PrelimNarrative:
On July 10, 2026, about 0745 eastern daylight time, a Sikorsky S-76D helicopter, N93RT, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Huntersville, West Virginia. The commercial pilot was fatally injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 positioning flight.
The pilot of the helicopter departed a private hangar near Glenville, West Virginia about 0710 to pick up the helicopter’s owner at his property. Preliminary ADS-B data showed the helicopter flying from near the departure point directly toward the destination landing zone until it was about 0.5 nautical miles (nm) northwest of the destination when the helicopter made a right turn. The helicopter was flying at an altitude of about 3,550 ft mean sea level (msl) when it made the turn to the right, away from the destination landing zone, which was located at an elevation of about 2,250 ft. 
A witness recorded a video of the helicopter when it was about 1.3 nm west southwest of the destination, and it showed the helicopter flying about 100 to 150 ft above ground level (agl). The video also depicted could ceilings that were about 200 to 250 ft agl.  The video showed the helicopter continuing down a valley toward the town of Huntersville, West Virginia with the landing gear extended, before making a right turn toward the destination. The witness, who watched the helicopter fly over his house, reported that the rotor wash from the helicopter was making the trees on his property sway as it passed overhead. 
Witnesses who were located closer to the destination stated that it was foggy around the time of the accident and estimated the cloud ceiling was between 100 and 200 ft agl.  They also stated that when they saw the helicopter it was partially obscured by the fog, with only the “belly” visible at various points. The described that as the helicopter passed over a ridge to the southwest of the destination, it continued east, perpendicular to the approach path they had seen the helicopter fly in the past. They also described that the helicopter pitched up just prior to impacting the mountainside. 
The accident site was about 0.15 nm southeast of the destination landing zone on the side of a mountain, at an elevation about 2,500 ft. The debris path was about 330 ft in length and oriented on a magnetic heading of about 110°. The debris area was on a slope that varied between 30° and 50° with the lowest debris located consisting of main rotor blade spars. The initial tree impact was about 200 ft in elevation below where the main wreckage came to rest, and those tree strikes were located about 40 ft the tree.
A majority of the helicopter was consumed by postimpact fire. Part of the tail rotor gearbox was impact-separated and was found near the tail section of the helicopter, both about 60 ft below the main wreckage. Both of the tail rotor control cables were found in the main wreckage and exhibited fire damage. A portion of one tail rotor control cable remained attached to the tail rotor control in the tail. The fuselage was unrecognizable and destroyed by postaccident fire. The main rotor head was found about 10 ft below the engines in the main wreckage. The main gearbox magnesium housing was entirely consumed by postaccident fire. The primary and multifunction flight displays were found in the burned portion of the wreckage and exhibited fire damage.
Both engines remained encased by the nacelle, came to rest inverted, and were damaged by postaccident fire. Both engine external and internal surfaces exhibited varying degrees of ash and soot accumulation. The left engine inlet case had been consumed by fire. A borescope examination of the 1st-stage high-pressure compressor (HPC) rotor showed all airfoils intact and full length, with no apparent deformation. Viewing through the exhaust duct confirmed that the T6 temperature-indicating probes remained intact. The 2nd-stage power turbine (PT) blades were also observed to be full length with no obvious damage. 
The right engine upper section of the reduction gearbox was perforated, exposing the internal gear system. A borescope examination of the 1st-stage HPC rotor showed all airfoils intact and full length, with no apparent deformation. Viewing through the exhaust duct confirmed that the T6 temperature-indicating probes remained intact. The 2nd-stage PT blades were also observed to be full length with no obvious damage.
The helicopter’s cockpit voice recorder/flight data recorder combination unit, along with two other devices with the capability of recording data in nonvolatile memory, were recovered and sent to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for data extraction and download.
The helicopter was retained for further examination.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s improper landing flare, which resulted in a hard landing.
AnalysisNarrative: The pilot reported that the purpose of the flight was to perform a traffic pattern circuit and a full stop landing. During the landing, he misjudged his altitude above the runway and the airplane landed hard as he initiated the landing flare. The nose landing gear struck the turf runway, collapsed, and the airplane nosed over and came to rest inverted. The fuselage and left wing were substantially damaged during the accident sequence. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

PrelimNarrative:
On July 12, 2026, about 1909 eastern daylight time, a Cessna 182J, N43TB, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Piseco, New York. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
According to a witness who lived near the Piseco Airport (K09), Piseco, New York, he was driving his truck down the road that paralleled the runway. He heard a very loud noise and turned to observe an airplane climbing from the runway before it banked to the left and impacted a tree line. 
Airport security video showed the airplane approaching runway 22, bounce, and start to porpoise. It bounced three times before it climbed and banked to the left. The airplane then disappeared from the video frame. Another security camera on airport property showed the airplane in a steep left bank angle before it impacted trees. 
The accident site was compact, and all major components of the airplane were identified. The wreckage was located in dense woods abeam the midfield point of the runway and had been consumed by fire. It came to rest inverted, oriented on a 210° magnetic heading, and was about 200 yards to the left of the centerline. 
The pilot held a private pilot certificate with ratings for airplane single-engine land, airplane single-engine sea. He reported a total flight experience of 1,020 hours on an application for an FAA third-class medical certificate, dated April 12, 2016. He had been approved for BasicMed since 2018. 
The airplane was manufactured in 1966 and powered by a Continental IO-470, 230-hp engine, driving a two-blade McCauley constant-speed propeller. The airplane was operated in Alaska for several years and was modified with the WREN 460 STOL conversion. According to the manufacturer of the modification, the airplane’s main spar was upgraded to a heavier spar that supported the newer flap system. It also included a new aileron system, a new stabilator system, and added a canard to the forward cowling just behind the propeller. The modification also added five feathering drag plates on the top of each wing to assist in turning the airplane at slow speeds. According to FAA aircraft registration records, the pilot purchased the airplane on February 20, 2026.

On July 12, 2026, about 1705 mountain daylight time, a Kaman Aerospace Corporation K-1200 (K-MAX) helicopter, N40HX, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident at Silver Jack Reservoir, Colorado. The pilot was fatally injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 133 external load firefighting flight.

The helicopter was operated under a call-when-needed contract with the United States Forest Service (USFS) and was conducting water bucket/fire suppression flight for the Gold Mountain Fire in the Uncompahgre Wilderness of the north-central region of the San Juan Mountains in Colorado. The firefighting helicopter was equipped with a 660-gallon Bambi MAX Bucket with PowerFill Max (water bucket) suspended from the helicopter by a 150 ft long line.

The helicopter was equipped with an Appareo AIRS-400 airborne image recording system that recorded video, ambient audio, and flight parameter data during the flight. The recovered device was examined at the NTSB Vehicle Recorder Laboratory, Washington, DC.

According to recovered flight parameter data, at 1607:41, the helicopter lifted into a hover at a remote helibase near Ouray, Colorado. At 1608:17, the helicopter’s ground speed and altitude began to increase, consistent with the helicopter departing the helibase.

The helicopter initially flew north-northwest along Hwy 550 toward Ridgway, Colorado, before it turned northeast and flew to the north end of Silver Jack Reservoir. The helicopter made a descending right 270° turn on the east side of reservoir. The helicopter then flew to the north-northeast over the reservoir where it refilled its water bucket. The helicopter then conducted firefighting operations about 2.7 nautical miles (nm) south-southeast of the reservoir. Based on the available data, the helicopter completed 5 water bucket drops over the forest fire.

Review of the recovered video content confirmed that visual meteorological conditions prevailed throughout the flight and the water bucket dip locations at the reservoir included a visible horizon, shoreline, and surrounding terrain features for vertical reference during external load operations.

Review of the previous five water bucket dips revealed that the pilot generally made large repetitive cyclic inputs while he maintained hover and were comparable to the large cyclic inputs that were observed during the final bucket dip that immediately preceded the accident. The enroute portions following the previous five water bucket dips, each with an external load of about 3,000 lbs, were unremarkable.

Review of the previous five water bucket drops revealed the pilot generally made large repetitive cyclic inputs while he maintained hover before the water drop. Immediately after each water release and after the helicopter transitioned to forward flight, the pilot’s flight control inputs were unremarkable while the helicopter was enroute to the reservoir dip sites.

During the final water bucket dip, the helicopter pitched up rapidly, accelerated in right yaw, and rolled right into an extreme unusual attitude. The turn/slip indicator showed full right deflections. The external load indicator rapidly increased from about 4,000 to about 7,700 lbs. A large aft cyclic movement was observed as the unusual attitude progressed and the cyclic continued moving aft until it was obscured in the field of view (FOV). The helicopter pitch then decreased rapidly, and the trees, shoreline, and water came back into the FOV. Based on external visual references and the attitude indicator, at the end of the video the helicopter was in an extreme right roll with the nose falling through the horizon toward the water.

The portions of the video that were reviewed, which included the final sequence of events, did not reveal any abnormal sounds or vibrations indicative of a rotorcraft system or engine malfunction during the flight.

There were two witnesses positioned on the dam at the north end of the reservoir. They reported seeing the helicopter enter the reservoir from the south to refill the water bucket. One of witnesses reported that after the helicopter refilled its water bucket it turned right (east) and descended into the reservoir upside down.

On July 22, 2026, the helicopter, water bucket, and 150 ft long line were recovered from the reservoir using a Boeing CH-47 Chinook helicopter. The wreckage was then loaded on a trailer and transported to a secure storage facility where it was examined.

Examination of the helicopter revealed impact-related damage primarily to the right-side of the fuselage. There were only fragments remaining of the windshield and door windows. The cockpit floor was displaced upward due to the impact-related damage to the right fuselage. The left side of the fuselage exhibited minor damage when compared to the right side of the fuselage.

The cyclic control system exhibited mechanical continuity from the cyclic stick to the L-cranks at rotor hubs, and then from the L-cranks to the spanwise blade control rod. Movements in forward, aft, left and right had friction from impact-related fuselage damage throughout the flight control system.

The collective control system exhibited continuity from collective stick to the rotor hub L-cranks, and then from the L-cranks to each spanwise blade control rod. Collective movements in up and down had friction from the collective stick friction block being dislodged and rubbing against the airframe.

The directional pedals had full range of movement in the cockpit with mechanical continuity from the pedals to the rotor hub L-cranks, and then to each spanwise blade control rod. The rudder control cable between the directional pedals and the rudder exhibited continuity from the pedals to aft section of the fuselage where the cable was cut to facilitate disassembly for transportation. The left side of the fuselage below the cockpit exhibited impact-related damage causing some binding of the rudder control rod below the cabin floor. The portion of the rudder control cable remaining in the aft tail section exhibited free movement and smooth control of the rudder surface.

Examination of the control module appeared to have full range of movement allowing the cyclic, collective and directional pedals all to have full continuity to their respective systems. Impact-related damage to the control module mounts displaced the module up from its normal position.

Based on photos of the helicopter at the accident site, the right stabilizer was observed partially separated from the aft fuselage. Examination revealed impact-related damage to the right side of the aft fuselage that pushed the left- and right- stabilizer bearings out of their supports. Additionally, the stabilizer system exhibited binding due to impact-related damage at the stabilizers. To relieve the binding, the control rod was disconnected from the stabilizer tube, which allowed full range of movement throughout the entire stabilizer system.

Examination of the N1 twist-grip engine control confirmed full continuity and freedom of movement to the engine connections. The N2 RPM engine control exhibited mechanical continuity and freedom of movement to the engine connections. Collective movements up and down were confirmed but had friction from the collective stick friction block that was dislodged and rubbing against the airframe.

Examination of the transmission, mounts, surrounding structure, and rotors shafts revealed no evidence of damage. The rotor hubs rotated freely by hand and/or through the input drive shaft. The transmission rotated freely, without any noticeable anomalies, in both directions. The freewheeling unit remained attached to the transmission input and operated as designed. Counterclockwise rotation of the clutch verified freedom of movement and no sprag engagement.

PrelimNarrative:
On July 13, 2026, about 1114 eastern daylight time, a Beechcraft 95-B55, twin-engine airplane, N55FD, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Metter, Georgia. The commercial pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
Surveillance video provided by the John Edwin Jones Sr Field/Metter Municipal Airport (MHP), Metter, Georgia, showed that the accident airplane taxied to the self-serve fuel tank after which both engines were shut down. The pilot then refueled the airplane from the 100LL self-service system. Refueling records obtained from the MHP airport management showed the pilot purchased 114.42 gallons of 100LL aviation gasoline. A surveillance video was obtained from an automotive gas station that abutted the airport property to the east. The video showed the pilot taxing before he departed from runway 28 at 1112.
Preliminary ADS-B data from a commercial data provider captured 4 data points after the airplane departed from MHP. The first was at 1112:54 and showed a ground speed of 89 knots at an altitude of 300 feet mean sea level (msl). The second data point was 1113:10 and showed a ground speed of 83 knots at an altitude of 400 feet msl. The third data point was 1113:26 and showed a ground speed of 82 knots at an altitude of 400 feet msl. The fourth and final data point was 1113:42 and showed a ground speed of 85 knots at an altitude of 400 feet msl. The accident site was located about 1,600 feet and 107° from the last ADS-B data point. The data showed that the airplane was airborne for about 1 minute and 50 seconds.
A pilot-rated witness observed the airplane’s departure from MHP. According to the witness, during the departure, he was concerned about a sound coming from the accident airplane during the takeoff roll. He described the sound as “choppy” and said he was concerned about the airplane’s longer than normal takeoff roll and the shallow climb. The witness did not observe the accident.
The accident site was approximately 1.3 miles southwest of MHP. The first identified impact point was in a tree approximately 30 ft above the ground. The second identified impact point was a larger tree that was broken at approximately 15 ft above the ground. The primary wreckage site was approximately 30 ft from the initial impact point, on a heading of 23° (true). The angle between the primary wreckage and the initial impact point on the tree was about 50°, consistent with a steep descent into terrain.
The airplane came to rest upright on a heading of 198° (true) and had been mostly consumed by a post-impact fire. All of the airplane's primary components were located at the primary wreckage site. Several pieces of wood with 45° cuts consistent with propeller strikes were found within the accident site.
Postaccident examination revealed that the airframe sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, both wings, and the empennage. The majority of the fuselage and the right wing had been consumed by a postimpact fire, while the left wing root was partially consumed by the fire. The nose cone had significant thermal damage, and there were no signs of aft crushing of the nose cone. The trailing edge of the left wing had impacted a tree at the accident site. The left wing tip displayed two indentations of the leading edge; however, there was no observed aft crushing damage to the rest of the leading edge. The right wing had been mostly consumed by the postimpact fire and the leading edge displayed crushing damage. The empennage remained partially attached to the fuselage and had some thermal damage; however, it remained mostly intact. The vertical stabilizer and rudder remained intact, and the vertical stabilizer displayed thermal discoloration and some melting of the plastic and rubber portions of the stabilizer. The right horizontal stabilizer and elevator exhibited upward bending deformation at their ends. The left horizontal stabilizer and elevator were relatively undamaged. 
Flight control continuity was established for the aileron, elevator, and rudder through breaks that were consistent with either the observed thermal damage or impact damage. All the control cables were continuous from their ends in the cockpit to their ends at their respective flight control bellcranks.
The left propeller remained attached to the crankshaft and displayed impact damage signatures. Both propeller blades were relatively straight, and there were no observed chordwise scratches or gouging. The right propeller remained attached to the crankshaft and displayed impact damage signatures. Both of the blades remained within the propeller hub. One propeller blade displayed significant S-bending deformation, twisting deformation, and polishing of the blade faces, as well as chordwise scratches. The other propeller blade displayed a small amount of twisting deformation near the blade tip as well as some polishing of the blade tip. 
The left engine remained partially attached to the airframe engine truss; however, the truss had separated from the rest of the airframe. The engine exhibited impact-damage signatures, with most of the damage occurring to the rear accessories and the forward-right side of the engine. A large piece of wood, consistent with one of the impacted trees, was wedged into the cowling right air inlet. The crankcase remained intact and was undamaged. The top, No. 6 cylinder through bolt was dislodged, and the bolt was extended about an inch from the cylinder flange. The crankshaft propeller flange remained attached to the rest of the crankshaft, and there were no visible cracks observed in the flange. All six cylinders remained attached to the crankcase and exhibited impact damage signatures, with the most damaged cylinder being the No. 5 cylinder. The top spark plugs were removed, and the cylinders were examined utilizing a lighted borescope. Examination of the No. 2 cylinder revealed that the piston had released from the piston pin and had broken up into multiple small pieces. Small portions of the piston and piston rings remained in the cylinder, and the piston pin remained attached to the connecting rod. Inspection of the No. 4 and No. 6 cylinders with a borescope showed small impact marks in the valve heads and pistons consistent with foreign object damage. The No. 1, No. 3 and the No. 5 cylinders displayed normal operating and combustion signatures. 
The oil pump was disassembled, and the gears contained a significant amount of metallic particles in the gears and the oil pump housing displayed scoring consistent with hard particle passage. The oil filter remained attached to the oil filter adapter; however, the adapter had impact separated from the oil pump assembly. The oil filter housing was cut open, and the filter pleats were visually inspected. The filter pleats contained a significant amount of metallic material within the pleats. 
The right engine remained partially attached to the airframe through the engine truss, cables, wires, and hoses. The engine displayed impact damage signatures concentrated to the bottom of the engine and displayed significant thermal damage to the rear of the engine. The crankcase remained intact, and there were no signs of a catastrophic internal engine failure. The crankshaft was rotated manually, and continuity was established between the crankshaft, camshaft, connecting rods and associated components. All six cylinders remained attached to their cylinder bays and displayed varying degrees of thermal-damage signatures. The top spark plugs and rocker box covers were removed from the cylinders. The cylinders were examined using a lighted borescope. The cylinder walls, piston faces, and valve heads displayed normal operating and combustion signatures. On July 9, 2026, about 1729 central daylight time, a Piper PA-30 airplane, N8154Y, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Tulsa, Oklahoma. The flight instructor and pilot under instruction were seriously injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. 
The flight instructor reported that while conducting training maneuverers in the practice area she heard a noise similar to “sputtering” from the right engine and noticed the RPM drop to about 1500 rpms. Shortly after the rpm drop, the noise stopped and the rpm returned to normal. However, due to unexpected right engine issue, she chose to return to the airport. While returning to the airport, the flight instructor reported that all the engine gauges were observed to be within their respective normal ranges. 
During the approach, the flight instructor took the flight controls from the pilot under instruction as she observed that the airplane was too high and drifting from the runway centerline. However, the flight instructor was unable to correct for the unstable approach and chose to perform a go-around. The flight instructor reported that the airplane suddenly rolled inverted to the right after she applied full engine power to perform the go-around. 
Video surveillance imagery showed the airplane start an initial climb during the go-around followed by a sudden inverted roll to the right and then impacting terrain in a vertical nose low orientation. The airplane sustained substantial damage to both wings and the fuselage. 
The airplane owner reported that both propeller governors had been recently removed, overhauled, and reinstalled. The airplane was retained for further examination.

On July 13, 2026, about 2236 eastern daylight time, a Smith Aerostar 601P, N800AA was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Lake Clear, New York. The private pilot and two passengers were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.

According to preliminary information from the FAA, the airplane was based at Monmouth Executive Airport (BLM), Belmar, New Jersey. Earlier on the night of the accident, the pilot flew uneventfully from BLM to Adirondack Regional Airport (SLK), Saranac Lake, New York. He intended to pick up two family members and return to BLM the same evening. FAA ADS-B data were available for the inbound flight; however, the airplane did not gain enough altitude on the outbound flight for FAA ADS-B data to be recorded.

SLK was located at 1,662 ft above mean sea level (msl) and runway 23 was 6,573 ft-long. Review of third-party commercial surveillance data revealed that the accident flight departed runway 23, at 2235:45. The last target was recorded 46 seconds later, at 2236:31, indicating a location about 1 mile from the departure end of the runway. The data also indicated that the airplane reached a maximum height of about 125 ft above ground level (agl), before descending and leveling off at 75 ft agl for the last five recorded targets, spanning 12 seconds. During that time, the groundspeed increased from 151 knots to 169 knots. 

Review of home security video near the accident site revealed an engine sound at 2236, followed by the sound of collision with trees. The wreckage was located about 4 hours later by first responders, and a postimpact fire had consumed a majority of the airplane. 

A debris path was observed in a nearby forest, beginning with a section of right wingtip, located about 1-mile beyond the departure end of runway 23. The debris path extended on a 230° magnetic course for about 1/2 mile, to the main wreckage. Severed trees, a section of right flap, and a small section of lower empennage were also located along the debris path. The wreckage came to rest flat and upright, oriented on a magnetic heading of 180°, at an elevation about 1,668 ft msl. 

All major components of the airplane were identified. Both engines were located near the main wreckage and both propellers remained attached to their respective engine. The empennage was located next to the left engine, and sections of both wings were identified near the main wreckage. The cockpit and cabin were consumed by fire. 

The pilot held a private pilot certificate with ratings for airplane single engine land, airplane single-engine sea, airplane multiengine land, instrument airplane, and rotorcraft helicopter. He reported a total flight experience of 1,025 hours on an application for an FAA third-class medical certificate, dated December 17, 2025. The pilot obtained an instrument rating on October 3, 2024. At that time, he reported a total flight experience of 890 hours; of which, 102 hours were at night. 

The airplane was manufactured in 1976 and powered by two Lycoming IO-540, 290-hp engines, each driving a three-blade Hartzell constant speed propeller. The airplane’s most recent annual inspection was completed on February 2, 2026. At that time, the airframe had accumulated 4,094 total hours of operation. The left engine had accumulated 79 hours since major overhaul (SMOH) and the right engine had accumulated 780 hours SMOH. 

Review of FAA Terminal Procedures, takeoff minimums for runway 23 at SLK, revealed instructions to climb 316 ft for every 1 nautical mile traveled, to ensure obstacle clearance, or perform a visual climb over the airport to 2,500 ft msl. 

The wreckage was retained for further examination. Additionally, a copy of the home security video was forwarded to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for sound spectrum study.

PrelimNarrative:
On July 9, 2026, about 1805 central daylight time, a Glasair 1RG airplane, N141CG, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Utica, Minnesota. The pilot received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot reported that the flight was for the purpose of checking the electric pitch trim system of the airplane. While testing the system in flight, at altitudes between 2,000 and 3,000 ft msl, the engine lost power. At this time the pilot had the electronic flight information (EFIS) screen of his avionics suite displaying mostly flight information. When the engine lost power, the pilot switched the EFIS to the engine management page and it showed that the airplane’s header tank was empty.
The pilot attempted to restore engine power but was unsuccessful. He executed a forced landing to a road. During the landing, while attempting to avoid obstacles along the roadway. The airplane went off the road and struck a culvert before coming to rest. During the forced landing the airplane sustained substantial damage to the forward fuselage.
Discussion regarding the airplane’s fuel system with the pilot and with the original builder of the airplane revealed that the airplane had a single main wing tank, and a fuselage mounted header tank. Each tank was connected to a selector valve which determined which tank the engine would draw fuel from. In addition, there was a transfer pump installed that allowed pumping fuel from the wing tank to the header tank. Any overflow of fuel from the header tank would return to the wing tank. The original builder stated that it was possible to leave the transfer pump on at all times with the selector valve set to the header tank. 
The pilot stated that during the accident flight the transfer pump switch was in the “on” position and he verified this when the engine lost power. Once the engine lost power the pilot switched the fuel selector to the main wing tank and attempted to restart the engine without success.  Further testing of the transfer pump is planned.

On July 10, 2026, about 1023 mountain daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Vans Aircraft Inc RV-12 airplane, N812MM, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Grand Junction, Colorado. The pilot and a passenger were uninjured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot stated that he picked up the airplane at Blake Field Airport (AJZ), Delta, Colorado, after a condition inspection was completed and planned to fly to Mineral County Memorial Airport, Creede, Colorado. After departure from AJZ, the Garmin G3X Touch display dimmed and shut down, which was immediately followed by a total loss of engine power. The pilot stated there was no electrical power to the starter switch, but the communication radio continued for function. The pilot then performed a forced landing to a field during which the airplane sustained substantial damage to the horizontal stabilizer.
The airplane was retained for further examination.

ProbableCause: The pilot's failure to maintain clearance from an antenna while maneuvering during a low-level aerial application flight.
AnalysisNarrative:
The pilot reported that while making a low-level aerial application pass over a corn field, he heard a loud bang and felt as if the airplane impacted something. He attempted to increase the engine power, but the engine did not respond to the throttle control inputs. The pilot performed an emergency hopper dump of the liquid chemical load and conducted a forced landing to a flat grass field, and a post-impact fire ensued.
The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, engine mount, elevator, and both wings. The propeller hub was found near a damaged antenna about .75 mi from where the airplane came to rest. The antenna was located inside of a metal fence, next to a small white building. The pilot reported that there were no pre-impact malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

PrelimNarrative:
On July 14, 2026, about 1105 eastern daylight time, an experimental Montana Coyote airplane, N448VQ, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Fredericksburg, Virginia. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 test flight.
Family members reported that the pilot was conducting a flight test after completing repairs to the airplane after a landing ground loop during a Phase 1 flight test on May 17, 2024. 
Video surveillance showed the airplane departing about 1049 from runway 24 at the Shannon Airport (EZF) in Fredericksburg, Virgina. ADS-B radar data then showed the airplane departing the traffic pattern to the south before returning to airport a few minutes after departure. At 1102, additional video surveillance showed the airplane on a final approach to runway 24. Starting at 1102:57, the start of a level right turn was captured with the airplane deviating to the right of the runway centerline to the right. At 1103:57, the bank angle suddenly increased followed by a drop of the nose with the airplane entering a descending right spiral. At 1103:05, the airplane disappeared behind a treeline in a nose low inverted right bank. A pilot-rated witness stated that everything seemed normal and that he could hear the engine operating normally with an increase in engine noise when the airplane was in the descending spiral. 
The airplane came to rest in an equipment storage lot about 0.13 nautical miles from the threshold of runway 24. The airframe was found on its right side with the right wing separated at the wing root. The left wing was partially separated at the forward spar. A small depression was located under the forward fuselage that contained fragments of the composite propeller and cowl.
Flight control continuity was established for the elevator, rudder, and right aileron from the control surfaces to their respective cockpit controls. However, the left aileron torque tube was found separated from the fuselage bellcrank with no bending or witness marks observed on the tube or bellcrank attachment housing. The right aileron torque tube remained secure in the bellcrank attachment housing. The torque tube was attached to the housing using four equally spaced rivets around the circumference of the tube.
The engine crankshaft was unable to be rotated by hand due to damage of the forward engine case. The magnetos were removed and rotated with a drill with spark observed on all leads. The fuel system was found compromised in numerous locations. Fuel was only observed in the fuel selector. 
The airplane’s Dynon SV-HDX1100 and both aileron torque tube and bellcrank assemblies were retained for further examination.

On July 10, 2026, about 1103 Pacific daylight time, a Canadair CF-5D, N845PS, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Mojave, California. The two pilots onboard were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.
The pilot reported that during the landing roll the left engine fire warning system initiated, which was followed by a right engine fire warning. He stated that he performed the emergency procedure and the airplane came to a stop on the runway, at which time both pilots egressed. 
A witness photographed the airplane in the airport’s traffic pattern prior to landing. A photograph showed the airplane trailing white vapor from the left side of the fuselage underneath the left wing and around the left engine exhaust. 
An airport surveillance video showed the airplane touchdown on the runway with white vapor trailing. The airplane continued to roll down the runway when the white vapor stopped and the airplane caught fire. The airplane came to a stop on the runway where the fire continued to burn near the empennage.  
The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and empennage. 
The airplane was relocated to a hangar for further examination.

On July 13, 2026, about 800 mountain daylight time, a Tag Aviation Pty Ltd Titanium Explorer gyrocopter, N665TE was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Larkspur, Colorado. The pilot passed away in the hospital five days after the accident. The gyrocopter was operated under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 as a personal flight. 
According to a friend of the pilot, the pilot flew the gyrocopter from Meadowlake Airport (FLY) Peyton, Colorado, to Central Colorado Airport (AEJ) Buena Vista, Colorado, 4 days before the accident. The pilot and his friend flew their respective gyrocopters around the Buena Vista area several times during that four-day period. The friend said that the gyrocopter was performing normally. 
On the morning of July 13th, the pilot filled the fuel tank with 91 Octane motor gas before he departed back toward FLY. The friend said that the pilot planned to circumnavigate Davis Airfield (AFF) Colorado Springs, Colorado, to the north and then fly back toward the east toward Peyton, Colorado. The pilot departed AEJ about 700. While enroute, he called another friend on his cellular phone to let him know that he was flying over Lake George in Park County, Colorado. He told the friend that everything was fine and he would call him again when he landed safely at FLY.
About 800, a witness walking her dog outside her home said that she heard the gyrocopter fly overhead. She said the gyrocopter was low and the engine was “struggling.” Then, the engine stopped and the gyrocopter fell through the trees. She reported that the pilot was conscious but not speaking and that fuel was dripping out of the fuel tank. 
The gyrocopter was relatively intact and came to rest on its right side under a group of trees. The rotor blades were bent and cracked. One of the rotor blade tips was sheared off. The three-bladed propeller was still attached at the hub, and the blades were flat and smooth. The needle on the Aviasport gyro rotor tachometer was fully in the red zone at 500 rpm.
According to the engine and airframe logbooks, N665TE would have been due for an annual condition inspection in September 2026. At the time of the accident, the airframe had accumulated about 50 hours, and the engine had accumulated about 400 hours.
The gyrocopter was retained for further examination.

On July 14, 2026, sometime between 1252 and 1356 CDT, a Luscombe 8A, N1164K, was substantially damaged when it crashed in a field near Canton, Texas. The pilot, who was the sole occupant, was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. 

The flight had originated from the pilot’s private airstrip where the airplane was hangared, which was oriented north to south. A farmer discovered the airplane wreckage about 800 ft northwest of the private airstrip, at about 1356. 

There were no eyewitnesses to the accident. The pilot sent a text message to a friend at about 1252, which was his last known communication. Additionally, a nearby resident reported hearing what sounded like an engine “winding up” for a few seconds, followed by less than a second of silence, then a “boom” sound.  He stated that he heard the sound within the general timeframe of the accident, but he was unable to identify the specific time.

The accident pilot purchased the airplane in December 2025. His wife told investigators that the pilot flew the airplane frequently and that they felt it did not produce sufficient take-off performance for them to fly together. She said he usually flew it in the morning or evening and had not flown the airplane much in high-temperature conditions. When she returned home from an appointment at around 1400, she observed the windsock located at the north end of the runway, which indicated the wind was from the north. She noted that the wind had been coming from the south earlier in the day. She said that the pilot typically took off to the south because the prevailing winds were generally from that direction, but on the day of the accident she believed he must have taken off to the north.


Figure 1: Overhead map view of accident location

The airplane impacted a field in a steep, nose-down attitude about 800 feet northwest of the northern end of the private airstrip. The longitudinal axis of the fuselage was oriented on a heading of about 349° magnetic and exhibited fore-aft crushing. All major structures and components of the airplane were located within the immediate wreckage area. Pieces of windscreen plexiglass were scattered forward and left of the primary wreckage, within about a 30-ft diameter. Disturbance of the surface soil was limited to the area located immediately under the wreckage.


Figure 2: Photo of airplane wreckage at accident scene

The right wing was displaced aft and the left wing was displaced forward. Compression wrinkling was observed along the top skin of the left wing along with forward bending at the wing root leading edge. The right wing was damaged at the outboard leading edge and the aft spar had separated at the fuselage. Both the left and right ailerons remained attached to their respective wings. The empennage remained intact and attached to the aft fuselage. Both elevators and the rudder also remained attached. The elevator trim tab was connected to the left elevator and articulated freely by hand. The upper fuselage had collapsed into the cabin.

The propeller remained attached to the engine crank flange. One blade was intact and exhibited no chordwise scratches or damage. The second blade was fractured and splintered near the blade root with aft bending.

On July 12, 2026, at 1018 mountain standard time, a Remos GX airplane, N126GX, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Glendale, Arizona. The flight instructor and student pilot were uninjured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.
According to the flight instructor, the student pilot was practicing landings at Glendale Regional Airport (GEU), Glendale, Arizona. The student performed a go around and, during the initial climb, he stated that the airplane’s pitch control was “delayed.” After taking the flight controls the instructor observed that the airplane did not respond to pitch control inputs. 
The flight instructor was able to maneuver the airplane using the ailerons, rudder, full nose up pitch trim, and engine power. During the final approach to runway 01, the airplane lost altitude and impacted terrain, resulting in substantial damage to the airplane’s fuselage.  
Examination of the airplane revealed that the rear elevator control rod had fractured about three inches forward of the elevator quick disconnect. (See figure 1.)

Figure 1: The separation in the rear elevator control rod, circled in yellow. 

According to maintenance records, the rear elevator control rod had been installed in December 2025 and had accrued 445 hours in service.

The airplane wreckage was retained for further examination.

InvestigationClass: Class 4 - Basic report with no Prelim publish

ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to compensate for the gusty and variable wind conditions, which resulted in a loss of control and collision with trees during takeoff.
AnalysisNarrative:
The airline transport pilot was attempting to take off from a grass runway in variable wind and light rain. During the takeoff, when the airplane was about 30 ft above the ground, the airplane rolled right toward trees on the side of the runway. The pilot was able to roll the airplane’s wings level; however, he was unable to avoid colliding with trees, resulting in substantial damage to the wings and fuselage. The pilot reported there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures of the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. 
A witness recorded video of the takeoff that captured both the airplane and a windsock. Review of the video revealed that the wind had shifted to a right crosswind during the airplane’s initial climb, immediately before the airplane rolled nearly 45 degrees, consistent with the pilot’s description of the airplane rolling to the right. The wind then shifted suddenly to a left quartering headwind as the airplane began to level; however, the airplane continued toward the trees off the right side of the runway.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to maintain clearance from a power line during a low-level aerial application flight.
AnalysisNarrative:
The pilot stated that he flew around the cornfield to identify hazards, noted the power lines, and then began aerial application operations. While spraying around a large tree the pilot saw the glint of the power line and attempted to avoid it but was unsuccessful. The pilot was unable to maintain sufficient main rotor RPM and entered an autorotation to the cornfield.  After landing in the field, the main rotor blades struck the corn stalks and the helicopter came to a rest on its side, resulting in substantial damage to the main rotor system, engine mount, fuselage, and tailboom. 
The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures of the helicopter that would have precluded normal operation.

PrelimNarrative:
On July 16, 2026, at 0701 Pacific daylight time, an experimental amateur built Vans RV-4, N98GB, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Yuba City, California. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
A review of recorded video from the Sutter County Airport, Yuba City, California, and a neighboring business, captured the airplane at various portions of the accident flight. One video showed the airplane departing runway 17 and then initiating a turn back to the airport. The airplane overshot runway 35 and traveled out of the frame of the camera. As the airplane traveled into view of a neighboring business’s video, it appeared the airplane was on the ground traveling in a northerly direction before it rotated along its vertical axis to the left about 270° and came to rest upright in an open field.
The airplane’s first identified point of contact (FIPC) was the airport’s northern perimeter chain link fence. The debris field was about 230 ft in length, oriented on a 348° heading and consisted of portions of wooden propeller blades and the rudder. The airplane came to rest upright on a 056° heading and remained mostly intact. Flight control continuity was established from the cockpit to all the flight control surfaces. 
The airplane was recovered to a secure location for further examination.

PrelimNarrative:
On July 16, 2026, about 0740 eastern daylight time, a Dakota Cub Super 18 airplane, N84AJ, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Plymouth, Massachusetts. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane operated under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 as a personal flight. 
ADS-B data obtained from the FAA and data extracted from the airplane’s Garmin G3X showed that the airplane departed from Plymouth Municipal Airport (PYM), Plymouth, Massachusetts, about 0632, and flew south towards Katama Airpark(1B2), Edgartown, Massachusetts, and then flew back towards PYM, generally staying below 1,000 ft above ground level. The airplane flew a path similar to a straight-in for runway 33 until it was about 1.4 miles from the departure end of the runway (see figure 1).

Figure 1. Overview of total flight
According to preliminary information provided by the Massachusetts State Police, eyewitnesses by Curlew Pond reported that as the airplane flew over the pond, the engine started to sputter. The airplane initially continued toward the airport but turned back toward the water, and then the engine noise went quiet. The airplane glided to the water and then nosed over inverted (see figure 2). 

Figure 2. Last portion of flight
The airplane was brought to a nearby shore, and turned back to the upright position. After initial documentation of the airplane, it was transported to the airport for further examination.
Postaccident examination revealed the magneto switch was selected to the BOTH position and the fuel pump switch was in the ON position. The fuel selector was selected to the left tank. Neither wing fuel cap was recovered with the airplane. The left fuel tank contained less than 10 ounces of fuel and the right fuel tank contained less than 4 ounces of fuel; neither fuel tank was breached. Fuel lines from the fuel tanks to the fuel selector remained secured and when opened contained fuel. Using a water detection paste, the fuel from the left fuel tank line contained some water and the fuel in the right fuel tank line did not contain any water. A fuel sample from the gascolator bowl contained a mixture of fuel and water. It is unknown how much fuel may have drained out of either tank while the airplane was inverted in the water. The fuel line from the engine driven fuel pump to the fuel servo was empty of fuel. The fuel servo’s fuel screen was free of visual contaminants. 
The pilot held a private pilot certificate with ratings for both airplane single engine land and airplane single engine sea.

PrelimNarrative:
On July 17, 2026, at 1748 central daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Vans Aircraft Inc RV-8A, N22SZ, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident in Mineral Point, Wisconsin. The commercial pilot was uninjured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot stated that while en route to Oshkosh, Wisconsin, he stopped at Iowa County Airport, Mineral Point (MRJ), Wisconsin, for fuel and to wait for visual flight conditions to improve at the destination airport. He then departed MRJ, and after climbing to 9,000 ft mean sea level, he switched fuel tanks and a “moment or so” later, the engine lost power. He then initiated a return to MRJ, during which he attempted several engine restarts. The engine restarted during the descent to MRJ, then lost power, restarted again, and continued to operate for the remainder flight to and taxi at MRJ. After the flight, the pilot stated that he talked to six or eight pilots at MRJ, two of which were mechanics, and a mechanic based at MRJ, about the loss of engine power that he had experienced. The group discussed mechanical and electrical fuel pump failures, carburetor icing, vapor lock, and test flying the airplane. 
On the following day, the pilot attempted a test flight of the airplane from MRJ. The pilot stated that the engine start for the test flight was “very clean normal start,” there were no hot start or fuel vapor problems, and the engine run-up was normal. He said that shortly after takeoff and early in the climb, the airplane engine began to run rough, and he decided to end the test flight and return to the airport. While turning left and climbing into the airport traffic pattern, the engine lost power. The pilot then decided to turn and land the airplane in the opposite direction since there was no engine power to fly an airport traffic pattern. During the turn, the engine started again but later lost power, and the airplane was high and fast. The pilot performed a forced landing on runway 11 where it impacted the runway surface. The airplane sustained substantial to both wings, the engine firewall, and an engine mount.
The airplane was retained for further examination.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s improper pitch control during landing, which resulted in a bounced landing, nose landing gear collapse, and nose over.
AnalysisNarrative: The pilot reported that during landing, the airplane began to porpoise. The nose landing gear subsequently collapsed, and the airplane veered off side of the runway and nosed over. The airplane came to rest inverted, resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage, vertical stabilizer, and rudder. The pilot reported that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s inadequate preflight and in-flight monitoring of the fuel quantity, which resulted in a total loss of engine power due to fuel exhaustion.
AnalysisNarrative: According to the pilot, he completed a preflight inspection but did not visually check the fuel quantity. Instead, he assumed the fuel was “at the tabs.” While completing the cockpit checklist he noted that the fuel gauges indicated about three-quarters full, but he did not check them again during the flight. After takeoff, the pilot climbed to 9,500 ft mean sea level to avoid reported turbulence below 5,000 ft. During the flight, he switched between the fuel tanks when prompted by his yoke-mounted GPS. He reported that personal matters and cellphone use distracted him. When the fuel in the right tank was depleted, he turned toward the nearest airport. The fuel in the left tank was then depleted, the engine lost power, and the pilot began an emergency descent. During the descent, the pilot identified a logging road for a forced landing. He was initially too high and made a left circling turn to line up with the road. The airplane struck trees and came to rest next to the road. The right wing and fuselage sustained substantial damage.
InvestigationClass: Class 4 - Basic report with no Prelim publish

PrelimNarrative:
On July 19, 2026 about 1440 Alaska daylight time, a DeHavilland DHC-2 airplane, N791PW was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Nondalton, Alaska. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 business flight. 
The pilot reported that he conducted a normal landing on a remote airstrip, and after touching down he applied the brakes, but the right brake did not respond. The airplane veered to the left, the pilot attempted to correct the left drift by adding additional right brake; the brake did not respond. The airplane ground looped and departed the runway which resulted in substantial damage to the right wing and right elevator. 
A postaccident examination of the brake system is pending.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s inadequate lookout, which resulted in a collision with ground equipment during taxi.
AnalysisNarrative:
The pilot reported that he performed four practice landings at the departure airport, to confirm landing performance, then continued to a private gravel airstrip. He overflew the airstrip and observed calm wind conditions, then performed another flyover to verify the runway was clear of obstructions. While on final approach, a gust of wind resulted in a temporary increase in airspeed then a touchdown farther than planned. After landing, during a “fast-taxi maneuver” he struck ground equipment that was obscured because of the tailwheel airplane’s nose-high pitch attitude. The landing gear collapsed, then the airplane then struck another piece of equipment, which resulted in substantial damage to the left wing. 
The pilot stated that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures of the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

PrelimNarrative:
On July 18, 2026, about 1440 central daylight time, a Robinson Helicopter Company R44, N484AT, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Adair, Iowa. The pilot was not injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 aerial application flight. 
The pilot stated that he was recently hired by the owner to complete agricultural spraying operations. He spoke with the pilot who flew the helicopter on the previous day and reported that the engine governor was slow to respond and that he should watch it during subsequent flights. The accident pilot decided to load the helicopter with water and complete a test flight to ensure normal operations and no governor malfunctions. The test flight was completed with no anomalies noted, and the governor was working normally. The pilot completed about 5 hours of flight time and sprayed about 600 acres without incident. Shortly before the accident, the pilot landed the helicopter on the refueler truck and added 1 quart of oil to the engine, then continued to spray another field. The pilot had completed 2 to 3 spray passes and climbed out of the field to turn around for another pass. During the turn, the low rotor rpm horn sounded so the pilot lowered the collective and increased the throttle, which increased the rotor rpm and the horn turned off. The pilot continued another spray pass and the low rotor rpm horn sounded again. He attempted to increase the throttle beyond the governor limitation, but the horn continued. The helicopter was flying about 60 mph and was about 15 to 20 ft above the field, so he executed an autorotation and landed in the mature corn. The helicopter slid in the field and rolled left, then came to rest upright. 
The responding FAA inspector reported that the helicopter sustained substantial damage to the main rotor blades, fuselage, and tailcone. Postaccident examination revealed that the governor control unit was not secured to its mounting location but was still connected to the airframe main wiring harness. 
The owner and company mechanic stated that the helicopter was recently purchased for the agricultural business and discovered that the previous owner had removed the governor control unit. They acquired another governor control unit and helicopter underwent an overhaul. When the helicopter was put back into service, the governor control unit was not secured to its mounting location. 
The helicopter was retained for further examination.

On July 18, 2026, about 1530 Pacific daylight time, a Piper PA-28-161, N8249B, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near San Bernardino, California. The pilot and pilot rated passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.

The pilot reported that while taxiing to the run-up area in preparation for takeoff at San Bernardino International Airport (SBD), San Bernadino, California, the airplane’s right main landing gear collapsed, and the right wing impacted the taxiway surface. 

Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that the right wing was substantially damaged. The airplane was recovered for further examination.

ProbableCause: The failure of the pilot to verify the loading hose had been disconnected before taking off and the failure of the loader to disconnect the fuel hose from the helicopter.
AnalysisNarrative:
The report provided by the company representative stated that the loader signaled to the helicopter pilot a thumbs up and walked down the stairs of the mobile loading platform. As the pilot was taking off, everything initially seemed normal until the pilot felt a tug on the helicopter. The helicopter pulled down and to the right and descended until it impacted the terrain in a right-side nose down attitude which resulted in substantial damage to the fuselage, tail boom, and main rotor.
After the accident it was noted that the dry break coupler had broken off the refueling hose from the mobile loading platform and remained attached to the helicopter. The company representative reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the helicopter that would have precluded normal operation.
When interviewed, the owner stated that the pilot was supposed to receive a thumbs-up or thumbs-down to indicate if the helicopter was ready to leave the platform. He also said the pilot was also supposed to visually verify that the fuel and chemical hoses were disconnected.
The pilot stated he took off the moment he saw the loader walk down the stairs and made no mention of looking for a thumbs up from the loader. The loader did not remember if he signaled the pilot with a thumbs up indicating that it was safe to take off.
InvestigationClass: Class 4 - Basic report with no Prelim publish

PrelimNarrative:
On July 16, 2026, about 1508 central daylight time, a Piper PA-24-260 airplane, N8606P, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Baraboo, Wisconsin. The pilot sustained serious injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot reported that for the cross-country flight, the airplane had about 6.5 hours of fuel onboard, and the planned flight only required about 2.5 hours of fuel.
A preliminary review of ADS-B data showed the airplane depart, about 1232, from the Mitchell Municipal Airport (MHE), Mitchell, South Dakota. The airplane traveled to the east toward the destination airport, the Baraboo/Wisconsin Dells Regional Airport (DLL), Baraboo, Wisconsin. About 22 miles to the west of DLL, the pilot maneuvered the airplane to the south of DLL. About 17 miles to the south of DLL, the pilot maneuvered the airplane to the north toward DLL. According to air traffic control, the airplane was cleared for the RNAV (GPS) runway 1 instrument approach at DLL.
As the airplane flew toward the approach end of runway 1, the airplane turned slightly to the west and then flew to the north over the various hangars, located to the west of runway 1. The airplane then maneuvered to the east, flying over runway 1. The pilot reported that the engine was not responding to his commands, but he did not hear any sputtering or popping noises. The airplane flew to the north of runway 1, the airplane turned to the west, and impacted trees. The pilot reported the airplane impacted trees because it could not produce climb power. The airplane came to rest upright on a flat grass field, on private property, located about 0.30 miles to the northwest of the approach end of runway 19.
The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and to both wings. The airplane was recovered from the accident site, and it was transported to a secure location for future examination.
A review of meteorological data from the closest weather reporting station, located at DLL, showed that the visibility at the time of the accident was about 1 3/4 miles, with moderate haze in the area, originating from large wildfires in Minnesota and Canada.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to maintain control of the airplane during takeoff, resulting in an aerodynamic stall and impact with water.
AnalysisNarrative: The pilot of the amphibious airplane reported that he was attempting to take off from a glassy water surface. The pilot had trouble getting the airplane “unstuck” from the water surface, so he pulled back on the control stick “extra hard.” This action broke the floats free from the surface tension but created a nose-high pitch attitude that resulted in the airplane entering an aerodynamic stall. The left float then impacted the water and it broke loose from the airplane before striking the underside of the left wing, resulting in substantial damage to the left wing. The airplane came to rest upright but slowly began to sink. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

PrelimNarrative:
On July 21, 2026, about 0815 mountain daylight time, an Enstrom F-28F helicopter, N8624B, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Malad City, Idaho. The pilot and pilot-rated passenger were not injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. 
The pilot in command, who was positioned in the left seat reported that the intent for the flight was to fly around the local area. After conducting a preflight inspection with no anomalies noted, he started the engine, conducted engine runup checks, increased the engine and rotor RPM to 100 percent and ascended to a hover. While conducting the helicopters in ground effect hover checks, he noticed that the manifold pressure was high, but still in the green. The pilot air taxied from the hangar parking area to the north toward the taxiway intersection near the approach end of runway 35 and saw that the manifold pressure was abnormally high. He landed the helicopter on the asphalt ramp to assess the instruments and conduct another magneto check, but when he rolled the throttle to flight idle, the engine lost total power. 
The pilot stated that with the engine and rotor RPM still married, he immediately engaged the starter and the engine restarted, but he noticed smoke emanating from the right side of the engine compartment, and there were flames on the lower left side of the engine. He attempted to shut down the engine by pulling the fuel/air mixture control on the instrument panel to the idle cut off position, but the engine continued to operate. He then turned the ignition switch to the off position to no avail, and he engaged the manual fuel shut-off located between the pilot and passenger seat, but the engine continued to operate. Unable to shut down the engine, the pilot and the passenger egressed the helicopter and searched for a fire extinguisher. Unable to locate a fire extinguisher, they contacted first responders, remained a safe distance from the burning helicopter and waited for the fire department to extinguish the blaze.
The wreckage has been recovered to a secure facility for further examination.

On July 20, 2026, at 1030 eastern daylight time, a Cessna 152 airplane was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Pell City, Alabama. The flight instructor and student pilot were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.
According to the instructor they departed St. Clair County Airport (KPLR), Pell City, Alabama, with full fuel tanks for a training flight. About four minutes after departure about 1,500 to 2,000 ft above ground level (agl), the engine lost all power and the instructor performed a forced landing to a field. After landing the airplane continued through a fence and the left wing impacted a tree.
According to a Federal Aviation Administration inspector that traveled to the scene the left fuel tank was ruptured. The airplane was recovered and an engine test run was performed. The engine did not run smoothly, and the throttle had to be pumped to keep the engine running.
The engine was shut down and secured for further examination.

ProbableCause: The flight instructor’s failure to maintain directional control during landing.
AnalysisNarrative: During an instructional flight, the flight instructor was demonstrating a landing. Upon touchdown, the flight instructor noticed that the airplane was right of centerline. He applied left rudder to realign the airplane with the centerline but overcorrected. The airplane veered sharply left, then he tried to correct with right rudder and the airplane veered sharply to the right. The airplane exited the runway surface and went through a ditch. The nose landing gear separated before the airplane slid through the grass and struck the concrete base of a tetrahedron. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the forward fuselage and wings. The flight instructor reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

PrelimNarrative:
On July 20, 2026, at 0643 central daylight time, a Piper J3C-65 airplane, N92432, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Richmond, Texas. The commercial pilot sustained serious injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The airplane impacted the roof of a house near the airport traffic pattern for Covey Trails Airport, Richmond, Texas. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and wings. The pilot stated that he did not remember the circumstances leading to and nature of the accident.
Postaccident examination of the airplane confirmed flight control continuity from the cockpit flight controls to the respective flight control surfaces. The two-blade wood propeller and metal propeller spinner did not display torsional features consistent with engine power.
The airplane was retained for further examination.

On July 23, 2026, about 1720 Pacific daylight time, a De Havilland DHC-3 Otter airplane, N709KA, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Eastsound, Washington. The pilot and two passengers were seriously injured, and eight passengers sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 135 scheduled air taxi flight. 
According to the operator, the flight originated from Kenmore Sea Base (W55), Seattle, Washington at 1630 with scheduled stops at Roche Harbor (WA03), Roche Harbor, Washington and Friday Harbor (W33), Friday Harbor, Washington. Preliminary ADS-B data showed that the airplane departed W55 about 1633 and maintained about 500 to 1,000 ft mean sea level (msl). The airplane remained over the water and generally travelled north over Rosario Strait. Once northwest of Lummi Island, the airplane turned west and passed north of Sucia Island. 
The operator stated that the pilot radioed the company operations center and reported inclement weather, which precluded the flight from continuing to WA03. The pilot informed the operator that he would return to Sucia Island, land, and wait for the weather to improve. The operator reported that there were multiple bays around Sucia Island where the pilot was authorized to land. ADS-B data showed that about 1619, when the airplane was about 11 miles northeast of WA03, it turned right about 180° and flew about 5 miles towards Sucia Island. Video imagery, from a witness who was near Shallow Bay, Sucia Island, showed the airplane at a low altitude and a nose-high attitude descending towards the water. When the airplane was about 4 ft above the water, the left wing dropped and the left wingtip and left pontoon float impacted the water. The airplane then landed with both pontoon floats on the water and continued forward where it subsequently impacted rocks. A passenger on the airplane reported that multiple small boats immediately arrived to remove the passengers from the accident site. A postaccident fire destroyed the fuselage after all passengers and the pilot had exited.   
The airplane was recovered to a secure hanger for further examination.

On July 24, 2026, about 1422 central daylight time, a Zenith Zodiac 601HDS experimental airplane, N27601, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Sioux City, Iowa. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The multi-leg visual flight rules (VFR) cross country flight departed from the Wittman Regional Airport (KOSH), Oshkosh, Wisconsin, with a final destination in Colorado. 
At 1236 on the day of the accident, ADS-B data showed the airplane departed the Pocahontas Municipal Airport (KPOH), Pocahontas, Iowa, on a southwesterly flight track. Upon reaching the vicinity of Holstein, Iowa, the airplane then flew west parallelling U.S. Highway 20 in the direction of Sioux City, Iowa. About 3 miles short of the U.S. Highway 20/75 intersection, the airplane began to track to the northwest, eventually turned north, and began climbing. After flying north, the airplane entered a right turn and descended until the last recorded data point which was located about a half mile southeast of the accident site.
The airplane was found in about 6 to 8 feet of water in a man-made lake near the shoreline. The vegetation along the shoreline on the side of the accident site, as well as the bank opposite the accident site about 80 to100 feet away, was intact with no indication of having been struck by the accident airplane. The main wing spar remained intact along its length but from the main landing gear outward on both sides, the wing structure and wing skins showed aft crushing and had mostly separated from the spar. The fuselage was deformed 90° from the wing spar.  The instrument panel, firewall, and engine separated from the front of the airplane and were located underneath and near the area the main wreckage came to rest. Upper engine cowling and windscreen fragments were scattered across the shoreline and a yard beyond the water. 
Divers and a local towing company were able to remove the airplane from the water. The major components of the airplane were present. Flight control cable continuity was established for the ailerons, rudder, and elevators. A visual inspection of the engine did not reveal any signs of a catastrophic engine failure. The wreckage was moved to a secure location for further examination.
According to KPOH personnel, the pilot purchased 14.7 gallons of 100 low lead fuel before departing. At the accident site, fuel sheen was present on the water and oil was present in the water during the recovery of the engine.
The National Weather Service (NWS) Area Forecast Discussion issued by the Sioux Falls, South Dakota, Weather Forecast Office at 1209 on the day of the accident reported instrument flight rules (IFR) to marginal instrument flight rules (MVFR) conditions would slowly improve through midafternoon. 
On the day of the accident around 1500, another pilot was flying west about 75 miles south of the accident pilot. He reported that conditions were worse than forecast, and he had to divert to avoid instrument meteorological conditions. He landed at an alternate airport and ended up driving home.
A review of FAA records showed the pilot held a private pilot certificate with a rating for airplane single engine land, but no instrument rating. The pilot, who was the airplane owner, built the airplane and he held a repairman experimental aircraft builder certificate for the airplane.

On July 22, 2026, about 1129 Pacific daylight time, an experimental amateur built Czech Aircraft Works Mermaid Skeeter 2 airplane, N42SK, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Cougar, Washington. The pilot was seriously injured. The airplane was operated under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
A review of a video provided by a witness showed the airplane at a distance while flying at a low altitude, in a right banking turn.  The airplane subsequently began to descend while in a right bank and impacted the water of Yale Lake. The airplane remained partially above water surface for an unspecified time before it ultimately became submerged. 
Recovery of the wreckage is currently pending.

ProbableCause: The separation of the right main landing gear axle, which resulted in a loss of control during the landing roll.
AnalysisNarrative: The pilot reported that after touching down, smoothly on centerline, the airplane veered right. He attempted to apply corrective control inputs which were not successful. The airplane then began to slide, which resulted in the left main wheel and subsequently the right main wheel separating from the landing gear. The airplane continued to slide on the main landing gear struts, with the lower left wing dragging on the runway, until the airplane came to stop on the edge of the runway nearly, and oriented nearly perpendicular to it. This resulted in substantial damage to the lower left wing and aileron. Postaccident photographs showed a rubber witness mark on the right main landing gear strut and fractures of both the main landing gear wheel axles. Given this information, it is likely that during the touchdown sequence the right main landing gear wheel axle began to separate, which resulted in the right main wheel coming into contact with the right main landing gear strut. The contact with the right main landing gear strut likely resulted in the right uncorrectable motion the pilot reported and subsequent sideload and separation of both main landing gear.

AnalysisNarrative: The flight instructor was providing instruction to the pilot toward a tailwheel endorsement. During their second flight of the day, the flight instructor demonstrated a normal traffic pattern and 3-point landing, after which the pilot flew the subsequent traffic pattern and landing approach. The airplane subsequently ground looped and sustained substantial damage to the right wing. The flight instructor reported that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

On July 23, 2026, at 1440 eastern daylight time, an American AA-1, N6132L, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Kearneysville, West Virginia. The pilot and pilot-rated passenger were seriously injured. The airplane was being operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.

A review of ADS-B data showed that the airplane departed from Eastern West Virginia Regional Airport (MRB), Martinsburg, West Virginia at 1345 and proceed about 20nm south where it performed a series of maneuvers before flying back toward MRB. During a postaccident interview, the pilot stated that while he was descending the airplane from 3,000 ft to 1,500 ft to enter the airport traffic pattern, the engine suddenly lost all power. Unable to reach the airport, he elected to make an emergency landing in a field about 5 nm south of MRB. During the forced landing, the airplane’s right wing and engine separated from the fuselage. The fuselage, left wing, and empennage were substantially damaged.

The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.
