PrelimNarrative:
On July 14, 2026, about 1725 Pacific daylight time, a Piper PA-24 airplane, N5002P, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident at Rogue Valley International/Medford Airport (MFR), Medford. Oregon. The two pilots were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The flight instructor reported that he and the pilot had intended to familiarize themselves with the airplane after it had been purchased by a new owner. Prior to the accident flight, the new airplane owner reported to the flight instructor that the prebuy inspection had identified some landing gear anomalies. Most of the anomalies were addressed during subsequent maintenance with exception of a delayed landing gear annunciation, which they were unable to duplicate. During the accident flight, one of the pilots asked the air traffic controller to observe if the landing gear was down. On the third circuit in the traffic pattern, the pilots heard the landing gear extend; however, the gear indication for the down and locked position did not illuminate. The pilot asked the tower controller to observe the landing gear position again, and the controller confirmed it was down. Nevertheless, about 200 ft - 300 ft above ground level, the landing gear down and lock position light illuminated and the pilot continued the approach and landing.
Shortly after touchdown, during the landing roll, the landing gear collapsed and the airplane subsequently came to rest on the runway. Postaccident examination by a FAA inspector revealed that the engine mount sustained substantial damage. 
The airplane was recovered and retained for further examination.

On July 24, 2026, about 1550 central daylight time, a Beech V35 airplane, N3707Q, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Carroll, Iowa. The pilot was not injured. The flight was operated under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 as a personal flight. 
According to the pilot, he departed from the Arthur N Neu Airport (CIN), Carroll, Iowa, and flew towards Stanton County Municipal Airport (JHN), Johnson City, Kansas. The pilot reported that shortly after takeoff, the engine started to run rough. He turned back towards CIN and noticed that the oil pressure began to decrease. About 5 miles from CIN, the oil pressure dropped to zero. When the airplane was about 3 miles from the airport, the engine started to smoke, and total engine power was lost. He performed a forced landing to a bean field. During the forced landing, the right aileron sustained substantial damage. 
A postaccident visual inspection of the engine revealed a hole in the crankcase above the No. 4 cylinder and additional case damage above the No. 3 cylinder. The oil dipstick showed little or no oil remained in the sump.
The airplane was retained for further examination.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to maintain clearance from a fuel farm fence while taxiing.
AnalysisNarrative:
During a turn while taxiing near a fuel farm at a slow speed, the airplane's left wing contacted the fuel facility fence. Following the initial impact, the airplane pivoted toward the fence, resulting in additional contact with the fenced enclosure. The collision resulted in substantial damage to the left wing and fuselage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
Following the accident, the pilot identified several areas to reduce the risk of similar occurrences. These areas included conducting a more deliberate visual assessment of obstacle clearance before initiating turns in confined ramp or taxi areas, requesting wing-walking assistance or external guidance when maneuvering near obstacles, and allowing additional taxi distance before beginning turns to increase wingtip clearance margins.

PrelimNarrative:
On July 27, 2026, about 2130 Alaska daylight time, a deregistered Piper PA-22-150 airplane, N4535A, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Chitina, Alaska. The pilot and two passengers were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
According to witnesses, the pilot and two passengers departed McCarthy Airport, McCarthy, Alaska, to drop off the passengers and supplies at the upper Dan Creek airstrip, located about 12 miles southeast of McCarthy. The upper Dan Creek airstrip is an uncharted private strip that is generally considered one way in and out, surrounded by steeply rising terrain, and go-arounds are not recommended.
Multiple witnesses, located on the ground in the vicinity of the airstrip, reported hearing the airplane approaching the southeast runway for landing at a normal approach power setting. The witnesses stated that they then heard the airplane’s engine increase to a high-power setting, then there was a moment of silence, followed by the sound of an impact.

The airplane impacted a berm on a rock-covered riverbank in a left-wing-low flight attitude about 740 ft north of the airstrip. The wreckage was oriented on a northwest heading. All four corners of the airplane were accounted for at the accident site. The outboard portion of the left wing was bent downwards and aft. The fuselage, inboard left wing, and portions of the inboard right wing were consumed by a postimpact fire.
During the onsite investigation, no preimpact anomalies were visually observed with the flight control system. The fuel selector was positioned on the left tank, and 100LL aviation fuel was present in the left wing. The throttle was found in the idle position and was bent in the direction of the pilot. The propeller blades exhibited rotational signatures including leading edge tip damage and chordwise witness marks, indicative of operation at a low-power setting upon impact.
The engine has been recovered to a secure facility for further examination.

On July 28, 2026, about 1949 mountain standard time, a Piper PA-28-180, N9062J, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Chandler, Arizona. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
Preliminary ADS-B data obtained from a commercially available source showed that the airplane departed runway 22R at Chandler Municipal Airport (CHD), Chandler, Arizona, at 1948:10. The airplane continued southwest on the departure leg and climbed to a reported GPS altitude of about 1,800 ft. The final recorded ADS-B point, at 1949:31, showed a reported ground speed of 45 knots and a descent rate of about 130 ft per minute.
Witnesses at a park about 0.5 miles southeast of the accident site reported observing the airplane flying southwest when they heard the engine sound cease. They stated that the airplane then entered a sharp right turn and descended rapidly. A dashcam video provided to the NTSB depicted the airplane in a steep right bank and rapid descent before ground impact.
The airplane impacted a commercial plumbing-supply yard about 0.7 miles from the departure end of runway 22L at CHD. The first identified impact point was a ground scar about 30 ft southwest of the main wreckage. The main wreckage was oriented on an approximate magnetic heading of 097° at an elevation of about 1,226 ft mean sea level. The forward fuselage rested on the concrete lot, while the aft fuselage and empennage extended across a curb into an adjacent dirt-and-gravel area. The engine, fuselage, cabin, wings, and empennage exhibited extensive thermal damage.
The wreckage was recovered to a secure location for further examination.

On July 24, 2026, about 14:32 Coordinated Universal Time, a Delta Air Lines Boeing 757-200, N662DN, powered by two Pratt & Whitney PW2037 turbofan engines, experienced a No. 1 (left) engine fire during initial climb from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Atlanta, Georgia. The captain and first officer (FO) were uninjured. The flight was operating under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 as a non-scheduled, maintenance ferry flight from ATL to Querétaro Intercontinental Airport (QRO), Mexico.
According to the flight crew, the pre-flight, taxi, and takeoff were uneventful. The captain was the pilot flying and the FO was the pilot monitoring. While climbing through 12,000 ft, a L ENG FIRE MASTER WARNING was displayed on the engine indicating and crew alerting system (EICAS) with an accompanying aural fire bell. The captain continued flying and the FO executed the engine fire checklist. The engine was successfully shutdown, one fire bottle was discharged, and the fire indication extinguished shortly thereafter. The crew declared an emergency, requested an immediate return to ATL, and performed an uneventful landing.
The crew did not observe any additional cockpit fire indications after landing and elected to vacate the runway and taxi to a gate. Post-landing inspection by airport rescue and fire-fighting (ARFF) found sooting and thermal damage on the No. 1 engine and nacelle components, extending up toward the pylon structure. Subsequent inspection by Delta Airlines maintenance found a tear near the top of the outer diffuser case.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to maintain control during a turn, which resulted in an aerodynamic stall.
AnalysisNarrative: The pilot reported that while performing agricultural spray applications, a vehicle parked on the road in the vicinity of the field he was spraying. He made a 360° turn waiting for the vehicle to move. During the turn, the airplane lost airspeed and entered an aerodynamic stall. The pilot attempted to recover the airplane from the stall by pitching the nose of the airplane down and applying full power. However, during the recovery, the airplane entered a secondary aerodynamic stall. The airplane impacted power lines and trees and then impacted a residential yard. The fuselage, wings, and horizontal stabilizer were substantially damaged. While departing from the turf runway, the flight instructor flew the airplane  in ground effect longer than was necessary and then turned left crosswind while still at a low altitude. The airplane’s left wing subsequently contacted a barbed wire fence, and the wire wrapped around the wing. The flight instructor returned to the airport, landed uneventfully, and removed the barbed wire from the wing. He subsequently performed a preflight inspection, and after nothing that the flight control surfaces were operating normally, returned to the airplane’s home airport uneventfully. Subsequent examination of the airplane revealed the left wing had been substantially damaged. The flight instructor reported that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures of the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 1, 2026, about 2301 mountain daylight time (MDT), a Cessna 172G, N1166F, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Blackfoot, Idaho. The pilot was fatally injured, and the two passengers sustained serious injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
A witness reported the pilot completed 3 takeoffs and landings for night currency before departing on the accident flight about 2300 MDT. 
Law enforcement received a 911 call reporting an airplane crash on a road adjacent to the airport, about 2301 MDT. No witnesses, surveillance video, or flight data captured the accident flight.
The airplane's first point of contact (FPOC) was marked by a ground scar about 33 ft inside the airport's eastern perimeter fence near the northeast corner of the airport. Paint chips, the right-wing tip and other debris extended from the FPOC through the perimeter fence to the main wreckage, which came to rest upright on the adjacent road about 30 ft beyond the airport boundary fence. The debris path was oriented about 058° magnetic, and the airplane came to rest on a heading of about 189° magnetic. 
Crushing and deformation were observed throughout the fuselage, wings, empennage, cockpit, and landing gear. The right wing exhibited leading-edge crushing and compression, with buckling of the upper and lower wing skins. The wing was bent upward near the root, with deformation extending into the midspan section of the wing. Portions of the wing skin were torn and separated. The left wing exhibited extensive buckling of the outboard wing skin and leading edge. The outboard wing was bent upward and aft, with wrinkling extending inboard.
The fuselage was crushed, with substantial damage to the cabin and aft fuselage. The vertical stabilizer and rudder exhibited crushing and deformation. The horizontal stabilizer and elevator were bent and partially separated at their attachment points.
The two-bladed McCauley propeller was separated from the engine crankshaft and was located within the debris field. Both blades exhibited extensive chordwise scratches along their surfaces. One blade was separated at the blade tip. The other blade exhibited bending near the outboard end, with the blade tip bent aft along with deformation. The propeller spinner was crushed and extensively deformed.
The airplane was retained for further examination.

On August 2, 2026, about 1608 central daylight time (CDT), a Beech E18S airplane, N210Q, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Guymon, Oklahoma. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 positioning flight.
The airplane was purchased by the pilot on June 22, 2026. According to the seller, the pilot was re-positioning the airplane to South Carolina. The seller stated that he had flown about 6 hours with the pilot in the accident airplane over two flights from June 21 to June 27. The pilot arrived on August 1 to pick up the airplane.
The flight took place over multiple time zones, all times referenced will be in CDT. On August 1, the airplane departed Lebanon State Airport (S30), Lebanon, Oregon, about 2108 and arrived at Winnemucca Municipal Airport (WMC), Winnemucca, Nevada, at 0015. The airplane was refueled with 175 gallons of 100 low-lead aviation fuel before departing about 0111, August 2. On August 2, about 0440, the airplane landed at Four Corners Regional Airport (FMN), Farmington, New Mexico. The airplane was refueled with 88 gallons of 100 low-lead aviation. The airplane departed FMN about 1258 for Guymon Municipal Airport (GUY), Guymon, Oklahoma. The airplane landed at GUY about 1509.
According to the GUY airport manager, the pilot refueled the airplane with 211.7 gallons of fuel and added oil to both engines. He spoke briefly with the pilot and discussed a fuel stop near Little Rock, Arkansas. At 1606, the pilot announced his departure from runway 18 at GUY on the common traffic advisory frequency (CTAF).
According to witnesses, after departing runway 18, the airplane was observed making a left bank and the pilot announced on CTAF that he was departing to the east. Witnesses observed the airplane make a turn to the east and continue the turn to the north while descending in a nose low, left-wing-low attitude. Multiple security videos captured the accident sequence. The footage was sent to the NTSB Vehicle Performance Division for further analysis. 
The airplane impacted a grass covered field in a wings-level, flat pitch attitude on a heading of about 015°. The aircraft came to rest upright about 80 ft north of the initial impact point. A post-impact fire consumed the majority of the fuselage and melted the wings and tail as seen in figure 1. All major components of the airplane were identified. Both engines were separated from the airframe and located near the main wreckage. Both propeller hubs remained attached to the engines. The propeller blades showed varying degrees of bending, twisting, chordwise scratching and polishing. Examination of the flight controls found no evidence of preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation.

Figure 1. Main wreckage
The pilot held a commercial certificate with ratings for airplane single-engine land, airplane single-engine sea, airplane multi-engine land, airplane multi-engine sea, instrument airplane and a BE-1900 type rating. Additionally, he held an Airline Transport Pilot certificate for rotorcraft-helicopter. He reported a total flight experience of 12,000 hours on an application for an FAA first-class medical certificate, dated December 24, 2025. 
The airplane was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.

On July?30,?2026, at 2356?mountain daylight time, a Cessna?172M airplane, N9650V, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Layton, Utah. The flight instructor was seriously injured, and the private pilot sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title?14 Code of Federal Regulations Part?91 instructional flight.

The flight instructor reported that he and the private pilot were conducting a longdistance night crosscountry instructional flight. As they were descending to land near the completion of the flight, the engine sputtered and then lost all power. The flight instructor configured the airplane for bestglide performance. While the flight instructor attempted to restart the engine, the private pilot completed checklist items, radioed air traffic control and declared an emergency. Both pilots reported that on about three or four occasions, the engine restarted and ran rough briefly, then lost power. The flight instructor determined the airplane had sufficient altitude and performance to glide to a runway landing at Hill Air Force Base (HIF), which was directly ahead. He reported that a gust of wind from a canyon hit the airplane from the right, resulting in an unexpected altitude loss. The flight instructor then determined the airplane would no longer reach the planned runway and performed a forced landing in a dark area near a roadway south of the airport. The airplane landed hard, nosed over and came to rest inverted in an intersection, sustaining substantial damage to the wings and fuselage.

A mobile phone video, recorded by a resident who lives near the accident location, showed the airplane descending low over a residential neighborhood. In the video, the engine produced a popping sound and was running sporadically.

A witness who was driving her vehicle on the roadway near the accident intersection reported that she observed something passing above. The witness then heard a loud crashing sound and observed an airplane overturned alongside the intersection. She noted that she did not hear sound coming from the airplane prior to the accident.

First responders reported seeing fuel pouring from the airplane wreckage, which continued to leak from the left wing for up to two hours after the crash.

The wreckage was transported to a secure facility and retained for further examination.

On August 2, 2026, about 0710 Pacific daylight time, a Cameron Balloons A-315, N315U, was not damaged when it was involved in an accident near Menifee, California. The pilot and one passenger were not injured, and one passenger was fatally injured. The balloon was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 skydiving balloon flight.
In a phone conversation, the pilot stated that after all the skydivers had exited the balloon and were safely on the ground, the balloon was descending. The pilot stated that it is their standard practice to open a bottle of champagne for the passengers who remained in the basket. He asked one passenger if he wanted champagne, which the pilot said he "just kind of grunted something" without really responding. While at an altitude of about 4,500 ft mean sea level, the pilot reached into a bag to retrieve drinks for the passengers and felt a very slight movement which he initially believed was one of the passengers had simply shifted position or turned around.  However, when he looked up, he noticed that one passenger had jumped out and was no longer in the basket. The pilot added that there was no sound, verbal statement, or warning that the passenger was going to jump out the basket in flight. 
The pilot radioed his ground crew and requested that they call 911. Subsequently, the pilot landed uneventfully.

On August 2, 2026, about 1318 central daylight time, a Robinson Helicopter Company R44 II helicopter, N26KL, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Bennett, Iowa. The pilot was not injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 agricultural flight.

The pilot reported that as the helicopter passed over a tree line he felt a vibration in the airframe and when the vibration increased he decided to perform an autorotation into the next field. According to the pilot, the helicopter descended rapidly from about 20 ft above the ground which resulted in a hard landing.

On August 4, 2026, about 1839 central daylight time, a Piper PA-24-250 airplane, N8422P, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Bethany, Missouri. The pilot received fatal injuries. The airplane was operated under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations as a Part 91 flight. 
The pilot, who was also the airplane owner, departed on a personal flight under visual flight rules from Peoria International Airport Peoria, Illinois, to Rapid City Regional Airport, Rapid City, South Dakota. Preliminary radar data showed that the flight climbed to an initial cruise altitude of about 13,000 ft msl after departure and operated at an altitude about 12,500 ft msl for about 90 minutes. The cruise altitude increased above 18,000 ft msl and into Class A airspace during the flight, which operated without air traffic control clearance or services. A review of weather data showed the flight entered convective activity after which it descended and impacted terrain. The airplane was destroyed by impact forces and a postcrash fire.
Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that it was not equipped with an installed breathable or a portable breathable oxygen system. The postaccident examination revealed no mechanical anomalies that would have precluded normal airplane operation.

On August 4, 2026, at about 1845 Pacific daylight time, a Cirrus Design Corporation SR22T airplane, N625LK, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Bend, Oregon. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
According to preliminary ADS-B data, the airplane departed from runway 35 at Bend Municipal Airport (BDN), Bend, Oregon, at about 1335. The airplane flew westbound, climbing to about 11,000 ft mean sea level (msl), before executing multiple turns above mountainous terrain about 33 miles west of BDN. Between about 1415 and 1610, the airplane maintained a looping, meandering flight path in the vicinity of BDN. At about 1610, the airplane began to fly in circles at about 5,000 ft msl 12 miles west of BDN.
The final ten seconds of data captured by the airplane’s recoverable data module (RDM) showed that the airplane’s left fuel tank sensor indicated 0 gallons of fuel remaining and the right fuel tank sensor indicated 1 gallon of fuel remaining. The RDM data also indicated that the airplane’s pitch moved from about 4° nose down to about 22° nose down and the throttle lever angle was at 92.3%. The RDM data terminated at 1845:50.
The airplane impacted terrain 12.5 miles west of BDN. The area was generally flat, with short scrub brush and standing dead trees. The first identified points of impact consisted of an area of fallen dead trees and a shallow impact crater. The wreckage path was about 175 ft long, oriented on a magnetic heading of 092°. The left wing, left aileron, right elevator, two propeller blades, left cabin door, fiberglass fragments, and fragments of the windscreen were distributed throughout the wreckage path. The main wreckage came to rest inverted on a magnetic heading of 333°. 
The airplane was recovered for further examination.

On August 4, 2026, about 1434 eastern daylight time (EDT), Marine One (VM1) a Sikorsky VH-3D, and Envoy Air flight 3742 (ENY3742), an Embraer E-170, were involved in a loss of separation about 2 miles north of Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA), Arlington, Virginia. There were no injuries reported to the passengers or crewmembers on board either aircraft. 
VM1 was a military Presidential transport local flight operating under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 from The Ellipse Park, Washington, D.C. ENY3742 was a scheduled domestic passenger flight operating under the provisions of Title 14 CFR Part 121 from DCA to Pensacola International Airport (PNS), Pensacola, Florida. At the time of the loss of separation, VM1 had departed The Ellipse when ENY3742 was departing runway 1 and beginning their initial climb. After the loss of separation, VM1 completed their local flight without incident while ENY3742 completed their flight to PNS without incident. Figure 1 below shows key locations and estimated position of both aircraft at FAA’s estimated closest proximity.

Figure 1. Key locations and estimated position of both aircraft at FAA's estimated closest proximity overlaid onto a street map in Google Earth.
As part of the investigative process, the NTSB invited qualified parties to participate in the investigation. Parties to the investigation include the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of the Navy (DON), and Envoy Air Inc. In accordance with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Annex 13, Centro de Investigação e Prevenção de Acidentes Aeronáuticos (CENIPA) of Brazil, representing the State of Design of the Embraer 170 airplane, was notified of the investigation.    
Certified air traffic control (ATC) audio recordings and Standard Terminal Automation Replacement System (STARS) radar data were provided by the FAA. Table 1 provides a summary of key communications between the DCA Airport Traffic Control Tower (ATCT) Helicopter Control (HC) and Local Control (LC) controllers and the flight crews of VM1 and ENY3742. The two transmissions in red italics were sourced from a third-party application: ATC – Live Air Traffic Radio. According to the disclaimer in their application, ATC audio in their application is sourced from Enhanced Radar (a company that builds Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven systems to transcribe, analyze, and optimize ATC communications and airspace operations) and processed with their Y4-small AI model. These transmissions were not received by FAA ATC radio receivers and were unable to be heard by the DCA ATCT HC or LC controllers. Note: The HC and LC positions operate on different frequencies and therefore, flightcrews and controllers can only hear what is being transmitted on the frequency they are using – in this case, VM1 was on the HC frequency and ENY3742 was on the LC frequency. 
Table 1. Summary of key communications between DCA ATCT (both HC and LC control), and flight crews of VM1 and ENY3742. All times are approximate and in EDT. (Communications in red italics were not able to be heard on FAA ATC frequencies.)

A preliminary FAA estimate of the closest proximity between VM1 and ENY3742 determined they were about .82 miles apart laterally and about 700 feet vertically, as shown in figure 2.

Figure 2. Radar flight tracks of both VM1 and ENY3742 overlaid onto satellite imagery with the FAA estimated closest proximity illustrated (.82 nautical miles (nm) lateral and 700 feet vertical).
Envoy Air Flight 3742 Flightcrew Statements
Postincident statements provided by ENY3742 flightcrew revealed the first officer (FO) was the pilot flying and the captain was the pilot monitoring. Both crewmembers recalled that after takeoff from runway 1, as the aircraft climbed and accelerated, the Terminal Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) announced a traffic advisory (TA) with “Traffic, Traffic.” At no time was the TCAS TA target acquired visually by either crewmember. The TCAS TA target symbol remained to the right and below their own-ship symbol the entire time. Both recalled seeing 600 feet of vertical separation being displayed on TCAS as the TA target passed behind their right wing of the own-ship symbol on the display. The captain added that at no time was the TCAS resolution advisory (RA) displayed, announced, or commanded.
DCA Helicopter Frequency Communications
Certified ATC audio recordings revealed that the first attempt to contact DCA ATCT was not received at all, and the second attempt was broken and completely unreadable (to which the controller advised on frequency). The frequency had been working normally and there were no known outages or reports of degradation of this frequency on the day of the event, nor was there a history of problems with this frequency according to FAA. As a result of the missed transmissions with VM1 on the day of the incident, FAA technicians from Spectrum Engineering conducted a coverage analysis and determined that there was not adequate line-of-sight to ensure communications between the radio transmitter/receiver sight and The Ellipse, where VM1 was temporarily operating from while construction was ongoing at the White House.
FAA Technical Operations Personnel Interviews
Postincident interviews were conducted with personnel from FAA’s technical operations responsible for the ATC radios used at DCA ATCT. Both technicians stated that there had been no documented history of reported problems with the HC frequency and had been no report on the day of the incident until after the incident had occurred. After finding the line-of-sight deficiencies in their coverage analysis done immediately after becoming aware of the problem, the FAA relocated the radios for the HC frequency from their location in a nearby residential neighborhood, to the top of the DCA ATCT. 
DCA ATCT Air Traffic Manager Interview
The postincident interview with the air traffic manager (ATM) also revealed that there was no known history of problems with the HC frequency from ATC. The ATM also reported that once the technicians had relocated the radios to the tower, ATC conducted radio checks with two separate Marine Helicopter Squadron One (HMX-1) aircraft located at The Ellipse and in the local vicinity and reported no deficiencies. Additionally, there were no deficiencies noted in communication with other helicopters in communication with DCA ATCT either.
Meeting Between DCA ATCT and HMX-1
DCA ATCT and HMX-1 staff met the week preceding the incident on July 30, 2026. According to the ATM, this was not a regularly scheduled meeting, but rather a meeting that had been requested by HMX-1 to discuss local operations and to express the need for more training flights within the DCA Class B airspace, and ATC wanted to discuss concern with recent reports of their not receiving the required 3 minute to liftoff call from HMX-1 flight crews. At that time, HMX-1 advised that communications “had been spotty,” and felt that may have been the reason. It was agreed that they would attempt other means of reaching the tower in situations where they were unable to reach them to provide the 3-minute call (for example, relaying through another aircraft), and on the day of the incident evidence showed they did. After not reaching them on their initial attempt, they had attempted to relay the 3-minute call through the helicopter facility at Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling, which was also unsuccessful.
Loss of Standard Separation
The FAA reported the preliminary estimated closest proximity between VM1 and ENY3742 as about .82 nm laterally and 700 feet vertically. This would meet the required minimum radar separation as set forth in FAA Order JO 7110.65BB, Air Traffic Control, paragraph 7-9-4, which required 1.5 nm lateral or 500 feet vertical separation within Class B airspace, between a VFR aircraft and any aircraft weighing more than 19,000

ProbableCause: The in-flight opening of the engine cowling, which resulted in engine baffling separating from the airplane and impacting the right elevator.
AnalysisNarrative: The pilot stated that he had performed a preflight inspection of the airplane and did not note any deficiency with the engine cowling’s security. About 7 minutes into the flight, the front right engine cowling opened and started flapping. The pilot declared an emergency with air traffic control and diverted to a nearby airport where he landed uneventfully. Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that engine baffling had separated from the engine compartment and impacted the right elevator resulting in substantial damage. Maintenance personnel examined the airplane after the accident and found that the cowling’s latch mechanism functioned normally with no mechanical irregularities.

On August 6, 2026, about 1030 central daylight time, a Beech H35, N5409D, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Bogalusa, Louisiana. The private pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
Preliminary ADS-B data showed the airplane departed Elm Creek Airpark (0TX6), Seguin, Texas, where the airplane was based, at 0617. The airplane arrived at George R Carr Memorial Air Field (BXA), Bogalusa, Louisiana, about 0915. According to the airport manager at BXA, the pilot wanted 40 gallons of fuel. He continued that the pilot “topped off” the left and right main fuel tanks and was adding fuel to the right auxiliary fuel tank when the fuel farm pump motor stopped working. The pilot had added 35 gallons at that point and told the airport manager that this would be enough fuel. 
The airport manager also reported that the pilot had wanted to put more fuel into the right side of the airplane to help “get the plane trimmed better.” The airport manager asked the pilot if he planned to use the crew vehicle to go into town to get something to eat, the pilot told him no, that they had left early and were on their way to Florida. Motion-activated surveillance cameras at the airport showed the pilot and passenger in the fixed base operator (FBO) building and the airport manager reported that he spoke with the pilot about the next leg of their flight to Florida. The pilot told him that they would stop on their way back to Texas the following Tuesday. The airport manager then left to begin working on the fuel farm pump and the cameras show the pilot and passenger leaving the FBO at 1013. The cameras that were pointed at the ramp did not capture any other footage of the pilot and passenger, or the accident airplane. The airport manager continued that while at the fuel farm working on the pump he saw the pilot doing a walkaround but did not watch the full preflight inspection and was not sure if the pilot sumped the airplane’s fuel tanks.  He then heard the pilot start the engine, which took two tries before it started. He watched as the airplane taxied out to the runway and heard the pilot perform an engine run-up. He then watched the takeoff roll, rotation, and initial climb before he turned and began putting tools away. When he exited the fuel farm pit and began to place his tools in his truck, he saw a smoke plume and went to the accident site where he found the airplane consumed by a postimpact fire. He did not report hearing any abnormalities in the engine noise during the engine run-up or takeoff/initial climb.
The accident site was located about 0.5 statute miles from the departure end of runway 36, the runway the airplane departed from, in a forested area. A pine tree about 10 ft aft and outboard of the right wing tip had two branches broken about 40 ft up the tree with the higher branch broken closer to the trunk. A large log was embedded in the cowling and cabin compartment of the wreckage, and a broken stump was observed under the fuselage consistent with the diameter of the embedded log. Multiple pieces of wood were observed with clean 45° angle cuts and the ends were singed. The wreckage came to rest on a true heading of about 300°, at an elevation of 148 ft mean sea level (msl). All major components of the airplane were located with the main wreckage. The wreckage debris field was contained to about a 15 yard radius encompassing the main wreckage. Postaccident fire damage was observed for about a 50 yard radius around the accident site.
The fuselage was mostly consumed by postimpact fire. The main cabin door was observed in the main wreckage and was substantially damaged by fire. The baggage door and emergency escape hatch were consumed by fire and not observed. The empennage was thermally damaged and remained attached to the fuselage via the control cables. Both stabilizers remained attached to the empennage. Both ruddervators remained attached to the stabilizers and the trim tabs remained attached to the ruddervators. Both wing leading edges were impact crushed aft to the forward spar and the upper and lower wing skin, aft of the forward wing spar, was wrinkled. The right wing impacted a tree, about 5 inches in diameter, about 5 ft from the base and slid down the tree removing bark until the wing came to rest on the ground. Both flaps and ailerons remained attached to their respective wings. The left flap actuator was measured, based on this measurement the flaps were at or near the “UP” position. The right flap actuator was consumed by fire and was unable to be measured. The landing gear actuator housing, motor, and landing gear extension handle were consumed by fire. The sector gear and main landing gear pushrods remained, and the position of the pushrods corresponded to the landing gear being fully extended or nearly so, if in an intermediate position. The faceplate for the tachometer was recovered with the needle fixed at a high rpm; due to thermal damage the exact reading could not be determined. All fuel tanks were destroyed by postaccident fire. When low pressure air was blown through the fuel selector it was found to be in the AUX position. The fuel strainer screen was examined and was unobstructed. The strainer bowl was examined and did not contain any debris or signs of corrosion.
The impact crater created by the engine was about 18 inches in depth. The engine exhibited impact and fire damage. Multiple accessories were impact separated from the engine. The throttle, mixture, and propeller controls were impact-separated. The airplane was equipped with one standard and one electronic magneto; both magnetos were impact-separated. The oil pan was destroyed by impact forces. The oil filter remained attached to the oil filter adapter and was not removed. The oil filler cap and dipstick remained installed in their respective locations.
The propeller remained attached to the engine crankshaft flange. Both propeller blades remained installed and attached to the propeller hub. The propeller governor remained attached to the engine and the governor actuator rod arm was impact separated. One propeller blade was curved slightly aft. The other blade exhibited significant S bending and twisting. The spinner was crushed around the propeller dome.
The airplane was recovered and retained for further examination.

On August 5, 2026, at 1117 mountain daylight time, a Cessna 177B, N34852, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Perris, California. The flight instructor and student pilot were not injured. The airplane was being operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.
According to both pilots, after completing a series of maneuvers, the engine lost power while positioning the airplane to practice S-turns at 1,500 ft AGL. Attempts to restart the engine were unsuccessful so the flight instructor performed an emergency landing to a field. During landing the airplane struck vegetation and nosed over, resulting in substantial damage to the left wing and fuselage. The pilots reported 44 gallons of fuel onboard at takeoff and they had been airborne about 1.5 hrs when the engine quit.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 7, 2026, about 1044 mountain daylight time, a Helicopter Transport Services (Sikorsky) CH-54A Skycrane Helitanker, N793HT, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Cove Fort, Utah. The pilot and copilot were fatally injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 133 aerial firefighting flight.
The helicopter, owned and operated by Helicopter Transport Services, was conducting aerial fire suppression operations under an exclusive-use contract with the United States Forest Service (USFS) in support of the Wide Mouth 2 Fire in central Utah. It was equipped with a 2,650-gallon water tank and a retractable hover-snorkel system.
According to the USFS, the helicopter departed Richfield Municipal Airport (RIF) about 1021 and proceeded toward the Wide Mouth 2 Fire to begin firefighting operations.
After departure, the flight crew established radio communications with the aerial supervisor and received authorization to enter the temporary flight restriction (TFR) area surrounding the fire. The aerial supervisor briefed the crew on the initial firefighting objectives, which included coordinated aerial water-drop operations. The helicopter proceeded to a predetermined water source, filled its tank, and then continued to the designated drop area as directed.
As the helicopter approached the drop site, the aerial supervisor transferred communications to the ground supervisor, who provided specific instructions regarding the target area. According to the ground supervisor, the helicopter arrived from the northwest, and he directed the crew to the location where water was needed. The helicopter then flew over the area to verify the target, and the flight crew confirmed they had identified the correct location.
The crew subsequently reported that they would make another pass before releasing the water load. While maneuvering in a right turn, the helicopter disappeared behind a knoll. The ground supervisor then heard a radio transmission stating, “Oh (expletive), we have a problem,” followed about one second later by, “Mayday, mayday, mayday.” No further communications were received from the helicopter.
The helicopter impacted rising terrain, and a post-crash fire consumed much of the airframe (see figure 1).

Figure 1. Aerial overview of accident site. (U.S. Forest Service Drone Photo)
The investigator-in-charge from the NTSB’s Alaska Regional Office, accompanied by an NTSB aerospace engineer and helicopter specialist, responded to the accident site and examined the wreckage on August 9, 2026. During the on-scene investigation, components were retained for further examination and testing. The results of those examinations are pending.
Recovery of the wreckage will take place when fire conditions and logistical considerations allow. A detailed examination of the airframe and engines is pending.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 7, 2026, about 1549 mountain daylight time, a Textron Aviation Inc. 172S, N1842E, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Provo, Utah. The flight instructor sustained serious injuries, and the pilot undergoing instruction was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.

The flight was operated by ATP Flight School under the callsign Career Track (CXK) 138 and was intended to provide preparation for the pilot undergoing instruction’s upcoming instrument checkride. The airplane was scheduled to depart for the practice area south of the airport via the “Golf Course” departure, a route that would have initially taken the airplane east over Provo Bay.

Preliminary air traffic control audio indicated that multiple aircraft operating in the vicinity of Provo Municipal Airport (PVU) in the period before the accident reported moderate to severe turbulence. One of those airplanes, which was also operated by ATP, reported descent rates exceeding 1,000 ft per minute while approaching Bird Island, a reporting point in Utah Lake about 5 miles southwest of the airport.

At about 1546, the accident airplane was cleared for takeoff from runway 18. ADS-B data showed that the airplane began a climbing left turn to the southeast with a groundspeed that varied between 68 and 75 knots. A few seconds later, the airplane began a rapid descent, accelerating to a groundspeed of about 96 knots before the last ADS-B target was recorded approximately 160 ft above the water, and 350 ft short of the accident site.



Figure 1 – ADS-B track

Security camera footage from multiple buildings located on the east side of the airport, facing west and south-southwest, showed several areas of tall dust formations moving through the surface area along and south of the airport during the time preceding the accident. One dust formation appeared to move across the departure end of runway 18 as the airplane entered the video frame in the upper-right portion of one of the cameras. A few seconds later, the airplane began to descend, and a splash was observed about 30 seconds later as the airplane impacted the water.

The airplane came to rest in marshland within Provo Bay, about 6,000 ft south-southeast of the departure end of runway 18. The main wreckage was semi-submerged in about 18 inches of water and resting on soft mud. The debris field extended about 100 ft in length. The first identified point of impact was the nose landing gear assembly, which had separated from the airframe. The remaining wreckage was concentrated to the east of that location.

The forward cabin section, engine, and both wings were submerged, with a section of a propeller blade tip visible above the water.

The wreckage was recovered for further examination.

On August 9, 2026, at about 1655 central daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Avid Mark IV, N77FB, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Arp, Texas. The private pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
According to witnesses, the accident airplane and a second airplane had landed in a grass field earlier in the afternoon. The accident airplane subsequently departed the field first and remained in the vicinity while the second airplane departed. Witnesses reported that after takeoff, the accident airplane was flying at a low altitude and appeared to be moving slowly as it maneuvered near the second airplane. The accident airplane then entered a steep left bank, followed by a steep descending turn. The airplane subsequently impacted trees and terrain adjacent to the field.
The airplane came to rest with all major components located at the accident site. The fuselage sustained impact damage, and both wings remained attached to the fuselage. Examination of the airframe confirmed flight control continuity, and no evidence of preimpact flight control anomaly was observed. Both wing fuel tanks remained intact and contained fuel. Examination of the engine confirmed mechanical continuity and compression on all cylinders. No evidence of a preimpact mechanical anomaly was observed that would have precluded normal operation.
An electronic flight instrument was recovered and retained for further examination.

On August 9, 2026 at 802 eastern daylight time, a Mooney M20E, N9257V, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Conway, South Carolina. The pilot was uninjured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot reported he planned to conduct an instrument flight rules (IFR) cross-country flight from Conway-Horry County Airport (HYW), Conway, South Carolina, to Berkeley County Airport (MKS), Moncks Corner, South Carolina. The pilot stated that he performed an engine run-up, which included a check of the magnetos, propeller governor and auxiliary fuel pump. He then departed runway 22, announced his intention to depart the area on the common traffic advisory frequency and switched to the terminal radar approach control frequency to activate his IFR clearance. Shortly thereafter, he noticed “sluggish” performance and decided to switch fuel tanks, which did not resolve the condition. He soon felt a vibration and noticed the engine running rough, which he described as continuing to “pick up and then back off.” About 1,000 ft mean sea level, he turned back to HYW before the engine lost power completely. The pilot stated that he could not reach the airport and soon began striking trees. The airplane came to rest upright, in dense woods. 
Post accident examination of the airplane by an FAA inspector revealed substantial damage to the empennage, fuselage, and both wings. The fuselage was crumpled and torn in multiple locations, and both the wings and tail sustained significant leading-edge damage. The engine case was not breached, and the engine oil dipstick was removed and showed about 8 quarts of oil. 
The pilot stated that he refueled the airplane after his last flight in June 2026 to a total of 52 gallons. The most recent maintenance logbook entry noted the replacement of the engine starter in July 2026. 
The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.

On August 6, 2026, about 1538 central daylight time, a PZL-Bielsko B1-PW-5 glider, N105WS, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Briggs, Texas. The pilot was fatally injured. The glider was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The glider was departing on an auto-tow launch at the time of the accident. According to witness statements, the glider achieved level flight at about 1,000 ft before release from the towline. Following the release, the glider yawed to the right and entered a descending spiral, completing about 7 to 8 rotations before impacting terrain west of the glider port. Witnesses reported that the glider impacted the ground in a near-vertical attitude.
The cockpit and forward fuselage were crushed aft during the impact. Both wings remained attached to the fuselage. The tail section and vertical stabilizer were partially separated, with the aft 4 ft of the tail boom folded over the aft fuselage.
The glider was retained for further examination.

ProbableCause: The fuel truck driver’s distraction and inadequate visual lookout, which resulted in a collision with an airplane.
AnalysisNarrative: The pilot stated that he had just landed on the runway and was instructed by the tower controller to exit the runway to the left and taxi to the hangars. After exiting the runway, he stopped past the hold short line to perform the after-landing checklist. While he was performing the checklist items, the airplane was struck from behind by a fuel truck, resulting in substantial damage to the airplane’s empennage, elevators, and fuselage. The fuel truck driver stated that he was looking at his phone while he was crossing the runway and when he looked up, he saw the airplane in front of him. He applied the truck’s brakes, but the truck struck the airplane.

On August 6, 2026, about 1355 eastern daylight time, a Piper Aircraft PA-32-260 airplane, N8791E, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Pinetown, North Carolina. The private pilot and two passengers sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
According to the pilot, after departing Martin County Airport (MCZ), Williamston, North Carolina, enroute to Ocracoke Island Airport (W95), Ocracoke, North Carolina, he climbed to and leveled at 3,000 ft mean sea level. About 10 minutes after establishing cruise flight, the engine experienced a total loss of power.
The pilot established the airplane's best-glide airspeed, transmitted a mayday call, and attempted to restart the engine. Unable to restore engine power, he selected a logging path within a wooded area for a forced landing. During the landing rollout, the airplane's left wing struck a tree. The airplane subsequently impacted another tree and came to rest in a ditch, resulting in substantial damage to the wings and fuselage.
The wreckage was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 10, 2026, about 1248 central daylight time, an experimental Velocity 173 FG Elite II airplane, N6954K, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Palmyra, Illinois. The pilot and two passengers sustained no injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal cross-country flight.
According to the pilot, 14 gallons of 100 low lead fuel was purchased prior to the flight at the St. Louis Regional Airport (ALN), East Alton, Illinois. The airplane departed from ALN about 1210, and the destination was the Whiteside County Airport (SQI), Rock Falls, Illinois, where the pilot based the airplane. The airplane climbed to about 7,500 ft msl and established a cruise flight configuration. About 15 minutes later, the engine sustained a total loss of power. The pilot declared an emergency with air traffic control. The pilot coordinated with the controller, and he decided to divert to the nearest airport, the Zelmer Memorial Airpark (5K1), Palmyra, Illinois. During the emergency descent, he attempted to restore the engine power. He noticed that partial engine power was restored by pulling the mixture control nearly to the idle cutoff position. He further noticed that further attempts at a richer setting caused a loss of engine power.
The pilot maneuvered the airplane for a straight-in approach to runway 18 at 5K1. He noted that the approach was too high and too fast. During the landing, the airplane departed the runway to the left. The airplane came to rest upright in a flat soybean field.
The experimental canard airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, the right wing, and the right canard. Postaccident examination found the fuel system to be intact, and the two wing fuel tanks were found to be more than half full. A fuel sample did not reveal any contamination. According to the pilot, there is no fuel selector valve assembly installed, only a fuel cutoff control. The two wing fuel tanks feed into a single header fuel tank. The airplane was recovered from the accident site, and it was transported to a secure location for future examination.
The composite airplane was built from a kit in 1998. A review of FAA records showed that the pilot purchased the airplane in May 2008. The airplane was equipped with a Lycoming Engines IO-360-C1D6 reciprocating engine and a MT-Propeller MTV-18-B/LD168-101 controllable pitch three blade wood-composite propeller.
A review of the airplane’s maintenance records showed that a condition inspection was performed by a mechanic on February 15, 2026, for the airframe, the engine, and the propeller. The airplane accumulated 23.7 hours since the condition inspection.

On August 5, 2026, at about 1034 mountain daylight time, a Van’s Aircraft RV-8, C-GFWR, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Great Falls, Montana. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The airplane departed Villeneuve Airport (CZVL), near Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, and landed on runway 21 at Great Falls International Airport (KGTF), Great Falls, Montana. During the landing rollout, the airplane veered right. The pilot applied engine power while attempting to regain directional control, and the airplane subsequently ground looped to the right and departed the runway. The left main landing gear collapsed, and the left wing contacted the ground. The airplane came to rest in the grass adjacent to the runway.
The airplane sustained substantial damage to the left wing, and fuselage. The pilot reported that the tailwheel assembly had been replaced about two weeks before the accident and that the accident flight was the airplane’s first flight and landing since the replacement.
The airplane was retained for examination.

On August 10, 2026, about 12:55 Pacific daylight time, a Cessna 180, N180DT, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near La Center, Washington. The flight instructor and pilot receiving instruction were seriously injured. The flight was being operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.
According to preliminary ADS-B, the airplane departed from runway 31 at Daybreak (WA46), La Center, Washington, about 1250, turned to the northwest, and climbed to 1,025 ft above ground level (agl). At 1251, the airplane made a turn to the east, and continued its climb to 2,200 ft. As the airplane passed the departure end of runway 31, it began a descent and about .5 mile east-southeast of WA46, the airplane made a left turn to the north. 1 mile northeast of WA46, at about 1,200 ft agl, the airplane made a descending 180° turn to the left, and flew southbound, approximately parallel with runway 13/31 at WA46, and about .45 mile from runway 13/31. About .40 mile east of the approach end of runway 31, about 250 ft agl, the airplane began a right turn and continued its descent until the end of the available flight track data. The last recorded data point was at 1255, about .23 mile southeast of the approach end of runway 31. (See figure 1)

Figure 1. Preliminary ADS-B flight track data of accident flight.
According to a witness who was positioned to the east of WA46, he observed the airplane shortly before the accident. He observed the airplane as it made the northbound turn, east of WA46, and then again as it flew southbound and began its turn toward the runway. He stated that as it was approaching, the engine sounded like it “backfired, as if the pilot was throttling back for landing”, and that otherwise, the airplane looked and sounded like most other airplanes he observes.
According to a family friend, the flight instructor stated to him that “they had been doing some practicing at Daybreak and that the engine lost power, they came up short and they had to put it in the trees.” The friend stated that the pilot had disclosed additional detail to him but did not share it with NTSB.
Due to ongoing medical circumstances at the time of this report, the NTSB has not received a statement of events from either pilot.
The airplane came to rest inverted, about 380 ft southeast of WA46. Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed substantial damage to both wings, the vertical stabilizer, and the fuselage. 
The wreckage was retained for further examination.

On August 10, 2026, at about 1835 mountain daylight time, an experimental amateur built Glasair Sportsman 2 Plus 2 airplane, N202AZ, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Pine, Arizona. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
According to preliminary ADS-B data, the airplane departed from runway 06 at Payson Airport (PAN), Payson, Arizona about 1827:07. The airplane flew on a northwest heading, climbing to about 5,850 ft mean sea level (msl) at 1831:51, before turning to the southwest above mountainous terrain about 7 nautical miles (nm) northwest of PAN. The airplane proceeded to the southwest and descended into a canyon, when the ADS-B signal was lost at 1835:47, about an altitude of 4,675 ft msl (about 680 ft above ground level and 136 ft above the canyon rim). 
The airplane impacted terrain about 3 nm west of the last ADS-B data point, on the northwestern face of a draw at an elevation of about 3,994 ft msl. The accident site area was comprised of roughly 45° sloping terrain with desert junipers and prickly pear cacti scattered along the rocky slope. The first identifiable point of impact (FIPOI) was a desert juniper with separated and damaged branches along with the left wing tip located at the base of the tree. The FIPOI was located about 791 ft above the base of the ravine, and about 1,300 ft below the ridgeline. The wreckage debris path was about 102 ft in length and oriented on a magnetic heading of 175°. The left wing, left aileron, left flap, right wing tip, fuselage, empennage, and engine were distributed throughout the wreckage debris path. A majority of the wreckage was consumed by a post impact fire. The fuselage came to rest in a right wing low, nose down attitude, on a heading of about 022 ° magnetic. The propeller was separated from the crankshaft aft of the propeller flange. Both propeller blades exhibited “S” bending, and leading-edge gouges. 
The wreckage was recovered to a secure location for further examination.

On August 9, 2026, at 1420 mountain daylight time, a Cessna 208B airplane, N247JP, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Salmon, Idaho. The pilot and eight passengers were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 135 on-demand air taxi flight.

The pilot reported that, after an uneventful flight from the departure airport, he joined the downwind leg of the traffic pattern for runway 17. While turning onto the base leg, he extended the wing flaps in preparation for landing and subsequently heard a loud “pop.” Immediately thereafter, the airplane made an aggressive, uncommanded roll to the left and banked to about 45°. The pilot attempted to regain lateral control by applying right aileron. He moved the control yoke to the full right aileron position and adjusted the aileron trim to the full right setting. The airplane touched down normally, and the pilot taxied it to the ramp without further incident.

Following the landing, a company mechanic examined the flight control systems and found substantial damage to the left wing spar. A preliminary examination identified a loose flap bolt that allowed the lower portion of the aft bellcrank to move freely. The aft bellcrank was designed to attach to the airplane with a bolt secured to an anchor nut assembly on its lower surface (see figure 1). The hardware will be retained for further examination.


Figure 1: Diagram showing the location of the loose bolt

On July 25, 2026, about 1630 central daylight time, a Cessna 150M, N18YZ, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Ferris, Texas. One pilot sustained minor injuries and the other pilot had no injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
Both pilots reported no abnormalities during the preflight. They added a quart of oil to the engine which was at 3.25 quarts when they checked. They fueled the airplane and taxied to the run-up area where the airplane showed normal indications during the preflight operational checks. 
The airplane departed from runway 13 at the Lancaster Regional Airport (LNC), Lancaster, Texas. During the initial climb the right seat pilot at the controls observed a climb rate of about 200 feet per minute and recognized the airplane was not producing sufficient performance to safely continue the flight. About 900 ft msl, the pilots agreed that clearing the power lines and trees ahead of them before initiating a turn was their priority. The engine was producing enough power to maintain airplane altitude but the airplane could not climb. After the airplane cleared the power lines and a residential area, the right seat pilot transferred control of the airplane to the left seat pilot and a turn back to the airport was initiated. As the airplane headed toward the runway, the engine began to run rough and the engine RPM decreased. About 3 miles from the airport the engine lost all power. Without enough altitude to glide to runway 31 an emergency landing was performed which resulted in substantial damage to the engine mount structure.
The airplane was retained for further examination.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 12, 2026, about 1906 eastern daylight time, a Staudacher ZZ 102 experimental airplane, N134ZZ, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Vicksburg, Michigan. The airline transport pilot and one passenger were seriously injured. The flight operated under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 as a personal flight.
Preliminary information provided by law enforcement indicated the airplane departed from Thrall Lake Airport (7MI3), Vicksburg, Michigan, and climbed to about 1,500 ft when it descended and impacted terrain. Both occupants were airlifted to hospitals, and the airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and both wings. 
According to the FAA aircraft records, the airplane was likely a unique build with only the accident airplane currently registered. The airplane was built in 2007 and purchased by the pilot in October 2021. According to a Barnstormers Facebook listing, dated November 8, 2025, the airplane had 210 hours total time, and the engine had 210 hours since major overhaul. 
Postaccident examination by FAA inspectors revealed the presence of fuel in both fuel tanks. However, when draining fuel from the fuel tanks, an orange substance was found in the fuel line. The airplane was retained for further examination.

The pilot was able to maintain control of the airplane and landed without further incident. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the left wing. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 15, 2026, 1755 Alaska Daylight Time, a China Airlines Flight Number CI-5265, Boeing 747-400F, registration B-18725, powered by four GE Aerospace CF6-80C2B1F turbofan engines, experienced an inflight fire indication during the initial climb from Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport (PANC). There were no injuries to the 4 crewmembers, and the airplane sustained minor damage. The flight was an international cargo flight from ANC to Taoyuan International Airport (RCTP), Taiwan.

According to the pilot, after takeoff at about 5,500ft above mean sea level (MSL), there was an audible fire warning and an "ENG FIRE 3" Engine-Indicating and Crew-Alerting System (EICAS) warning indication illuminated. The crew discharged one fire extinguishing bottle and shutdown the No. 3 engine. During the inflight shutdown procedure, electrical AC Bus Tie 3 tripped and electrical AC Bus 3 de-energized, which resulted in the left-hand autopilot disengaging and the loss of multiple instruments on the captain’s side. The crew engaged the Center autopilot and declared Mayday with air traffic control (ATC). ATC vectored the airplane to a holding pattern to jettison fuel prior to landing, but the fuel jettison control system failed. With the No. 3 engine fire warning no longer illuminated following discharge of the fire extinguishing bottle, the airplane remained in a holding pattern to burn enough fuel to be under the overweight landing limits at PANC. The airplane landed uneventfully approximately two hours after takeoff.

A post incident examination of the airplane by maintenance personnel revealed fire damage to a lower section of the left-hand engine cowl and evidence of an undercowl fire on the left-hand side of the engine. 

The NTSB traveled to the incident site. As part of the investigative process, the NTSB invited qualified parties to participate in the investigation. These included representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), GE Aerospace, and Boeing. The Taiwan Transportation Safety Board (TTSB), representing the State of the Operator, assigned an Accredited Representative; the Civil Aviation Administration (CAA) of Taiwan and China Airlines were named as a technical advisor by the TTSB.  The investigation team traveled to ANC to examine the airplane. A pressurization check of the fuel manifolds with  nitrogen gas revealed a crack in the left-hand (inboard) fuel manifold tube, located adjacent to fuel nozzle number 24 at approximately the 9 o’clock position on the engine. The engine was later removed from the airplane and shipped to an engine repair and overhaul facility for further examination. 

This investigation is ongoing..

On August 13, 2026, about 1302 central daylight time, a Mooney M20G airplane, N6916N, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Luling, Texas. The pilot received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 personal flight.
According to ADS-B data, the flight originated from the David Wayne Hooks Memorial Airport (DWH), Houston, Texas, about 1058. The airplane proceeded to the west-southwest toward San Antonio, Texas, for about an hour. About this time, the pilot contacted San Antonio Approach Control and declared an emergency. The pilot informed the air traffic controller that the airplane’s engine had lost power. The controller advised the pilot of an airport 7 miles northeast. The pilot requested a vector to the airport which the controller supplied. The pilot later reported having the airport in-sight before the airplane’s position reports ceased.
The pilot reported that he executed a forced landing to a road. He said that during the landing roll, the airplane’s left wingtip contacted vegetation along the side of the road which pulled the airplane to the left. The main landing gear went onto the shoulder of the road and the airplane veered off the road and struck trees. The airplane sustained substantial damage to its left wing.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to maintain clearance from trees during the landing approach.
AnalysisNarrative: According to the pilot of the tandem seat biplane, while conducting a short-field landing approach to the runway threshold, he was having trouble seeing his aiming point past the front passenger. He subsequently misjudged the airplane’s descent rate during a turn, and the left wing struck a tree beside the runway overrun. The airplane struck the ground and was consumed by a postimpact fire. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

ProbableCause: The pilot's failure to maintain clearance from power lines while maneuvering at low-level altitude during an agricultural operation.
AnalysisNarrative:
The pilot reported he was conducting aerial pollination in a corn field. Before beginning the pollination, the pilot flew an inspection circuit around the area to identify potential hazards and observed a center-pivot irrigation system and the power lines along the east and west sides of the field. The pilot reported that he completed about 3/4 of the field pollination and had two passes remaining. While turning the helicopter to enter another pass, the pilot focused on the target row, lost sight of the power lines, and the helicopter struck a power line wire with the tail rotor. 
Following the wire strike, the pilot elected to perform a precautionary landing. During the landing, the helicopter contacted the ground on the right skid, bounced, and yawed slightly to the right before it came to a stop. 
A post-accident examination of the helicopter revealed substantial damage to the right rear aft strut mounting area, and damage to the pilot seat floor structure at the forward strut attachment. The pilot reported that there was no evidence of any preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the helicopter that would have precluded normal operation.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 14, 2026, about 1459 central daylight time, a Gulfstream Aerospace G-IV airplane, N406JS, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near St. Louis, Missouri. The three crew members and 7 passengers were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations part 135 on-demand air taxi flight.
According to the crew, they received a STEER BY WIRE FAIL Crew Alerting System (CAS) message before departure from Eagle County Regional Airport (EGE), Eagle, Colorado. They completed the appropriate checklist and the message cleared. While on approach to Runway 8R at Spirit of St. Louis Airport (SUS), St. Louis Missouri, after lowering the landing gear, the crew again received a STEER BY WIRE FAIL CAS message. The crew completed the checklist; however, the message did not clear.
The airplane landed on the runway and as the nose wheel contacted the runway it began to shimmy. The nose landing gear (NLG) separated from the airplane followed by a collapse of the left main landing gear. The airplane veered left into the grass and came to rest upright. During the accident sequence, the airplane sustained damage to the lower fuselage and left wing.
According to the pilot, during the preflight inspection, the airport ground crew was unable to install the pip pin that goes into the NLG torque link that is used to engage and disengage the scissor link with the Nose Wheel Steering actuator for the NLG. The pilot was able to install the NLG pip pin which has a secondary safety pin that is normally installed into the pip pin to help ensure it remains engaged. The pilot reported that he forgot to install the secondary safety pin.
Postaccident examination of the runway and surrounding grass areas found several items of debris. The NLG pip pin, which is normally seated in the NLG torque link, was found separated from the NLG with three ball locks remaining as seen in figure 1. The NLG pip pin normally has four ball locks; the missing ball lock and the NLG upper scissor link could not be located. Examination of the NLG revealed that the safety pin was found intact in the open position and with the separated NLG still attached to its lanyard cord as seen in figure 2.

Figure 1. Nose landing gear pip pin.


Figure 2. Nose Landing Gear with open safety pin and torque link depicted.
The airplane was equipped with a cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder, which were removed and sent to the National Transportation Safety Board Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, DC, for download. The wreckage was retained for further examination.

ProbableCause: The collision with a deer during touch-and-go landings.
AnalysisNarrative:
The pilot reported that during the landing roll on runway 27 he observed three deer crossing the runway. The pilot initiated a go-around and heard a loud bang during the maneuver. The pilot subsequently flew a traffic pattern and returned for landing, unaware that the deer strike had damaged the right main landing gear and separated a portion of the landing gear assembly. During the subsequent landing, the airplane veered to the right and struck a runway marker sign, which resulted in the collapse of the left main landing gear. The airplane then skidded into the grass area adjacent to the runway and came to a stop.
The airplane sustained substantial damage to the aft lower fuselage structure. The pilot reported no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airframe or the engine that would have precluded normal operation. A review of the airport directory found a remark to alert pilots to deer on and in the vicinity of the airport.

On August 12, 2026, at approximately 2305 eastern daylight time, a Robinson R44 Raven II helicopter, N861MP, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Anthony, Florida. The pilot and passenger sustained minor injuries. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
According to the pilot he had departed a private residence and had climbed to about 700 ft agl when the helicopter started to shake violently. Shortly thereafter the low rotor rpm warning system came on, the pilot lowered the collective and entered an autorotation. During the autorotation, the pilot applied full throttle and the engine and rotor rpm recovered into the normal operating range. As the pilot initiated a climb the engine lost all power again and the pilot made an emergency landing in a field; the helicopter came to rest on its right side. 
The helicopter is being relocated to a secure location; a detailed examination of the engine and airframe is pending.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 15, 2026, about 1300 eastern daylight time, an experimental, amateur-built Zenith 601 HDS airplane, N601EZ, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Ripley Landing, West Virginia. The private pilot was seriously injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.

The pilot departed Jackson County Airport, Ravenswood, West Virginia (I18), with the intention of practicing touch and go landings at the airport. The pilot reported that during the left turn onto the downwind leg of the airport traffic pattern, the engine lost all power. The pilot turned the airplane towards the airport but did not have enough altitude to glide to it. The pilot made an emergency off field landing in a tree clearing about 1.2 miles south-southeast of the airport. Upon touchdown, the nose gear impacted terrain, the airplane then nosed over and came to rest inverted. The pilot was trapped under the wreckage until the following day when he was located by first responders about 0900.

The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to properly stow the motor in preparation for approach and landing that resulted in a loss of airspeed and an inadvertent aerodynamic stall and spin.
AnalysisNarrative:
The pilot of the electric motor glider stated that in preparation for decent and landing to the destination airport, he selected the system enable switch to off instead of selecting the motor mast position selector to down. The motor then windmilled, which resulted in the motor and mast losing power, and the glider quickly lost airspeed. The glider then entered an aerodynamic stall and spin. The pilot stated that in an attempt to recover from the spin, he pushed down on the control stick and applied rudder, but the glider pitched up violently. While in an unusual attitude and at a low altitude, the pilot was unable to regain control and deployed the ballistic parachute. During the deployment, the parachute rocket went through the right wing, but the parachute still deployed and the glider impacted terrain in an inverted attitude. The glider sustained substantial damage to the right wing. 
The pilot attributed the rapid loss of the glider’s airspeed due to the drag induced from the windmilling propeller and thought that the windmilling propeller also inhibited airflow over the vertical and horizontal stabilizer, which prevented recovery from the stall and spin. The pilot stated there was no mechanical malfunctions or failures with the glider that precluded normal operation.
