AnalysisNarrative: The flight instructor stated that student pilot was practicing off airport landings in the helicopter. After conducting a normal approach, they transitioned the helicopter into a hover about 2 to 3 ft above the ground. While at a hover, and with both the student pilot and the flight instructor touching the controls, the flight instructor turned his attention to clearing the tail rotor. While the flight instructor’s attention was focused outside the helicopter, the helicopter drifted to the left, descended, after which the left skid contacted the ground. The helicopter (dynamically) rolled on to its left side resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage, main rotor system, tail rotor system, and empennage. PrelimNarrative:
On August 14, 2026, about 1040 eastern daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Zenith Cruzer, N673BK, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Chatham, Massachusetts. The pilot and the pilot-rated passenger received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 flight test.
According to the pilot and the owner/builder of the airplane, the accident flight was the airplane’s fourth during its phase one testing.  The previous three flights were uneventful except for oil temperature anomalies. The owner/builder had adjusted the oil cooler position and the purpose of the accident flight was to verify whether repositioning the oil cooler improved the engine oil temperature readings.
The pilot stated that the accident flight was delayed a short time until wind conditions improved. After observing other aircraft operating in the airport traffic pattern, the pilot and the owner/builder decided to proceed with the flight. The preflight inspection, engine runup, and flight control checks were normal. Shortly after takeoff, the pilot reported that the left wing dipped, followed by the right wing, and that the airplane subsequently rocked laterally from side to side. The pilot announced to the owner/builder there was a problem and decided to land the airplane on the remaining runway. Video surveillance footage from the airport showed that the airplane impacted the runway in a left wing down attitude, after which the main landing gear collapsed and the nosewheel separated from the fuselage.
The wreckage was retained for further examination.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 17, 2026, about 1446 central daylight time, an Aviat Aircraft Inc A-1B airplane, N299CA, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Pilot Grove, Minnesota. The two pilots received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 aerial photography flight. 
The pilot in the rear seat stated they were conducting an aerial photography flight and had flown for about 5 ½ hours that day. During the flight, the front seat pilot was manipulating the flight controls and noted that the airplane was not responding normally. They observed that the left aileron had partially detached from the wing and the outboard end was hanging down. The front seat pilot executed an emergency landing to a field. During the landing, the airplane nosed over and sustained substantial damage to both wings and the empennage. 
Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that the left outboard aileron hinge bracket was fractured. The airplane was retained for further examination. 
A review of NTSB records revealed that the airplane was involved in a similar accident in 2017 involving an inflight failure of the left outboard aileron hinge bracket assembly.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s descent below the glidepath and collision with trees during a missed approach.
AnalysisNarrative: The instrument-rated pilot had planned a cross-country flight with an intermediate fuel stop. While enroute, he noted that the weather conditions at the planned fuel stop airport had deteriorated, so he elected to divert to another airport. While performing an RNAV instrument approach to the diversionary airport, the pilot reported that he entered instrument meteorological conditions and experienced “some disorientation.” He described that the airplane may have deviated left of course and descended below the glidepath. The pilot subsequently decided to initiate a missed approach and applied full engine power. During the initial climb, the airplane contacted treetops but continued to climb. The pilot observed damage to the left wing and declared an emergency with air traffic control. The air traffic controller then provided the pilot with radar vectors to another airport, where the pilot completed an instrument approach and landed without further incident. A postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that the wings and horizontal stabilizer were substantially damaged. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 19, 2026, at 1852 eastern daylight time, a Bell Helicopter Textron Canada 407, N873ST, and a Cessna 150H airplane, N23330, collided in flight near Carlisle, Pennsylvania. The two commercial pilots onboard the helicopter were seriously injured, and the helicopter was substantially damaged. The commercial pilot on board the airplane was fatally injured and the airplane was destroyed. The helicopter was operated by the Pennsylvania State Police (PSP) as a public aircraft. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
According to the PSP, the helicopter crew departed from Capital City Airport (CXY), Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and flew to Carlisle Airport (N94), Carlisle, Pennsylvania, about 15 nautical miles away, to conduct flight instruction training exercises at the airport. ADS-B flight track data obtained from the FAA revealed the helicopter crew flew a straight in approach to runway 28 at N94 and crossed about 50 ft above the runway threshold at 1851. The helicopter then slowly descended and transitioned into a hover taxi about 1,800 ft down the 4,008-ft-long runway before exiting the paved surface to the north over a grass-covered field.
While the helicopter was approaching the airport, ADS-B data showed that the airplane crossed over the airport to the northeast, then made left turns to enter a left crosswind leg to downwind leg of the traffic pattern for runway 28 (figure 1). A witness stated that he heard the airport Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF) communications between the helicopter flight crew and the airplane pilot; one of the helicopter pilots told the airplane pilot to extend his downwind. The airplane pilot acknowledged the communication. 

Figure 1 – ADS-B flight track data for the helicopter (green) and airplane (yellow) during their approaches to the airport.
During a postaccident interview, the flight instructor onboard the helicopter stated that they saw the airplane on the helicopter’s Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System first, then saw the airplane while it was on the crosswind leg of the airport traffic pattern. The flight instructor then made a radio call stating the helicopter’s position on final approach. The airplane pilot asked if they wanted him to extend his downwind, and the flight instructor responded, “yes, extend your downwind.” The airplane pilot acknowledged and stated that he was number two for landing. 
Airport surveillance video combined with ADS-B flight track data showed that the pilot turned onto the left base leg of the traffic pattern about 2,500 ft from the runway 28 threshold and continued his approach. Shortly after the pilot initiated the left turn onto base leg, ADS-B track data was lost. Airport surveillance video captured the remainder of the flight. 
There were three security cameras on the airport that captured the aircraft immediately before and during (figure 2) the approach of both aircraft. Timestamped airport security camera footage showed the helicopter on short final approach to runway 28. The helicopter crossed over the runway threshold while the airplane was on the left base leg. About 30 seconds later, the airplane crossed over the threshold as the helicopter was still over the runway. The airplane’s wings rocked to the left and right as the airplane flew low over the runway surface, and it appeared to make several lateral and vertical movements as it flew over the runway with the flaps extended. The airplane did not touch down on the runway. As the airplane approached the helicopter, the helicopter hovered off the runway and transitioned over the grass field, with its nose still oriented toward the departure end of runway 28 and parallel to the runway. The helicopter pilots stated that due to the helicopter’s position and orientation relative to the runway, they were unable to observe the approaching airplane, which was behind them. 

Figure 2: Airport security camera locations labeled A, B, and C, showing their orientation relative to the airplane and helicopter’s direction of travel down runway 28.
The airplane continued to fly along the runway with the wings rocking before it pitched up and began climbing. After the airplane reached the apex of its climb, about 1 1/2 wingspans above the runway, the right wing dropped and the airplane immediately turned right and descended towards the northwest. The helicopter was in a hover about 50 ft north of the runway when the approaching airplane’s wings rolled level, before it rapidly pitched up, and collided with the rear of the helicopter, striking the tail rotor and main rotor blades. About 8 seconds elapsed from the time the helicopter exited the runway surface until the collision. 
The following four still video images (figure 3) from two of the airport security cameras show the time, locations, orientation of the aircraft and their relative position to each other. 

Figure 3 Four still video images from cameras A and C showing the airplane and helicopter as they maneuvered in the vicinity of the runway. The airplane is circled in yellow, and the helicopter is circled in blue.
Following the collision, the helicopter’s main rotor blades and tail boom separated. The main wreckage of the helicopter, consisting of the entirety of the fuselage, cockpit, engine, and transmission remained relatively intact and fell onto its left side before coming to rest. 
During the collision, the airplane separated into four major sections; the engine compartment, wings, empennage, and lower fuselage were spread over a distance of about 250 ft along a magnetic heading of about 330°. Additional parts of the airplane were significantly fragmented and spread throughout the area in a fanlike pattern. 
All major portions of the helicopter and the airplane were accounted for at the accident site and recovered. Damage signatures to both aircraft including paint transfer marks, and cuts to the fuselages were indicative of a collision. Postaccident examination of both aircraft revealed no evidence of any preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation. During the onsite examination of the airplane, the flaps actuators were observed to be in the retracted position. 
The wreckage of both aircraft, along with avionics capable of recording digital data were recovered and retained for further examination.

On August 19, 2026, about 1920 central daylight time, a Para-Ski VX powered parachute, C-IFBY, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Westport, South Dakota. The pilot sustained serious injuries, passenger 1 sustained fatal injuries, and passenger 2 sustained minor injuries. The powered parachute was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
A witness reported that they observed the accident aircraft depart from a field towards the west. The witness looked away for about one minute, and when the witness looked back the aircraft had already impacted terrain. The aircraft impacted terrain, collided with a barbed wire fence, and came to rest on its side with substantial damage to the fuselage.
Initial reports revealed that the pilot was seated in the front seat with passenger 1 seated in his lap and passenger 2 was seated in the rear seat as seen in figure 1.

Figure 1. Seat configuration
The accident aircraft does not meet the requirements as outlined in Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 103 to be considered an ultralight vehicle. The aircraft fuel capacity exceeded 5 gallons and is configured for operation for more than a single occupant. The pilot holds an FAA remote pilot certificate for small unmanned aircraft systems.
The powered parachute was retained for further examination.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 20, 2026, about 1300 eastern daylight time, a Diamond Aircraft Ind Inc DA20-A1, N83RF, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Bristol, Maine. The pilot was fatally injured, and the pilot-rated passenger sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. 
The pilot-rated passenger reported that the flight originated from Brunswick Executive Airport (BXM), Brunswick, Maine, with intentions of overflying points of interest before landing at its intended destination of the Knox County Regional Airport (RKD), Rockland, Maine. About 20 minutes after departure, they observed a low engine oil pressure indication and the pilot elected to divert to RKD. Shortly thereafter, they experienced several “buffets” from the engine along with an odor of smoke in the cockpit, which was followed by a total loss of engine power. The pilot initiated a right turn and performed a forced landing on a state park road about 24 miles southwest of RKD. During the landing, the airplane traversed a grassy area, impacted trees and shoreline rocks, and then came to rest inverted in about 4 ft deep water along the Pemaquid Harbor shoreline. 
The identified touchdown point was three linear tire impressions in the grass about 50 ft in length, consistent with main and nose landing gear, about 40 ft from the road on a 220° magnetic course, and about 540 ft from the main wreckage. The airplane impacted a sign about 65 inches above ground level and 80 ft from the tire impressions. A green wingtip navigation light was observed at the base of the sign. The airplane then struck a raised wooden structure surrounding a horseshoe pit and two trees that were located about 40 ft apart near the shoreline (see figure 1). All major components of the airplane were located at the accident site. 
Figure 1. – Annotated Google Earth image of the accident site.
The airplane was recovered to a secure facility, and a postaccident examination was conducted. The left wing exhibited impact damage to its outboard leading-edge and aft wing root. The right wing was separated from the fuselage with impact damage noted to its outboard leading-edge. The flaps were observed fully extended, consistent with a landing configuration. Impact damage was noted to the top of the horizontal stabilizer. Rudder and elevator control continuity was established from the flight controls in the cockpit to the respective flight control surfaces in the empennage. Aileron control continuity was established from the flight controls in the cockpit to the left aileron and the right aileron impact separated control tube. The engine cowlings and canopy were fragmented. The pilot and copilot 4-point restraints remained attached and could be latched and unlatched without any anomalies. Both engine propeller blades were fractured with no rotational abrasions or leading-edge damage. 
The engine’s reduction gear box was fractured from impact forces. The crankshaft could not be rotated by hand. Examination of the engine revealed the No. 4 cylinder exhaust valve face was separated from the stem, and a hole was observed in the piston dome with impact damage noted to the interior of the cylinder and head. Residual oil was noted in the interior of the crankcase and about 2 quarts of oil was present in the reservoir. The oil pump rotated freely when actuated by hand. There was no evidence of an in-flight or postaccident fire.
The wreckage was retained for further examination.

On August 20, 2026, at about 1145 Alaska daylight time, a Cessna 441, N128EZ, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Cape Newenham, Alaska. The two pilots and six passengers were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 135 on-demand air taxi flight.

Radio communications between Anchorage Air Route Traffic Control Center (ARTCC) and the flight crew indicated that, following departure from Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport (ANC), Anchorage, Alaska, the flight crew established communications with the ARTCC while enroute to Cape Newenham LRRS Airport (PAEH), Cape Newenham, Alaska. At the time of departure, the most recent METAR from PAEH reported 10 statute miles (SM) visibility and cloud ceilings at 800 ft above ground level (agl). At about 1016, the flight crew received weather information for PAEH and requested the RNAV Runway 15 approach. The ARTCC subsequently cleared the flight crew to descend at their discretion to 6,000 ft mean sea level (msl).

At 1027, the controller cleared the flight crew to cross the RNAV (GPS) Runway 15 Initial Approach Fix (IAF), RRLND, at or above 5,000 ft msl and cleared the flight for the RNAV Runway 15 approach. The flight crew responded that they did not want to begin the approach at that time and requested holding instructions.  The controller subsequently cleared the flight crew to hold at RRLND with an expected further clearance (EFC) time of 1100. At 1043, the flight crew reported entering the hold at RRLND. The controller acknowledged the report and revised the EFC time to 1130, or earlier upon pilot request. At that time, the Automated Weather Observing System (AWOS) at PAEH reported the wind from 280° at 7 knots 1/4-mile visibility, patches of fog, and overcast 300 ft agl. 

At 1102, the flight crew requested and was subsequently cleared by the controller for the RNAV Runway 15 approach. At that time the PAEH AWOS reported 3 miles visibility, mist, and a broken ceiling at 300 ft agl. At 1114, the crew reported they were executing a missed approach, advised the controller that they were operating in visual meteorological conditions, and canceled their IFR clearance. At 1124, the flight crew again contacted ARTCC, reported that the weather conditions at PAEH had improved, and requested an IFR clearance for a second RNAV Runway 15 approach. After confirming the crew could maintain terrain and obstruction clearance to 4,500 ft msl, the controller assigned a transponder code, established radar identification, and cleared the flight for the RNAV Runway 15 approach via IVUXE upon reaching 4,500 ft msl.

Between 1127 and 1135, the flight crew coordinated with the controller regarding routing for a second RNAV Runway 15 approach. After initially requesting direct routing to IVUXE, the flight crew later requested routing via WAGEN. The controller subsequently cleared the flight crew, upon reaching 4,500 ft msl, to proceed direct to WAGEN, then IVUXE, and direct to PAEH. After reporting level at 4,500 ft msl and later established on the WAGEN-to-IVUXE transition, the flight crew was cleared for the RNAV Runway 15 approach and approved to change frequencies. At that time the PAEH AWOS reported 1/4 mile visibility, fog, and an overcast ceiling at 300 ft agl. No further radio communications were received from the flight crew.

According to preliminary ADS-B data, the airplane departed from runway 7L at ANC at 0911:54. After departure the airplane climbed to an altitude of about 625 ft msl and initiated a climbing right turn to a southwest heading. 

At 0924:29, the airplane climbed through an altitude of about 16,175 ft msl and entered a right turn to a westerly heading. The data showed the airplane continued climbing to flight level 280 while proceeding west toward PAEH. When the airplane was about 123 miles northeast of the Initial Approach Fix (IAF) RRLND, it began a descent. The airplane crossed RRLND at about 10,375 ft msl and subsequently performed a series of descending turns in the vicinity of the GPS fix, consistent with holding. 

At 1104:31, while at an altitude of about 4,400 ft msl, the airplane turned westbound toward the Intermediate Fix (IF) IVUXE. At 1107:31, the airplane approached IVUXE at about 2,100 ft msl and initiated a left turn toward the Final Approach Fix (FAF) KRSSS. The last recorded altitude north of KRSSS was about 1,025 ft msl prior to ADS-B contact being lost at 1110:13. When ADS-B resumed at 1111:16, the airplane continued on the final approach, until contact was lost at 1111:40, the airplane was about 2.3 miles north of the Missed Approach Point (MAP) CFKMW at an altitude of about 425 ft msl. (See figure 1.)


Figure 1: Preliminary ADS-B flight track between 1040:28 and 1111:40, depicting the airplane’s hold near RRLND, its turn to the south near IVUXE, and the last data point between KRSSS and CFKMW.
ADS-B contact was reestablished at 1114:21 while the airplane was on a northerly heading at about 1,300 ft msl. It continued northbound past IVUXE and approached FELTI (located about 21 miles north of IVUXE) at about 2,100 ft msl. The airplane then completed a 180° left turn to a southerly heading toward IVUXE. At 1130:04, the airplane had climbed to an altitude of 3,925 ft msl and had initiated a right turn to the west, as it approached the WAGEN IAF. Between 1132:40 and 1135:56, there were several periods where ADS-B contact was lost. When ADS-B contact resumed at 1135:56, the airplane was at 4,425 ft msl on an easterly heading toward IVUXE.

At 1138:15, the airplane was at an altitude of about 2,850 ft msl when it initiated a right turn near IVUXE. At 1141:14, the airplane crossed KRSSS at about 2,400 ft msl and continued southbound along the approach course. At 1143:18, the airplane crossed the MAP CFKMW at about 1,000 ft msl. The airplane continued beyond CFKMW, while it descended to about 600 ft msl, until ADS-B contact was lost at 1143:51. At that time, the airplane was about 1.3 miles north of the runway 15 threshold at PAEH. (See figure 2.)


Figure 2: Preliminary ADS-B flight track between 1114:21 and 1143:51, depicting the airplane flying northbound after executing a missed approach. The airplane subsequently initiated a second approach.
A review of the RNAV (GPS) RWY 15 instrument approach plate, PAEH, dated 09 July 2026, showed Lateral Navigation (LNAV) Minimum Descent Altitude (MDA) as 1320 ft and 3 miles visibility. The MAP was located 2.2 miles north of the runway 15 threshold. Two cautions were noted: “1) Rwy located on slope of 2306’ mountain. High terrain both sides and S end of rwy.” and “2) Successful go-around improbable if initiated past the MAP.” 

Technicians who were stationed at the facility near PAEH provided statements to investigators. One technician stated that he performed a routine inspection of the runway at about 0900 on the morning of the accident. As part of this inspection, he drove the length of the runway to check the condition of the runway surface and to ensure there was no wildlife within 100 yards of the runway. At that time, he did not observe any anomalies or foreign objects on the runway and did not see any wildlife. The technician noted that he typically performs another runway inspection to ensure the runway is clear before an airplane is expected to land; however, he was unable to complete a runway inspection for the accident airplane’s arrival because of thick fog that blanketed the runway.

According to the second technician, the facility featured a dedicated weather building located about 0.3 miles west of the approach end of runway 15. The building housed an aviation radio and terminal that displayed weather information from the AWOS equipment, which was located near the runway. In addition, charts and photographs in the weather building provided the distances and elevations of nearby landmarks.

ProbableCause: The glider’s encounter with atmospheric conditions where lift was not sufficient to maintain flight.
AnalysisNarrative: The pilot of the glider was on a local flight and reported that the thermal lift began to dissipate. The glider’s empennage separated from the fuselage and was substantially damaged. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the glider that would have precluded normal operation.

ProbableCause: The flight instructor’s failure to maintain airplane control during landing in gusting wind conditions.
AnalysisNarrative: The flight instructor reported that during the instructional flight, a thunderstorm developed in the area so they returned to the airport.  About five miles from the airport, he obtained the weather information and noted the wind was from 210° at 7 knots, but the wind speed increased as they approached the airport. On short final the airplane encountered an unexpected windshear, which resulted in a significant sink rate. Airport surveillance video of the accident revealed that the airplane touched down with the right main landing gear first, then veered to the left side of the runway and into the grass. As he applied full power to go around, a gust of wind lifted the right wing, the left wing struck the ground, and the airplane spun left about 360°. The airplane sustained substantial damage to both wings and the fuselage. The flight instructor reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 18, 2026 at 1100 eastern daylight time, a Cessna 172L, N3866Q, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Micanopy, Florida. The flight instructor and student pilot were uninjured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.
The flight instructor reported that during the power recovery to a power off stall the student pilot was having trouble pushing the throttle back in during the recovery portion of the procedure. The flight instructor attempted to demonstrate the maneuver and when he attempted the power on recovery the movement of the throttle did not increase the engine power. When the throttle was pushed in it would forcibly push back out on its own. They ran through their checklist as they attempted to return to the runway. The engine continued to run at idle speed as they made a force landing to a dry lakebed. During the landing rollout the nose wheel traveled into a marshy area and the airplane nosed over. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the wings.
An inspection of the throttle control system is pending.

ProbableCause: The misfuelling of the airplane by the refueler. Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s failure to verify that the airplane had been properly fueled prior to departing on the accident flight.
AnalysisNarrative:
The pilot of the reciprocating, multi-engine airplane reported that, after takeoff while climbing to altitude, the #1 cylinder on the right engine was running hot. He leveled the airplane at 5,000 mean sea level (msl), but the cylinder continued to run hot, so he elected to feather the propeller and shut down the engine. As he attempted to navigate to an airport, he noticed that the other engine was beginning to deteriorate and he was no longer able to maintain altitude. He attempted to increase power on the remaining engine but about 2 miles from the airport he performed a forced landing to a cornfield. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the right engine mount, fuselage, and empennage as a result.
A first responder on scene sampled fuel from one of the airplane’s fuel tanks with a paper towel and reported that the fuel did not have any color to it. She also reported that the fuel smelled like diesel fuel. A postaccident interview with the fueler at the departure airport confirmed that he had topped off the airplane with “pre-mixed Jet-A.” The airport manager at the departure airport confirmed that the fueler used Jet-A fuel when filling the airplane. A fuel receipt was provided by the airport manager, and was signed by the pilot, that showed the airplane had been fueled with 145 gallons of Jet-A.
In an interview with the pilot, he reported that he did not specifically tell the fueler that he wanted 100LL in the airplane. He also stated that he did read the fuel receipt after fueling and that they “wanted to get home” so they “got in the airplane and left.” The pilot did not inspect or sample fuel from the airplane’s tanks after the fuel was added.

ProbableCause: The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during the final approach in variable and gusting wind conditions. Contributing to the accident were localized wind effects associated with mountainous terrain and with nearby convective activity.
AnalysisNarrative:
During an approach to a grass airstrip in mountainous terrain, the airplane encountered variable and gusting wind conditions near the runway environment. The initial attempt to land on runway 27 resulted in a go-around after the airplane encountered an estimated 17 knot tailwind. The pilot then maneuvered the airplane for a landing on runway 09.
The pilot reported that the airplane was stabilized on final approach to runway 09 with full flaps and an airspeed of about 65 knots. During short final a gust from the right displaced the airplane left of the runway centerline. The pilot was unable to correct for the displacement before the left wing struck trees adjacent to the runway which resulted in a loss of control and impact with terrain. The pilot reported that this was his first flight into the airstrip.
A witness reported that wind conditions increased from calm to about 15 knots gusting to 25 knots during the airplane's initial approach to runway 27 and that thunder was audible in the vicinity of the airstrip. The witness observed the airplane left of the intended approach path before it struck trees north of the runway centerline.
Weather review shows active convective activity near the accident site, including a convective SIGMET for thunderstorms over the state. Radar imagery at the time of the accident depicted precipitation echoes about 6 miles southeast of the airstrip. Although the forecast winds aloft were light, localized effects associated with nearby convective activity, including turbulence, downdrafts, outflow winds, and rapidly changing wind conditions, likely existed near the airstrip at the time of the accident.
The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, both wings, and the empennage. The pilot reported that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 26, 2026 about 1317 Alaska daylight time, a Piper PA-24-260 airplane, N9485P, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Seldovia, Alaska. The pilot and three passengers were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot and three passengers departed from Merrill Field Airport (PAMR), Anchorage, Alaska, for a day flight to Seldovia Airport (PASO), Seldovia, Alaska. A witness at the Seldovia airport heard the airplane approaching to land on runway 16 and the airplane appeared to be coming in fast. He then heard a series of bounces which sounded hard and abnormal. The first bounce was loud and not a normal touchdown sound. He heard a second bounce which also sounded hard and abnormal. He visually saw the third bounce and believed that the nosewheel hit the ground first. He then heard the engine go to full throttle. He stated that the aircraft pitched up very high and possibly had a tail strike. A witness working with heavy equipment near the end of the runway saw the airplane and noted the airplane was unusually low to the ground just past the end of the runway. He further noted that the accident airplane had attempted to land in the opposite direction of other airplanes that had been landing. Multiple ground witnesses reported seeing the airplane unusually low to the ground, the engine being very loud, and the airplane impacting a tree before descending into the water.  
The FAA’s chart supplement for the airport notes that surface of the Seldovia Airport runway is gravel and the length is 1,845 ft. The slope to clear obstructions for runway 16 is 11:1. The supplement notes 158 ft trees, 1,735 ft from runway 16 and 110 ft left of the centerline. For runway 34, the supplement notes an 89 ft tree, 995 ft from the runway, and 140 ft right of the centerline.
The Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) weather station at the airport at the time of the accident was reporting wind from 020 at 5 knots with wind gusts at 9 knots.  
The airplane came to rest about 2,200 ft from the end of runway 16 into the Seldovia Slough. A detailed wreckage examination is pending.

On August 27, 2026, about 1051 eastern daylight time, a Piper PA-18A 150, N2368P, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near New Smyrna Beach, Florida. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 banner tow flight.
According to the pilot, he conducted a normal preflight inspection in preparation for banner towing operations. During the inspection, he noted that the engine oil quantity was one quart low. He added one quart of oil and completed the remainder of the preflight inspection. The pilot confirmed that the fuel tanks were full and reported no other anomalies.
After takeoff, the pilot completed a successful banner pickup. He reported climbing to approximately 1,000 ft before reaching the shoreline. As the airplane crossed the shoreline, the pilot turned north and initiated a descent. While descending through about 600 ft above ground level (agl), the pilot began adding engine power to level off at 500 ft agl. When he advanced the throttle, he heard a loud pop, followed by a total loss of engine power.
While maintaining control of the airplane, the pilot determined that the beach was too crowded to safely conduct a forced landing. He elected to perform a forced landing to the water instead. The airplane touched down on the water and subsequently nosed over, coming to rest inverted. 
The wreckage was retained for further examination.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 30, 2026, about 1250 eastern daylight time, a Consolidated Aeronautics Inc., Lake LA-4-200, N6185V, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Ithaca, New York. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
According to preliminary ADS-B data received from the FAA, the airplane departed Ithaca Tompkins International Airport (ITH), Ithaca, New York about 1156. The flight track data was consistent with the airplane performing low approaches or landings at multiple lakes during the flight. According to FAA air traffic control audio recordings provided by the FAA, the pilot contacted ITH air traffic control tower, and reported that he was 8 miles west of the airport. The pilot was instructed by the controller to report when the airplane was 4 miles from the airport. At 1233:01 the final segment of the flight track showed the airplane began a gradual descent from 2,300 ft mean sea level (msl) at 113 knots ground speed.  At 1233:30 the airplane continued its descent through 2,200 feet msl and began a 180º right turn and had decelerated to 87 knots ground speed.  At 1234:18 the airplane continued descending through 1,500 ft msl and stabilized at 61 knots ground speed.  At 1234:25 the last track data point showed the airplane on a westerly ground track, at 1,401 ft msl (about 300 ft above the elevation of ITH), and 61 knots ground speed.  
The wreckage was located in a wooded, rural area at the end of a gravel driveway. The airplane came to rest in a nose-down attitude, and all major components of the airplane were accounted for at the accident site. The final approach heading was about 262º magnetic. Broken branches were observed in a tree that was about 40 ft high and 120 ft before the initial ground impact point. 
The airplane fuselage was a hull-type designed for water landings. The nose of the airplane was substantially damaged, with aft crushing and crumpling. The empennage remained attached to the fuselage and sustained no damage. The engine was mounted above the fuselage on a structural pylon located aft of the cabin and between the wings and drove a two-blade pusher propeller. The forward engine cowlings were impact-fractured and cracked.
The outboard section of the right wing was impact fractured and crushed along the leading edge and contained embedded vegetation. The left wing exhibited aft crushing along the leading edge, buckling at the midpoint, and was torn at the rivet line above the left-wing float. 
The instrument panel was fragmented. Flight control continuity was established from the flight control surfaces through impact-fractured control tubes and cables to the cockpit area. The fuel valve was positioned to ON, and fuel line continuity was established from the main fuel tank to the engine.
The airplane fuel system consisted of a bladder-type 40-gallon main tank under the pylon and two 7-gallon auxiliary tanks located in each of the wing floats.  The tanks were intact with no evidence of breaching. No fuel was present in the main tank or auxiliary tanks. The finger screen was observed at the bottom of the main tank, was clear of debris, and was unobstructed.  
The three electrically-operated boost pumps were tested with a 12-volt power source and operated normally. The fuel lines were tested for restriction by blowing air through them from the main tank to the engine they were found to be unobstructed.  After wing removal, the auxiliary fuel lines from the wing float tanks to the fuselage were tested for restriction by blowing air through them and they were found to be unobstructed; however, the auxiliary fuel lines could not be tested from the fuselage to the main tank
Mechanical continuity of the engine was established by rotating the propeller by hand.  Thumb compression and suction were confirmed on all cylinders during post-accident examination of the engine. The engine was equipped with two standard magnetos that remained secured in their housing and both produced spark on all the leads when tested. Oil was present in the oil sump, and no contamination or metal particles were present inside the oil filter. Trace amounts of fuel were observed within the engine-driven fuel pump and fuel servo inlet line. No fuel was observed in the flow divider. All of the fuel injection nozzle lines were secure and the injection nozzle lines and nozzles were unobstructed.  
The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 31, 2026, about 1131 Pacific daylight time, a Mooney M20C, N2783W, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Hood River, Oregon. The pilot and flight instructor were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.
A witness reported that the airplane was based at Jernstedt Airfield (4S2), Hood River, Oregon, and was conducting a local flight approximately 10 miles southwest of the airport while maneuvering in the Parkdale Valley area. One witness reported observing the airplane perform several maneuvers characterized as “aerobatic-type tricks” before it entered a nose-down attitude and collided with terrain. Additional witnesses stated that the two pilots were conducting stall-practice maneuvers as part of a flight review at the time of the accident.
The accident site was located on sloping terrain at an elevation of approximately 1,502 ft mean sea level (msl). The wreckage came to rest atop an agricultural debris pile in an approximate 30° nose-down attitude on a magnetic heading of about 220° and resulted in a crater measuring approximately 5 ft in diameter and 3 ft in depth beneath the wreckage.
The aft fuselage and empennage remained largely intact but exhibited downward bending aft of the passenger compartment. All major structural components of the airplane were located at the accident site, and the wreckage debris was confined to an area within approximately 50 ft of the main wreckage. The first identified point of contact (FIPC) was the trees directly above the wreckage. A displaced section of fence adjacent to the wreckage had damage consistent with contact from the airplane's right wingtip. 
The wreckage was subsequently recovered to a secure facility for further examination.

On August 28, 2026, about 0145 Pacific daylight time, an IAI 1124A Westwind airplane, Canadian registration C-GIAW, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident at Harry Reid International Airport (LAS), Las Vegas, Nevada. The two pilots, and three medical crew members were not injured. The airplane was operated by SkyCare Air Ambulance and Charter as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 129 air ambulance flight. 
According to the pilot, during the takeoff roll, the airplane’s left main tire burst when the airplane reached about 130 knots indicated, which was followed by an audible “thud” sound.  The airplane then veered left and the pilot retarded the throttle levers, deployed the idle thrust reversers and pushed hard on the brakes and right rudder. In an attempt to regain control of the airplane the pilot released the left brake. However, the airplane exited the left side of the runway and traversed the runway safety area before it came to rest in an adjacent taxiway. The left main landing gear collapsed, and the right tire blew during the accident sequence. The runway surface revealed two parallel tire marks to the left of the runway centerline about midfield that were accompanied by irregular tire signatures and shredded tire material and brake components. The airplane’s lower fuselage sustained substantial damage. 
The airplane was recovered to the ramp area at LAS for further examination.

The pilot, who was also the owner of the airplane, stated that he was departing from J-22 Ranch Airport (16FL), Milton, Florida, after the completion of some avionics related maintenance. The engine run-up was normal, and the magneto test was within the normal range. He was performing a soft field takeoff from the grass runway with “1 notch” of flap extension. After the airplane lifted off the runway and climbed about 30 ft, the engine lost partial power and the rpm dropped from 2,400 to 1,700 rpm. He then leveled the airplane about 200 ft above the ground to gain airspeed, but the airspeed did not increase. The pilot attempted to land in a peanut field; however, the airplane contacted treetops prior to the field and impacted the ground, which resulted in substantial damage to both wings. 
The wreckage was retained for further examination.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 30, 2026, about 0905 Pacific daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Zenith CH701, N701WJ, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident at Byron Airport (C83), Byron, California. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.

The airplane had previously sustained damage in an accident at Byron in 2019 (see NTSB report WPR20LA035). It was subsequently repaired by the pilot, with work including reconstruction of the aft fuselage, construction of a new rudder, and fabrication of a new set of wings.

Following completion of the repairs, engine and systems testing was conducted. The day before the accident, additional taxi tests, high-speed runs, and takeoff tests with immediate landings were performed at Byron, with no anomalies reported.

On the day of the accident, the pilot taxied the airplane to the run-up area following which he conducted two additional cycles of high-speed taxi and takeoff tests on runway 23. After observing normal operation, the pilot elected to takeoff and remain in the traffic pattern. While climbing through approximately 300 ft agl, the pilot observed a decrease in engine rpm followed by a total loss of power. The pilot reported that his attention was focused on returning to the airport for landing and he did not have sufficient time to troubleshoot the loss of engine power.

The pilot maneuvered the airplane toward the airport and landed in a grass area adjacent to the runway. During the landing roll, the airplane struck a ditch and nosed over.

The airplane sustained substantial to the leading edges of both wings, left-wing strut, rudder and aft fuselage.

The airplane was retained for further examination.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s loss of directional control during the rejected takeoff, which resulted in a runway excursion. Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s decision to abort the takeoff after the airplane had accelerated above its normal rotation speed. Also contributing to the accident was the flight school’s non-standard engine break-in takeoff procedure.
AnalysisNarrative:
The pilot stated that the purpose of the flight was to conduct the break-in of a newly installed engine and that this was his first engine break-in flight. Before departure, the pilot received a briefing from the chief flight instructor regarding the engine break-in procedures outlined in the school’s Engine Break-In Checklist.
The pilot stated that during the takeoff roll, about 900 ft down the runway, he realized that the throttle was not in the takeoff position and advanced it full forward. About halfway down the runway, he evaluated that he would not reach his intended rotation speed of 75 knots and aborted the takeoff. During the aborted takeoff, at 60 knots, the airplane briefly became airborne before settling back onto the runway. The airplane continued decelerating, but departed the runway surface near the runway 36 hold-short line and came to rest in a ditch.
The airplane sustained substantial damage to the engine mount. The pilot reported that there were no pre-accident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.
The chief pilot and the owner/operator reported that the operator's engine break-in procedures required pilots to rotate at 75 knots and establish a shallow climb for better engine cooling. A review of the pilot operating handbook shows that a normal takeoff rotation speed is about 55 knots. A review of the Lycoming Service Instruction No. 1427C, Reciprocating Engine Break-In and Oil Consumption, directs operators to conduct a full-power takeoff in accordance with the applicable POH and does not specify an increased rotation speed for engine break-in operations.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 27, 2026, about 1625 eastern daylight time, a Hawker Beechcraft Corporation 400A airplane, N199TT, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Newark, New Jersey. The airline transport pilot and commercial pilot were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 positioning flight.
The airplane departed from Nantucket Memorial Airport (ACK), Nantucket, Massachusetts, destined for Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), Newark, New Jersey. At 1615 the airplane was vectored to the ILS runway 22L approach for landing at EWR. According to the pilots, the automated terminal information service (ATIS) was reporting 1 1/2 miles visibility with thunderstorms and rain showers. The captain, who was the pilot monitoring during the initial approach observed and called out the runway approach lighting and runway environment. He then took over the controls from the copilot and continued flying the approach. During short final approach, a sudden heavy rain shower appeared, and both pilots lost sight of the runway.  
According to the pilots, the captain executed a go-around; however, the airplane continued to descend. The copilot stated they experienced possible wind shear and a loss of airspeed. The airplane’s right wing dropped, dragged across the runway surface and impacted several runway edge lights. The impact resulted in substantial damage to the right wing leading edge and right flap; the wing sustained dents and a puncture to the leading edge. The right flap could not be fully retracted and remained partially deployed. The airplane subsequently climbed and the pilots diverted to Morristown Municipal Airport (MMU), Morristown, New Jersey, about 15 nautical miles to the northwest. During the flight to MMU, the pilots declared an emergency due to flight control issues after which the airplane landed without further incident.  
The airplane’s cockpit voice recorder (CVR), Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGPWS), and nonvolatile memory from other avionics were secured for download.

PrelimNarrative:
On September 1, 2026, about 1142 Pacific daylight time, a Cessna 560XL airplane, N562JL, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Porterville, California. The two pilots sustained minor injuries, and the four passengers were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 135 business flight.
A review of ADS-B data provided by the FAA showed that the airplane departed Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK), Oakland, California, about 1106, and flew on a southeast track to its planned destination of Porterville Municipal Airport (PTV) Porterville, California. The data showed that the airplane reached a maximum cruise altitude of about 25,000 ft mean sea level (msl). The airplane lined up for final approach to runway 12. On about a 1 nautical mile final approach, the airplane’s altitude was about 1,000 ft msl and the groundspeed was about 245 knots. The last data point, about 1,800 ft from the runway threshold, showed the airplane about 600 ft msl, with a groundspeed of about 234 knots.
According to the pilot, about 30 miles from the destination, the Los Angeles Air Route Traffic Control Center (ARTCC) controller cleared them to descend to 16,000 ft msl. The controller then cleared them to descend to 9,000 ft msl followed by a descent to 6,000 ft msl. About 10 miles from PTV, they were about 5,000 ft msl and 250 knots. The controller then advised them of the airport’s location and the pilot cancelled his instrument flight rules clearance. On the visual straight in approach, the airplane was estimated to cross the runway threshold between 225-250 knots and floated about a third to halfway down the runway. Upon touchdown, the captain applied heavy braking. The airplane continued down the 5,960 ft long runway and then exited the end of the runway, breached a fence, crossed two roads, and came to rest in a field. The pilots and passengers safely egressed though the airplane’s main door. 
Postaccident examination revealed that the airplane’s wings sustained substantial damage. The airplane wreckage was recovered to a secure facility.

AirportName: Midland International Air and Space Port
ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during landing in gusting wind conditions.
AnalysisNarrative:
The pilot of the tailwheel equipped airplane reported that he performed a three-point landing in gusting wind conditions. During the landing roll, the wind lifted the right wing and he attempted to correct with right aileron, but the right wing struck the ground. The airplane then skidded to the left and he attempted to correct with rudder before the left wing struck the ground. The airplane nosed down and came to rest on the runway. The airplane sustained substantial damage to both wings and the top of the fuselage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. 
The pilot reported that he and other pilots in the area observed dust devils during the flight. Based on the observed conditions, it is possible that that airplane encountered a dust devil during landing.

PrelimNarrative:
On September 1, 2026, at 1220 Pacific daylight time, a Cessna 150E, N3037J, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Siler, Washington. The pilot and pilot rated passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot reported that he was conducting a cross-country flight from Jefferson County International Airport (0S9), Port Townsend, Washington to Packwood Airport (55S), Packwood, Washington. The pilot established a cruise altitude of 5,500 ft mean sea level above a cloud layer. Once the airplane was no longer above clouds and was approaching their intended destination, he initiated a descent, reduced engine power, and applied carburetor heat. Subsequently, the pilot noticed a 300 rpm decrease and that the engine was running rough. He advanced the throttle; however, engine rpm did not increase. The pilot attempted to restore engine power by enriching the mixture, cycling the magnetos, and cycling the carburetor heat. Despite his attempts, the pilot was unable to restore engine power and initiated a forced landing to a riverbed since the airplane was unable to maintain altitude. During the landing sequence, the airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage.
The airplane was retained for further examination.

PrelimNarrative:
On September 1, 2026, at 2225 central daylight time, a Cessna 210K, N9420M, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Dawson Springs, Kentucky. The private pilot and passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot reported that about 10 minutes after departing from Madisonville Regional Airport (2I0), Madisonville, Kentucky, while climbing through about 4,500 ft mean sea level (msl) he heard a bang. Subsequently the engine began to shake and vibrate severely. The pilot continued that after the bang the engine “lost useful power but initially continued running.” He looked at his oil pressure and noted that it had dropped to zero, and multiple exhaust gas temperature (EGT) and cylinder head temperature (CHT) readings were dropping. The pilot attempted to glide to and land at Tradewater Airport (8M7), Dawson Springs, Kentucky. Because the airport was not equipped with airport lighting, and the pilot was unable to locate the airport in the dark.
About 2,800 ft msl the pilot lowered the landing gear and selected a road to conduct the forced landing. During the landing the airplane impacted a power pole before landing on the roadway. During the landing roll the airplane contacted a guardrail and another utility pole which resulted in substantial damage to both wings, the horizontal stabilizer and elevator.
Postaccident examination of the engine revealed that the crankcase was breached, with a broken connecting rod visible near the No. 6 cylinder. The airplane was recovered and retained for further examination.

On September 3, 2026, about 0815 eastern daylight time, an experimental, amateur-built Evolution airplane, N305PV, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Tampa, Florida. The commercial pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.

According to preliminary information obtained from the FAA, an instrument flight rules (IFR) flight plan was filed for the accident flight departing from Tampa Executive Airport (VDF), Tampa, Florida, with a destination of Elizabeth City Regional Airport (ECG), Elizabeth City, North Carolina. Review of air traffic control data revealed that the pilot acknowledged and correctly read back his IFR clearance and takeoff instructions. The instructions were to fly runway heading (050°) to 2,000 ft and expect 17,000 ft, 10 minutes after departure. No further communications were received from the accident airplane.  

Review of ADS-B data and security video revealed that the airplane lifted off and turned left, approximately halfway down the 5,000-ft-long runway, at a groundspeed about 80 knots. The airplane flew a 180° left turn in a nose-high, steep left bank, before it descended nose-down into terrain. 
 
The wreckage was located in a wooded area of a state water management facility, about 1/3-mile northwest of the touchdown zone for runway 5 at VDF. A debris path was observed, originating with severed tree branches, followed by ground scars, and then terminating at the main wreckage. The debris path was approximately 70 ft-long, on a magnetic course of 220°, and at a descent angle about 35° through the trees. The wreckage came to rest inverted, on a magnetic heading of 310°, and a majority of the airplane’s composite airframe was consumed by a postcrash fire.

All major components of the airplane were identified. The engine remained attached to the firewall at the front of the wreckage. Three of the five composite propeller blades remained attached to the hub. The inboard sections of both wings were located behind the engine. The empennage was consumed by fire with the exception of a rudder counterweight and pieces of the rudder that were located underneath the main wreckage. 

The pilot held a commercial pilot certificate with ratings for airplane single engine land, airplane single engine sea, and instrument airplane. He was operating under the provisions of BasicMed with his most recent examination and course completed on April 25, 2026. Review of training records revealed that he reported 1,203 total hours of flight experience when he began initial transition training for the make and model airplane on August 26, 2025. 

The airplane was assembled from a kit in 2020 and issued an FAA experimental airworthiness certificate. It was powered by a Pratt and Whitney PT6A-135A, 550-horsepower turboprop engine, driving a five-blade constant speed Hartzell propeller. The airplane’s most recent condition inspection was completed on August 26, 2026. At that time, the airframe and engine had accumulated 581 hours since new.

The wreckage was retained for further examination.

PrelimNarrative:
On September 3, 2026, about 0932 mountain standard time, a Bell OH-58, N480FT, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Deer Valley, Arizona. The pilots did not sustain any injuries. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.
The helicopter instructor reported he and a pilot-rated student departed from Phoenix Deer Valley Airport, Phoenix, Arizona to practice approaches, hovering autorotations, and autorotations with a power recovery in the local area. After completing the approaches and a hovering autorotation without incident, the instructor landed the helicopter and briefed the student about the autorotation with a power recovery procedure. 
Shortly after, the instructor and the student both demonstrated a successful autorotation with a power recovery. With the instructor on the controls and the helicopter about 500 ft above the ground (agl) and 70 knots indicating, the instructor initiated the third autorotation. The instructor noted that the entry was smooth and announced the main rotor rpm settled around 100% and that the N1 needle was around 62%, at idle engine power. About 200 ft agl and 60 knots, the instructor rolled the throttle to full power and joined the rotor rpm needle with the engine's rpm needle. 
As the helicopter crossed about 50 ft agl, the instructor initiated a flare and about 10-15 ft agl, he applied slight aft cyclic to slow the descent rate and terminate the recovery to a 3-5 ft agl hover. During the aft pitch control input, the low rotor RPM warning horn became audible and the instructor noted that he did not receive an engine response after he increased the throttle setting. The instructor quickly raised the collective lever to cushion the landing; however, the helicopter continued its descent and impacted terrain. Subsequently, the main rotor system separated from the mast and the helicopter sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, main rotor system, and drive train. 
The airplane was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.

On September 3, 2026, about 1518 mountain daylight time, a Cessna T206H airplane, N919CW, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Dunton, Colorado. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The flight was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 aerial survey flight.
According to the operator the pilot and camera operator departed Grand Junction Regional Airport (GJT) Grand Junction, Colorado, completed their survey work and were returning to Belen Regional Airport (BRG) Belen, New Mexico, about 300 nautical miles south-southeast. The pilot was receiving VFR flight following from Denver Center and had been advised radio coverage may be intermitted due to the mountainous terrain. Review of preliminary automatic dependent system broadcast (ADS-B) data revealed the airplane departed GJT about 1341 and conducted aerial survey operations for about 45 minutes and then proceeded southeast between about 8,500 to 10,900 ft mean sea level (msl). 
The pilot’s route of flight took them slightly east of Dolores Peak, a 13,289 ft mountain with a ridgeline that extends from the peak to the east. On the flight earlier in the day from BRG to GJT the airplane passed over a ridgeline about 1.5 miles east of Dolores Peak, about 500 ft above ground level (agl). As the airplane approached Dolores Peak on the return flight, about 2 minutes from the ridgeline the airplane was about 500 ft agl and 101 knots. About 1 minute later and 1 mile from the accident site the airplane was 50 ft agl and 80 knots. At 1518 the airplane made a slight right turn and impacted trees and terrain. The final ADS-B target was located above the accident site. A hiker in the area stated that it was windier than normal the day of the accident.

Figure 1 Preliminary Flight Track Data; Final segment of the accident flight track of N919CW with track details.
The airplane impacted heavily wooded rising terrain in a wings level attitude at an elevation of 10,770 ft msl and was orientated on a 300° magnetic heading. The debris path was about 340 ft long and contained all major components of the airplane. The initial tree strike separated the left horizontal stabilizer. The left wing came to rest near the cockpit and fuselage. The right wing came to rest about 25 ft beyond the main wreckage. Flight control continuity was partially established; complete continuity could not be confirmed due to impact and thermal damage. Portions of the flight control cables were fragmented due to a large tree trunk; the breaks were consistent with impact overload. The engine was separated from its mounts and was located near the main wreckage and exhibited thermal damage. The propeller was separated from the engine; two of the three propeller blades were observed. One blade was straight, the other exhibited minor s-bending with a deep trailing edge gouge about mid-span of the de-ice boot. 
The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.

On September 3, 2026, at 2004 eastern daylight time, a Piper PA-28-180, N7635W, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Dallas, Georgia. The flight instructor and student pilot were seriously injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.
The student pilot and flight instructor reported that the purpose of the flight was to perform practice takeoffs and landings at Paulding Northwest Atlanta Airport (PUJ), Dallas, Georgia. The student pilot arrived at the airport and performed a preflight inspection of the airplane. He sampled the fuel and found no contaminants, then checked its quantity with a fuel stick. He also checked the engine oil quantity and reported there were 6 quarts indicated on the oil dipstick. The flight instructor stated that he also checked the fuel and oil on the airplane and noted that there was nothing abnormal with the airplane. 
They then started the airplane and taxied to runway 13 for departure from PUJ. The student and flight instructor both stated that before departure, they performed an engine runup and did not notice anything abnormal. After departure they performed a series of uneventful touch-and-go landings at PUJ. During the accident touch-and-go, on initial climb the engine “cut out.” The flight instructor reported the airplane’s nose pitched down and the engine rpm abruptly dropped, but the propeller continued rotating. The student pilot reported that the flight instructor took control of the airplane and intended to land on a nearby road. Unable to reach that road, the flight instructor performed a forced landing in a densely wooded area. 
Preliminary review of ADS-B data showed that shortly after crossing the departure end of runway 13, and about 175 ft above ground level, the airplane turned left to the northeast. The airplane stopped climbing, continued to the northeast toward a road, and began descending. Just south of the road, the airplane turned east. Shortly thereafter ADS-B data showed no additional movement of the airplane. 
An on-scene examination by an FAA inspector found the airplane fuselage laying on its right side, with substantial damage, and both wings separated and suspended in trees. The airplane was equipped with avionics that were capable of recording flight data. They were recovered and sent to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory for data download.  
The airplane’s most recent 100-hour inspection occurred on September 1, 2026. The accident flight was the fifth flight after that inspection.
The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.

On September 2, 2026, about 2007 central daylight time, a Six Chuter SR7XL experimental light-sport powered parachute, N5617X, was involved in an accident near Amery, Wisconsin. The pilot was seriously injured. The powered parachute was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot was conducting a post maintenance test flight after he had just completed a condition inspection on the powered parachute. During the inspection he had changed several hoses. The pilot told a witness the engine just quit. The powered parachute impacted trees while attempting to land and the pilot was seriously injured.
The powered parachute was recovered and retained for further investigation.
