PrelimNarrative:
On September 5, 2026, about 1345 Pacific daylight time, a Grumman AA-5, N6510L, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Fresno, California. The pilot and 3 passengers were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
Surveillance video showed that the pilot and passengers boarded the airplane at the airplane owner’s residence at Sierra Sky Park Airport (E79), Fresno, California, and shortly after taxied to the approach end of runway 30. Another video showed the airplane begin its takeoff roll and subsequently abort the takeoff about halfway down the runway. The airplane continued down the runway, turned around at the departure end and taxied back to the runway approach end. At this time, the pilot texted the owner about a radio problem she was experiencing. About two minutes later the pilot taxied the airplane to the owner’s residence, which was located on the airport. According to text messages, the owner contacted a mechanic to troubleshoot the radio issue and a few minutes later the mechanic approached the airplane after it had been shut down. Shortly after, the airplane was observed taxiing towards the runway. 
According to witnesses located near the runway, the airplane taxied to the approach end of runway 30 and then started its takeoff roll. The airplane lifted off the runway about 1,000 ft from the departure end and pitched up hard into a nose-high attitude. Witnesses reported that the engine sounded weak and that there were no misfires or sputtering. The airplane continued down the runway at about 30 ft above ground level (agl). Surveillance video showed the airplane maintain a nose-high attitude about 30 ft agl as it overflew the remaining runway. A video, which captured the airplane further down the runway, showed it about 40 ft agl as it flew out of view in a nose-high attitude. 
The accident site was located in a washout at the top of sloping terrain, near impacted trees, about 1,000 ft northwest from the departure end of runway 30. The first identified point of contact was a large branch near the top of a 40 ft tree that had recently been topped to comply with FAA clearance regulations for the airport. Broken limbs and branches were spread out at the base of the impacted trees. The airplane came to rest upright in a washout near the impacted trees and was positioned on a magnetic heading of about 285°. The nose landing gear separated from the airplane and was found uphill in the washout near the impacted trees. The airplane was mostly consumed by postimpact fire. About an acre of surrounding terrain was burned by the fire.
The wreckage was relocated to a secured facility for further examination.

On September 5, 2026, about 2105 eastern daylight time, a Piper PA-28-181, N7653F, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Ludlow, Massachusetts. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
According to preliminary ADS-B data, at 2054, the airplane departed from runway 14 at Northampton Airport (7B2), Northampton, Massachusetts, en route to Plymouth Municipal Airport (PYM), Plymouth, Massachusetts. Once clear of the runway, the airplane made a climbing left turn to a ground track of 088°. At 2056, the airplane turned right to 158° while continuing to climb to an altitude of 5,000 ft mean sea level (msl). During that time, the airplane made a series of slow left and right turns but remained relatively on course. At 2102, the airplane turned to about 180° and started to climb. Preliminary air traffic control information indicated that the controller at the Yankee Terminal Radar Approach Control contacted the pilot to inquire about the sudden turn to which the pilot responded that he was “correcting.” The airplane then began a climbing left turn to about 5,400 ft msl and a ground track of 023°. At 2103, the airplane began a right turn and spiral descent from an altitude of about 5,600 ft msl. The descent rate in the turn reached a rate of 11,520 feet per minute (fpm). As the turn tightened, the descent rate decreased to between 4,000 and 7,000 fpm and the airplane reached a maximum ground speed of 186 knots. The final ADS-B data point was recorded at 2104 at an altitude of 900 ft msl with a groundspeed of 162 knots, a vertical descent rate of 3,968 fpm and a ground track of 005°. 
The airplane impacted a wetland area 1,063 ft from the last recorded ADS-B data point. The wreckage path was oriented on a heading of 166° and was confined to an area 50 ft long by 30 ft wide. The airplane was severely fragmented and there was no post impact fire.
The airplane wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.

On September 6, 2026, about 1353 eastern daylight time (EDT), 21 Air flight 7598, a Boeing 767-33A, N1997A, overran runway 30 after landing at Miami International Airport (MIA), Miami, Florida and subsequently impacted two ground passenger vehicles. The two crewmembers aboard the airplane sustained minor injuries. Five people on the ground sustained fatal injuries and three people on the ground sustained serious injuries. The airplane sustained substantial damage to include a postcrash fire on the right wing. Flight 7598 was a domestic cargo flight operating on behalf of Amazon.com Services LLC under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121 from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport (SJU), San Juan, Puerto Rico, to MIA.
In response to the accident, the NTSB traveled to MIA on September 7, 2026, to document the accident site and collect perishable evidence to support the investigation. As part of the investigative process, the NTSB invited qualified parties to participate in the investigation. These parties included the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), The Boeing Company, General Electric (GE) Aerospace, 21 Air, Miami-Dade Aviation Department (MDAD), National Air Traffic Controllers Association (NATCA), and 21 Air Pilots Association (TAPA). 
The parties were formed into specialized investigative groups led by NTSB group chairmen in the areas of Structures, Systems, Powerplants, Air Carrier Operations and Human Performance, Air Traffic Control (ATC), Airports and Survival Factors, Hazardous Materials, and Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR). NTSB specialists for Meteorology and Aircraft Performance were on site to collect information in their respective fields. A Flight Data Recorder (FDR) specialist at the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, DC conducted work on the FDR recovered from the accident airplane. NTSB Chairwoman Homendy was the Board Member on scene.
History of Flight
On the day of the accident, flight 7598 was the third flight for the accident airplane and the second flight for the accident flight crew. According to flight crew interviews, the captain and first officer (FO) reported for duty about 0530 EDT on the day of the accident. The accident flight crew flew the accident airplane from MIA to SJU as flight 7521, which departed MIA about 0635 EDT and landed in SJU about 0858 EDT. Flight 7521 was the first time the accident flight crew had flown together. For flight 7521, the FO was the pilot flying and the captain was the pilot monitoring.
Flight 7598 departed SJU about 1124 EDT and was scheduled to arrive into MIA about 1428 EDT. For flight 7598, the captain was the pilot flying and the FO was the pilot monitoring. Flight 7598 was cleared for landing on runway 30 from MIA airport traffic control tower (ATCT)/terminal radar approach control (TRACON) about 1349 EDT when the airplane was about 12 nautical miles from the runway 30 displaced threshold. According to Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) Out and FDR data, flight 7598 was about 105 ft above ground level (agl) at a groundspeed of 177 kts as it crossed the threshold of runway 30. 
The accident airplane touched down about 3,750 ft past the threshold at a groundspeed of 160 kts. The airplane continued down runway 30, crossed the departure end of the runway at 113 kts, impacted the localizer and the Medium Intensity Approach Lighting System with Runway Alignment Indicator Lights (MALSR) at the northwest end of the runway at about 100kts, and departed the paved surface and onto the grass (see figure 1). The distance between the end of the paved surface to the location the accident airplane came to rest was about 1,200 ft.
The last recorded groundspeed on the FDR was 65 kts, reached shortly after the accident airplane impacted an airport perimeter fence and traversed a public road (NW 67th Avenue). Prior to impacting the airport perimeter fence, the accident airplane impacted a Ford Econoline passenger van traveling on an airport perimeter road parallel to the perimeter fenceline (see figure 2). Of the seven occupants in the passenger van, five sustained fatal injuries and two sustained serious injuries. While traversing NW 67th avenue, the accident airplane impacted a Toyota Corolla Cross sport utility vehicle (SUV). The sole occupant in the SUV sustained serious injuries. 
The accident airplane impacted a chain link fence surrounding a parking lot and came to rest about 1,200 ft from the paved surface of runway 12/30. The captain egressed the airplane out of door 1L and the FO egressed out of the right cockpit window. About 1353 EDT, MIA ATCT/TRACON activated the alert phone in response to the accident. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue at MIA responded with 5 Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting (ARFF) units, with additional mutual aid resources dispatched following the initial response.

Figure 1. NTSB aerial imagery superimposed on a satellite view of the area of the runway excursion. 

Figure 2. The impacted Ford Econoline van (left) and Toyota Corolla Cross SUV (right).
Crew Experience
The captain held an airline transport pilot certificate with a type rating for the Boeing 767 that he received on May 18, 2026. The captain was hired by 21 Air in April 2026. He had accrued about 7,267 total hours of flight experience, as reported in his interview with NTSB investigators, of which 150 hours were in the accident airplane make and model. The captain also had about 2,700 hours of flight experience in the Boeing 737. On September 5, 2026, the captain flew two flights comprising an outbound from MIA to El Dorado International Airport (BOG), Bogotá, Colombia, and a return flight from BOG to MIA. According to the operator’s records, the return flight departed BOG about 0441 EDT and arrived about 0902 EDT. The captain was subsequently off duty until the morning of the accident.
The FO held an airline transport pilot certificate with a type rating for the Boeing 767 that he received on April 2, 2025. The FO was hired by 21 Air in February 2025. He had accrued about 2,800 total hours of flight experience, as reported in his interview with NTSB investigators, of which 800 hours were in the accident airplane make and model. The FO also had about 400 hours of flight experience on the McDonnell Douglas DC-9. On September 3, 2026, the FO flew two flights comprising an outbound from MIA to Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI), and a return flight from BWI to MIA. According to the operator’s records, the return flight departed BWI about 2209 EDT and arrived into MIA about 0033 EDT on September 4, 2026. The FO was subsequently off duty until the morning of the accident.
Airplane and Operator Information
The Boeing 767 is a two-engine widebody airplane that can be configured to carry passengers or cargo. The accident airplane was manufactured in June 1994 and was originally delivered as a passenger-carrying configuration. The airplane was subsequently converted to a freighter configuration in June 2016. The accident airplane was equipped with GE CF-6 engines. At the time of the accident, the airplane had accumulated a total time of about 110,077 flight hours and 24,505 flight cycles.
21 Air is a cargo airline with corporate headquarters in Greensboro, North Carolina, and operations based in Miami, Florida. At the time of the accident, the company operated 22 airplanes (including the accident airplane) composed of a mix of Boeing 757 and 767 airplanes.
Meteorology
An Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) is located at MIA. The main ASOS sensors are located near the approach end of runway 9, near taxiway S1, while additional ASOS sensors are located about 600 ft southeast of the accident site. At 1313 EDT, the MIA ASOS generated a Special Report (SPECI) that reported, in part, variable wind at 3 kts, visibility of 10 statute miles or greater, thunderstorms, scattered cumulonimbus clouds at 3,000 ft agl

On September 7, 2026, about 1015 eastern daylight time, a Mooney M20F airplane, N9546M, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Titusville, Florida.  The pilot was fatally injured.  The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
Airplane position data revealed that the flight departed from runway 36 (taxiway Charlie intersection) at the Space Coast Regional Airport (TIX), Titusville, Florida. About 1015:07, the airplane overflew the departure end of the runway. About that time, it entered a left turn and climbed to a maximum altitude of about 220 ft mean sea level (msl). The left turn continued until the final data point was recorded at 1015:27. The altitude associated with the final data point was 220 ft msl, and the airplane was oriented on a southwest heading at that time. 
Surveillance video footage from a camera located at the Executive Jet Center fixed base operator depicted the airplane as it departed. Initially, the airplane became airborne and began to climb. However, soon afterward, it entered a descent. As it neared the end of the runway, the airplane began to climb again and subsequently entered a left turn. The turn continued until the airplane ultimately descended behind an intervening tree line.  Shortly afterward, a plume of smoke was visible rising above the trees.
A witness positioned outside the museum on the east side of the airport reported observing the airplane. Initially, she thought that the pilot was descending to execute a touch-and-go but then the airplane started to climb. She noted “a lot of noise” from the airplane as it climbed; however, that noise stopped shortly afterward as it neared the end of the runway. The airplane then entered a left turn and, ultimately, impacted power lines.
The airplane struck a set of powerlines before coming to rest inverted on the westbound traffic lanes of Route 405/Columbia Blvd immediately north of the airport property. A post-impact fire ensued. The accident site was about 0.29 miles northwest from the departure end of runway 36.  

Figure 1 – Aerial view of accident site
The cockpit area, including the instrumentation and avionics, was consumed. The outboard section to the left wing was separated and located near the main wreckage consistent with the powerline impact. The aft fuselage was deformed and buckled that was consistent with impact forces. The empennage remained attached with exception of the upper 2-ft section of the rudder which was separated and located in the debris path.  The nose landing gear and left main landing gear were in the extended position. The right main landing gear was separated and located in the debris path.

Figure 2 – Airplane at accident site

On September 7, 2026, about 1337 central daylight time, an experimental STOL CH701 airplane, N101XV, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Neosho, Missouri. The pilot and passenger sustained fatal injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 personal flight.
According to a friend, the pilot had flown to the Neosho Hugh Robinson Airport (EOS), Neosho, Missouri, to assist him with some airplane maintenance. The maintenance consisted of temporarily removing and installing the accident airplane airspeed indicator into another airplane to allow for a ferry flight. After that ferry flight, the airspeed indicator was reinstalled and “tested” in the accident airplane. The pilot departed in the accident airplane with another friend about 1334. 
A witness reported that the airplane departed EOS with no issues observed during the takeoff or initial climb. After he observed the initial climb, he got back into his vehicle and did not observe any further portion of the flight. 
At 1335:39, a dash camera video recording, positioned about 0.80 nautical miles east of the airport, captured the airplane on the left crosswind for runway 19. The airplane tracked west to east before starting a left turn toward the northwest at about 1335:47. At 1335:50, the recording showed an unknown object departing and falling away from the airplane. The airplane continued the left turn and entered a nose down descent before disappearing behind a tree line. 
The accident site was located in an open field about 0.48 nautical miles east of the departure end of runway 19. Impact ground scars and debris were consistent with the airplane impacting terrain in a nearly vertical nose down attitude (see figure 1). 

	Figure 1. Accident site overview 
Postaccident examination revealed that the left inboard leading-edge PegaSTOL slat was separated and not found within the vicinity of the main wreckage. The PegaSTOL wing slat system is manufactured by Dédalius Aviation Inc. A couple of days after the accident, the leading-edge slat was found by law enforcement about 0.14 nautical miles southwest of the accident site (see figure 2). 

	Figure 2. Left inboard leading-edge slat. 
The airplane was retained for further examination.

On September 7, 2026, about 1720 Pacific daylight time, a Cessna 172N, N734ZK, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near San Diego, California. The flight instructor and student pilot were fatally injured. The airplane was being operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.
Preliminary ADS-B data showed the airplane departed Montgomery-Gibbs Executive Airport (MYF), San Diego, California about 1615. The airplane remained in the local airport traffic pattern for the duration of the accident flight, performing nine left-hand visual traffic patterns to runway 28L.
Airport and nearby business security cameras captured portions of the accident flight as the airplane approached the runway and as the pilots performed multiple go around maneuvers. Witnesses also observed the airplane and described the airplane as flying very erratically during multiple go-around maneuvers, pitching upward steeply after the go-around was initiated, flying very slow, and “stalling” before the airplane recovered. 
On the nineth approach the airplane can be seen in one of the videos flying low near the ground as it approached the runway, nosing over, pitching up and then nosing over a second time. The airplane then entered a steep nose high pitch attitude prior to the runway 28L threshold. The airplane appeared to attain about 45° pitch up attitude while about 100 to 200 ft above ground level.  The airplane entered a steep left descending turn and impacted runway 28L near the runway threshold. The airplane came to rest on taxiway B and a post impact fire ensued.
The wreckage was examined on scene. The fuselage, inboard wings, and cowling sustained heavy thermal damage. The inboard sections of both wing fuel tanks were partially consumed by fire. All primary flight controls were identified at the accident site. Flight control continuity was confirmed from the cockpit controls to each flight control surface. The engine was examined and the crankshaft was rotated in its normal direction of rotation.  Thumb compression was obtained on all four cylinders. Equal movement of all intake and exhaust rocker arms was observed on all cylinders. The aluminum fixed pitch 2-blade propeller remained attached to the crankshaft propeller flange. Blade “A” exhibited rearward bending and torsional twisting along its blade length with its tip missing. Blade “B” was mostly thermally consumed by the post impact fire. Two sections of propeller tip were found between the initial impact marks and the main wreckage. Each portion of blade tip found was twisted, fractured, and heavily scored. No anomalies were identified that would have precluded the normal production of engine power.

On September 7, 2026, about 1248 central daylight time, a Cessna 337C airplane, N2657S, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Brenham, Texas. The pilot sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 post-maintenance test flight.
According to the pilot, who is also a mechanic, he had recently purchased the push-pull configuration airplane on September 3, 2026. The airplane had been based for the last several years with the previous owner at the Brenham Municipal Airport (11R), Brenham, Texas. According to the aviation operations manager at 11R, he refueled the airplane prior to the flight. All four of the fuel tanks were topped off with 100 low lead fuel and he ensured the four fuel tank caps were all secured.
The pilot reported there were no issues noted during the runup sequence. The airplane taxied from the ramp to runway 16 for the local area flight. During the takeoff sequence, the pilot reported the rear engine sustained a total loss of power at the point of rotation. The pilot performed a forced landing on a ranching property, about 0.85 miles to the southeast of the departure end of runway 16. The airplane came to rest upright on a flat grass field, right next to a metal fence and barn.
The airplane sustained substantial damage to both wings, the fuselage, and the empennage. The airplane is pending recovery from the accident site to a secure location for future examination.
The airplane, which is known as a Super Skymaster, was built in 1968. The airplane was equipped with front and rear Continental Motors IO-360-C reciprocating engines and McCauley Propeller Systems D2AF34C59 (front) and McCauley Propeller Systems D2AF34C61 (rear) two-blade aluminum propellers.
According to the meteorological reporting station located at 11R, the calculated density altitude near the time of the accident was 2,571 ft.

On September 6, 2026, about 1800 Pacific daylight time, an experimental Pitts Model 12 airplane, N491X, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Lake Stevens, Washington. The pilot sustained serious injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
According to the pilot, after departing Frontier Air Park (WN53), Lake Stevens, Washington, he began practicing a series of aerobatic maneuvers in the vicinity of the airport. During a spin, the airplane experienced what the pilot described as a partial loss of engine power. After recovering from the spin, the pilot applied full power, but the engine did not respond. The pilot attempted to troubleshoot by activating the electric boost pump; however, the engine remained at idle power. The pilot stated that he determined he would not reach the runway and aimed for a treed area between two homes. The pilot further stated that, while attempting to extend the airplane's glide at low altitude, the airplane subsequently entered a right spin. The pilot reported that he regained control of the airplane, rolled the wings level, and flared before impacting terrain.
Multiple witnesses captured video of the accident sequence and the aerobatic maneuvers that preceded the accident. The videos show the accident airplane recover from a series of spins at a low altitude, make a right turn, and fly wings level for several seconds before entering another spin and descending below the tree line. The propeller can be seen rotating, and engine noise is audible throughout the recorded accident sequence.

Figure Accident airplane at accident site (NTSB Photo)
The airplane impacted a treed area between two homes and came to rest on its left side (see figure), which resulted in substantial damage to the wings and fuselage.
The wreckage was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.

On September 8, 2026, about 1100 central daylight time, a Boeing-Stearman A75L300 airplane, N680HW, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Bogue Chitto, Mississippi. The pilot sustained minor injuries and the passenger was uninjured. The airplane operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot reported that in cruise flight, the passenger reported that oil spray was coming in the cockpit and he could smell burning oil from the engine. The pilot saw that oil pressure had decreased and began to divert to the nearest airfield. When the oil pressure read zero, the pilot shut the engine down and performed a forced landing on a road. During the landing, the airplane’s lower right wing collided with a road sign, and the pilot subsequently lost control of the airplane.  The airplane then turned and veered through a fence and came to rest in a pasture. During the accident sequence, the fuselage and the upper and lower wings sustained substantial damage. 
A visual inspection of the engine by responding FAA inspectors did not locate an obvious source for the reported loss of oil. The airplane was retained for further examination.

On September 5, 2026, at 1422 eastern daylight time, a Bell 47G-4A, N797WS, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Alcoma, Florida. The pilot was not injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. 
The pilot reported that about 43 minutes after takeoff, he felt the helicopter momentarily yaw to the left twice. About 10 seconds later he heard a brief “metallic grinding noise,” which was followed by a loss of altitude, at which point the pilot performed a forced landing. The helicopter came to rest in trees resulting in substantial damage to the engine mounts, pitch change linkage, and tailboom. 
The helicopter was recovered and retained for further examination.

On September 7, 2026, about 1255 eastern daylight time, a Cirrus Design Corp SR22, N521LM, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Ashland, Ohio. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot stated that during landing at Ashland County Airport (3G4), Ashland, Ohio, the airplane’s right brake did not operate. The left brake operated normally, and the airplane began to veer to the left. He kept the airplane on the centerline of the runway utilizing rudder controls; however, when the airplane slowed down it departed the left side of the runway and contacted two runway lights, which resulted in substantial damage to the wing and firewall. 
Examination of the airplane by an FAA inspector revealed that the right brake disc was circumferentially fractured. 
The brake disc was retained for further examination.

PrelimNarrative:
On September 8, 2026, about 0044 mountain daylight time, N393JW, a Beech 200, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Roswell, New Mexico. The two pilots and two of the medical crew members were not injured, a third medical crew member received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 135 Air Medical flight. 
The airplane departed Albuquerque International Sunport (ABQ), Albuquerque, New Mexico, about 2350, on an instrument flight rules (IFR) flight plan to Roswell Air Center (ROW), Roswell, New Mexico.  
According to the pilots, the pilot flying was performing his initial operating experience (IOE) flight, the pilot observing was evaluating the IOE flight, and the flight had been uneventful. A stable approach to runway 17 was flown, and both pilots confirmed seeing 3 green landing gear down indicator lights. The pilots stated that the airplane crossed the runway threshold at 110 kts and the pilot flying began the airplane’s landing flare. The airplane touched down harder and sooner than he expected, and the airplane bounced. During the bounce, the airplane began to roll to the left, and the pilot observing announced, “my controls.” The pilot observing assumed control of the airplane, leveled the wings, and reestablished the airplane’s landing flare. During the second landing flare, the pilot observing (now flying) retracted the flaps “to settle the aircraft”, and thought the airplane was rolling on its landing gear. The airplane continued to sink toward the runway and the pilots subsequently heard the fuselage scraping the pavement. The pilot observing (now flying) secured the engines to assist with slowing the airplane, and it came to a stop about 1/3rd down the length of the runway. 
Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that both main landing gear were collapsed, and the lower fuselage sustained substantial damage. 
The wreckage was retained for further examination.

PrelimNarrative:
On September 10, 2026, about 1545 eastern daylight time, a Beech 99 airplane, N799CZ, and a Diamond DA20 airplane, N84VV were involved in a ground collision accident at the Willow Run Airport, Belleville, Michigan. N799CZ received minor damage and N84VV received substantial damage. There were no injuries to either the pilot of N799CZ, or the student pilot and flight instructor on-board N84VV. N799CZ was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 135 cargo flight, and N84VV was operated as a Title 14 CFR Part 91 instructional flight.
The pilot of N799CZ reported that after starting the airplane’s engines, he set the parking brake and then turned around to turn on the airplane’s oxygen bottle which was located behind his seat. While turned he noticed what he thought was a loose cargo strap but discovered that the strap was not loose. When he turned back around the airplane had moved and the propellers began striking the tail of the other airplane. He stopped and shut down the airplane.
Both the flight instructor and student pilot of N84VV reported that they had completed their preflight inspection of N84VV and had started the airplane’s engine and were stationary. As they were preparing to taxi, they felt the airplane getting struck by N799CZ. They noted that they did not see N799CZ from the cockpit before the collision. Following the collision, they shut down the airplane and deplaned.
N84VV received substantial damage to the left horizontal stabilizer, left elevator, vertical stabilizer, rudder, left wing flap and left wing aileron.

PrelimNarrative:
On September 7, 2026, about 1059 central daylight time, a Cessna 172N airplane, N734NM, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Panama City, Florida. The student pilot and flight instructor were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.
The flight instructor reported that this was his second flight of the day in the accident airplane, and that there were no abnormalities experienced during the first flight. Prior to the accident flight, a preflight inspection and engine run-up were completed with no indication of any abnormalities. A normal takeoff was accomplished with the airplane accelerating normally to rotation speed. During initial climb, about 300 ft above ground level, both pilots observed a loss of engine power, despite the throttle and mixture controls being in the full forward position. The flight instructor continued that there was no smoke, vibration, or “catastrophic engine noise” coincident with the loss of power. The flight instructor took control of the airplane and executed an emergency forced landing, straight ahead, onto airport property. During the forced landing, the airplane’s right wing struck a runway approach light which resulted in substantial damage.
The airplane was retained for further examination.

PrelimNarrative:
On August 10, 2026, about 1800eastern daylight time, a Piper PA-24-250, N6985P, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Union City, Ohio. The flight instructor and the private pilot were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14?Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.

The flight instructor reported that he was giving a flight review to the airplane owner because the owner’s flight review was expired. Prior to the initial departure, an engine run-up was performed and “everything was normal.” The flight departed from Portland Municipal Airport (PLD), Portland, Indiana with about 55 gallons of fuel on board (nearly full) and proceeded to Randolph County Airport (I22), Winchester, Indiana, where a full stop landing was performed. The engine was secured before being restarted a few minutes later for another flight. Another engine run-up was performed with no discrepancies reported. 

The flight departed from I22 with the fuel selector position to the right fuel tank and the pilot climbed to 3,500 ft mean sea level where he performed air work for about 45 minutes. The flight instructor then asked the owner to come out of slow flight and go back to cruise flight. After leveling out of the turn the flight instructor reported that the engine “had a complete failure [but] the propeller was wind milling.” The flight instructor directed the owner to establish best glide airspeed, turn on the fuel auxiliary boost pump, and change the fuel selector to the left tank, which he did. While maneuvering for a nearby field the flight instructor “cycled the engine primer 4 times to get fuel to the engine…” but that did not restore engine power. At that time the airplane was at 200 ft above ground level and the owner lowered the landing gear. The airplane came to rest upright in the field with the nose and left main landing gear extended and the right wing resting on the ground.

While the airplane was being recovered from the accident site, the left and right fuel tanks were drained, and contained about 12 gallons and 5 gallons of fuel, respectively. The recovery of the airplane was delayed due to the wet condition of the field. The airplane was retained for further examination.

PrelimNarrative:
On July 15, 2025, at about 1440 Pacific daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Murphy Moose SR3500 airplane, N80TM, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Quinault, Washington. The pilot received minor injuries, one passenger received serious injuries, and one passenger was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
According to the airplane’s records, it had originally been constructed in Canada with a Vedeneyev M14P radial engine. In November 2023, it was imported to the United States and was altered to accommodate the installation of a Pratt & Whitney Canada T-74 (PT6A-20) engine. The pilot subsequently purchased the airplane in September 2024.
The airplane was based at Olympia Regional Airport (OLM), Olympia, Washington. On the morning of the accident, the pilot did not note any anomalies with the airframe or engine during his preflight inspection. The pilot and passengers boarded the airplane, and flew to Sekiu Airport (11S), Sekiu, Washington. After having lunch in Sekiu, they departed for the return flight to OLM. (See Figure 1).

Figure 1: The airplane’s flight path and the location of the accident site, depicted in the yellow inset.
According to the pilot, about 20 minutes after departure from 11S, the engine sound changed, and the engine began to exhibit a “weird vibration.” Shortly thereafter, the Master Caution light on the instrument panel illuminated, and the engine experienced a total loss of power. When the pilot realized he would not be able to glide the airplane to a nearby lake, he extended the flaps slow the airplane in anticipation of the forced landing. The airplane subsequently impacted densely forested, mountainous terrain within Olympic National Park. (See Figure 2).

Figure 2: An aerial photograph of the accident site. (Courtesy of the US Navy).
The pilot reported he lost consciousness during the accident and did not regain consciousness until hours later. After removing the passengers from the airplane, the pilot manually activated the Emergency Locator Transmitter (ELT) and called 911. According to records provided by the National Park Service, the Olympic Park Dispatch was notified of the call at about 1840. The accident site was determined to be unreachable by foot, and at about 1915, a rescue helicopter from Naval Air Station Whidbey Island was dispatched to recover the airplane occupants. At about 2204, dispatch was notified that the airplane occupants had been hoisted into the rescue helicopter by long line.
The wreckage has been retained for further examination.

On July 16, 2025, at 1402 central standard time, a Beech K35, N5353E, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Sylacauga, Alabama. The private pilot sustained serious injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. 
According to the pilot, the airplane had a remanufactured engine installed about 30 hours prior to the accident. The remanufactured engine had experienced maintenance issues with the magnetos, spark plug fouling, and abnormal cylinder temperatures with the number four cylinder. Maintenance personnel replaced all of the spark plugs with new spark plugs and maintenance runups were conducted that showed no abnormal operation. 
After departing on the accident flight, about an hour into the flight, the pilot reported that the number one cylinder head temperature dropped below 300 degrees and was accompanied by a “high” exhaust gas temperature. The pilot contacted air traffic control and attempted to divert to Northeast Alabama Regional Airport (GAD), Gadsden, Alabama. The engine began to run rough and the pilot cycled the ignition switch with no change. The pilot declared an emergency, and he was given radar vectors to Merkel Field Sylacauga Municipal Airport (SCD), Sylacauga, Alabama. The airplane could not maintain altitude and he conducted a forced landing into wooded terrain about 1-mile west of SCD. The airplane came to rest inverted and both wings, the fuselage, and the empennage sustained substantial damage.
The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.

On July 17, 2025, about 1122 eastern daylight time, a Piper PA-46-310P, N460WW, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Sunset, South Carolina. The commercial pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 positioning flight.

The pilot stated that as part of his preflight inspection he added two quarts of oil to bring the engine to a total of 6.5 quarts. After departure during climb at full power the manifold pressure increased and decreased, which should have been between 35 and 36 inches of mercury (inHg). During that same time there was a corresponding exhaust gas temperature (EGT) variation. He leaned the fuel to air ratio which helped, but while over mountains he decided to continue away from them while monitoring the situation. While continuing to climb passing five or six thousand ft mean sea level (msl) the engine began vibrating with fluctuating power; the No. 2 cylinder EGT was rising and decreasing, with a corresponding engine vibration. The No. 2 cylinder head temperature (CHT) was about 100º cooler than normal, while turbo No.1 was 300 to 400° cooler; otherwise the engine gauges were in the green arc. He continued the climb then during cruise flight with the manifold pressure at 25 inHg, the No.2 cylinder EGT was reading very low 700 to 800º. Because he was above a cloud layer and unsure of the bases of the clouds due to a low instrument flight rules Airmet, he initiated a descent from 14,500 ft msl to 12,500 ft msl to not have to deal with hypoxia until he could find an area free of clouds.

After a few minutes he noted the oil pressure was at the yellow/bottom of the green arc and decided to maneuver towards Pickens County Airport (LQK), Pickens, South Carolina. The oil pressure light illuminated and with a cloud opening and the engine still developing power he reduced engine power, lowered the landing gear and after descending a few thousand ft the engine RPM increased to 3,000. He pulled the propeller control back and contacted Federal Aviation Administration air traffic control and requested to proceed direct to LQK. He then raised the landing gear and advised the controller of the situation. He slowly applied engine power, but the engine became extremely rough, and he heard a “pop” sound followed by oil spray on the windshield with smoke coming from the engine cowling. Unable to reach LQK, which was 9 to 10 nautical miles away from his present position, he decided to perform a forced landing on a golf course.

He turned back towards the golf course and applied full power but there was no change in engine rpm. He cleared trees then touched down on a golf course fairway landing up hill. After landing the main left gear separated and the nose landing gear collapsed allowing the propeller to contact the ground. After exiting the airplane he noted oil from the front of the engine cowling to the wind screen and along the length of the bottom fuselage.

Postaccident inspection of the accident site revealed that airplane came to rest about 315 ft from the initial touchdown point. A path of oil was noted exiting the right side of the nose cowling onto the windshield, and the Continental Aerospace Technologies TSIO-550-C (1) engine only had 3/4 quart of oil registering on the oil filler gauge and rod. Multiple holes were noted in the engine crankcase, the left magneto was separated, and a fractured connecting rod was observed.

The airplane was recovered and retained for further examination.

ProbableCause: The flight crew’s failure to use the airplane pre-landing checklist and failure to extend the airplane’s landing gear before landing.
AnalysisNarrative:
The flight instructor and the student were conducting a simulated single engine approach to landing when the accident occurred. During the landing approach, the flight instructor was monitoring other aircraft traffic in the area, and the student asked the instructor a question, which distracted the instructor from performing his normal prelanding checks and verifying that the airplane’s retractable landing gear was extended. As the approach continued, neither the student nor flight instructor noticed that the landing gear was not extended. The airplane landed with the landing gear in the retracted position. The airplane received substantial damage to the structural external longerons on the bottom of the fuselage.
As a result of the accident, the flight school implemented additional training for instructors and students regarding checklist usage and additional crew procedures have been implemented to verify landing gear extension prior to landing. Additionally, the review of the accident will be included in future safety meetings.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to establish and maintain the airstrip centerline during takeoff, which resulted in the airplane’s right wingtips contacting the corn that bordered the airstrip.
AnalysisNarrative: The pilot was departing from a 100-ft-wide grass airstrip in the tailwheel-equipped agricultural biplane. The pilot reported that during the takeoff run, as the tail of the airplane came up, the right wingtips contacted the corn that bordered the airstrip. The airplane subsequently veered further into the corn and spun around. The airplane’s wings, fuselage, and empennage were substantially damaged during the accident. The pilot reported that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation of the airplane.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to maintain pitch control during takeoff. Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s inexperience in the accident gyroplane.
AnalysisNarrative:
The pilot was performing a post inspection test flight of the gyroplane. Prior to the flight, the pilot noticed the control stick pressures were greater than he had experienced with other gyroplanes he had previously flown. The gyroplane’s owner and a mechanic explained the gyroplane’s trim system to the pilot who then adjusted the trim to a setting he assumed would be sufficient to maintain control when the gyroplane was airborne. 
During takeoff, the gyroplane pitched up and when the pilot attempted to arrest the motion, the backstick forces on the control stick were greater than expected. The pilot lost control of the gyroplane as it continued to pitch upwards, so he reduced the engine power. The gyroplane had pitched to about 60° nose high, rolled left, and impacted the ground resulting in substantial damage. 
The pilot had flown several models of gyroplanes but had no flight experience in the accident gyroplane. After the accident, the pilot further learned that the gyroplane’s trim had previously been modified with a heavier trim spring which made this gyroplane respond differently than other gyroplanes.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to maintain proper airspeed and altitude during the approach which resulted in a runway overshoot and subsequent landing in a lake. Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s delayed remedial action to abort the landing.
AnalysisNarrative:
During the approach to the turf runway, the pilot noticed the airplane was “high and a little fast” but she thought she could correct the altitude and the airspeed. The airplane “floated down” the runway and she realized the airplane would not be able to land in the remaining runway available, so she raised the flaps. The airplane flew over the remaining runway available, landed in a lake near the departure end of the runway, and nosed over.
The airplane sustained substantial damage to the right wing. The pilot reported there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airframe or the engine that would have precluded normal operation. The pilot further reported that the accident could have been prevented by advancing the throttle before raising the flaps and aborting the landing before flaring when she realized the airplane was too fast on the approach.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control while landing with a crosswind.
AnalysisNarrative: The pilot reported the accident occurred while landing following the Phase 1 test flight. During the landing roll, with the nosewheel still off the runway, the airplane suddenly pitched down and veered left. The pilot attempted to regain directional control with a right rudder pedal input, but the airplane continued to veer left and departed off the side of the runway into the grass where the nose landing gear collapsed and the right wing struck the ground. The fuselage and right wing sustained substantial damage during the runway excursion. The pilot stated that there were no mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. At the time of the accident, the pilot was landing the airplane on runway 27 with wind from 320° at 4 knots.
InvestigationClass: Class 4 - Basic report with no Prelim publish

ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to attain an appropriate touchdown point during landing, which resulted in a runway overrun and collision with a fence.
AnalysisNarrative: The pilot reported the purpose of the flight was to perform a quick check of all the airplane’s systems prior to conducting a long cross-country flight the following week. While returning to the pilot’s home airport, the pilot reported that he was too high and fast during his final approach. The pilot elected to continue with the landing and touched down on the runway approximately mid-field. The pilot reported that he was “travelling too fast to stop before the end of the runway,” despite the use of heavy braking. The airplane exited the end of the runway and impacted a fence that surrounded the airport perimeter, substantially damaging both of the airplane’s wings. The pilot reported there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation of the airplane.

PrelimNarrative:
On July 17, 2025, about 2358 mountain daylight time, a Piper PA-28-180, N7186W, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near West Yellowstone, Montana. The pilot and two pilot rated passengers were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. 
The pilot and two pilot rated passengers had planned to complete a series of flights together, while two of the three pilots were building night, cross country flight time. 
According to preliminary ADS-B data provided by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the airplane landed on runway 01 at Yellowstone Airport (WYS), West Yellowstone, Montana, at 2246, and departed from runway 19 at 2353. Once airborne, the airplane’s flightpath drifted left of the runway centerline, then remained on a parallel course to the runway’s extended centerline. About 3 miles southwest of WYS, the airplane initiated a left turn to the south. About 45 seconds later, the airplane turned left to a southeasterly heading. About 28 seconds later, a right turn was initiated and continued until the end of the flight track data. No altitude information was recorded within the ADS-B data. 
According to the pilot of another airplane that landed at WYS near the time of the accident, he was inbound on an instrument flight plan and had been cleared to fly the ILS approach to runway 01 at WYS. When he was about 10 miles from WYS, he transmitted on the WYS common traffic advisory frequency (CTAF), his position and intention to fly a straight in approach to runway 01. As he completed his radio transmission, he heard a transmission from what he felt was the pilot of the accident airplane, however, it did not offer a clear description of its position. The pilot of the approaching airplane transmitted a second time and asked for position clarification from the accident pilot, who subsequently responded, “…I’m trying to get to…(garbled).” The approaching airplane’s pilot then saw aircraft lights in the distance below his airplane that were moving toward the southeast.  The pilot of the approaching airplane transmitted a third time, “Are you on a left crosswind?” No further radio transmissions from the accident pilot were heard and the approaching airplane landed without further interaction with the accident pilot.
The approaching airplane’s pilot stated that at the time he flew the instrument approach into WYS, it was “very dark” and there was no landscape illumination from the moon or ground lights, other than the runway lights.
On July 18, 2025, at 1121, an Alert Notice (ALNOT) was issued following reports from family members, that the pilots could not be reached by phone, and confirmation from the airplane’s rental management company, that the airplane had not returned to its home airport. The wreckage was subsequently located by the Montana Department of Transportation Aeronautics Division, about 5.5 miles southeast of WYS, 410 ft west of the last ADS-B data point, at an elevation of about 7,580 ft msl. 
Examination of the accident site revealed that the airplane impacted wooded terrain near the top of a geographical plateau. The debris field was about 200 ft in length, from the first identified point of contact (FIPC), and was oriented on a magnetic heading of 266°. The main wreckage was located about 160 ft from the FIPC. A portion of the main wreckage came to rest in a nose low attitude, and a portion came to rest inverted. The inverted portion of the main wreckage was oriented on a magnetic heading of 299°. All major components of the airframe, flight controls, engine and propeller assembly were observed throughout the debris field.
The wreckage was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.

ProbableCause: The ground crews improper parking of N247BZ, which left its tail protruding into the taxiway, and the JA986A flight crew’s failure to maintain adequate clearance while taxiing.
AnalysisNarrative:
All Nippon Airways flight 9397, JA986A, a Boeing B787-10, collided with Breeze Airways flight 509, N247BZ, an Airbus Canada BD-500-1A11 (A220), while taxiing for takeoff at Charleston International Airport (CHS), Charleston, South Carolina. There were no crew injuries and two minor passenger injuries onboard N247BZ and no injuries to crew onboard JA986A. The left wingtip of NH9397 contacted the rudder of the N247BZ, resulting in substantial damage to both airplanes. 
Breeze Airways flight 509 was scheduled to operate from Harry Reid International Airport (LAS), Las Vegas, Nevada, to Norfolk International Airport (ORF), Norfolk, VA. Due to weather in the vicinity of ORF, the flight crew of flight 509 coordinated with the Breeze Airways dispatch team and a decision was made to divert to CHS. Dispatch coordinated with the ground service provider and CHS airport operations and was granted permission for flight 509 to park on the remain overnight (RON) ramp, spot R1, see figure 1.



 
Figure 1. Excerpt of Jeppesen 10-9 Airport Diagram Chart.
After landing, the N247BZ flight crew taxied to the RON ramp and was marshalled by ground personnel into spot R6. After shutting down the engines and starting the auxiliary power unit, the flight crew observed ground personnel approaching with air stairs and turned OFF the fasten seatbelt sign. The captain opened the cockpit door and used the public address (PA) system to inform the passengers of the plan to refuel. 
Upon returning to the cockpit, the ground personnel contacted the flight crew and stated they needed to reposition the aircraft to allow a Boeing aircraft to taxi behind them. At that time, the captain turned the seatbelt sign ON, coordinated with the flight attendants, and made a PA announcement for the passengers to return to their seats for aircraft movement. The captain kept the parking brake engaged while waiting for passengers to be seated and the ramp personnel connected the tug. At that time, the flight crew felt the aircraft suddenly and violently “jolt”. The captain queried the ground personnel and was informed that the wing of JA986A hit their tail.
JA986A was a ferry flight from CHS to Tokyo International Airport (HND), Tokyo, Japan, with a stop at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Los Angeles, California. The flight crew consisted of two captain qualified pilots; the pilot flying (PF) was seated in the left seat, and the pilot monitoring (PM) was seated in the right seat. The PF had operated out of CHS before, but at a different time of day. The PM had not flown out of CHS. 
The JA986A flight crew reported they received clearance to taxi to runway 15 via taxiway M. While taxiing on taxiway M, the flight crew observed good visibility but noted that it was dark and there was no taxiway centerline lighting guidance. The flight crew observed N247BZ parked ahead of them, facing West in the RON parking area (nose in), and the other airplanes were parked facing East (tail in). The flight crew assumed that the aircraft was parked for the night and was positioned in a “normal” parking spot, however as they taxied closer to the parked airplane, they thought it was “closer than normal”. 
The PF stated he was going to offset to the right, “just to be safe”. The PM indicated that he was attempting to monitor the right wing, by pressing his face against the windshield. While passing behind N247BZ, the flight crew felt a light vibration, similar to taxiing over an uneven surface. The JA986A flight crew stopped the airplane and requested airport personnel inspect their wing for potential damage, see figures 2 and 3.

Figure 2. Photograph of N247BZ (left) and JA986A (right) after the collision. (Source: Breeze Airways)

  
Figure 3.  The left photo shows the damage to the vertical stabilizer and rudder of N247BZ
The right photo shows the damage to the left wing on JA986A. (Source: Breeze Airways)
JA986A sustained damage to the left raked wing tip and removable tip assembly. The removable wing tip is not considered a primary structure however the upper and lower panels of the raked wing tip are, and this damage adversely affects the structural strength requiring a major repair or replacement. Therefore, this was considered substantial damage.
Charleston Regional Aviation Authority (CRAA) provided a RON ramp parking diagram, which indicated that all odd numbered parking spots were to be tail-in parking spots and R1 was designed to hold an A220 airplane. All even spots were to be nose-in parking spots and R6 was designated for smaller airplanes. The diagram also depicts a clearance line, indicating the boundary of the ramp area and taxiway M. Photographs provided by the CRAA depicted the nose gear of N247BZ on the lead-in line to spot R6 and main landing gear beyond the clearance line, see figures 4 and 5.

Figure 4. Excerpt of CHS RON parking diagram. (Source: CRAA)

Figure 5. N247BZ nose wheel positioned prior to the RON ramp spot R6 stop bar. (Source: CRAA)
A postaccident review was conducted between Breeze Airways, CRAA, and the ground service provider. According to Breeze Airways, the ground service provider manager elected to park N247BZ on R6 due to ramp spacing for ground service equipment and the fuel truck. Additionally, they had previously parked an A220 on R6 for “gas and go” situations and had no issues. Prior to arrival, ground personnel had not cleared the ramp area of equipment and stopped the airplane with the tail beyond the ramp clearance line. Furthermore, N247BZ flight crew were unfamiliar with the RON ramp and the appropriate orientation of airplanes. They stated that the Jeppesen charts did not indicate parking directions, only spot locations. Lastly, CHS airport operations did not have prior knowledge of Boeing aircraft movements, therefore they were unaware of the potential for traffic on taxiway M.
InvestigationClass: Class 4 - Basic report with no Prelim publish

ProbableCause: The pilot’s improper landing flare and subsequent failure to maintain directional control during the landing in a crosswind condition.
AnalysisNarrative: The pilot reported that he flared too high during the landing, possibly due to a runway width illusion. The airplane bounced on contact with the runway and then began to weathervane into the crosswind. The pilot stated he performed control inputs to minimize the ground loop but was unsuccessful and the right wing scraped the runway. Contact with the runway resulted in substantial damage to the right wing and aileron. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. At the time of the accident, the pilot was landing the airplane on runway 28L with wind from 200° at 8 knots.

PrelimNarrative:
On July 19, 2025, about 2050 central daylight time, a Kolb Firestar airplane, N55161, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Meadow Grove, Nebraska.  The pilot was fatally injured.  The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
A family member reported that the pilot departed his private airstrip about 1610.  Local authorities were notified of the accident about 2050 when a property owner noticed the airplane in his soybean field.  There were no witnesses, and the exact time of the accident is unknown.
The accident site was located in a soybean field about 0.3 mile south of the departure airstrip.  Initial ground impact was about 50 ft from the wreckage, and the impact path was oriented on a southwest heading.  The forward portion of the fuselage was crushed aft, and the cockpit area was compromised.  The left wing was separated at the root and retained by the wing strut.  The right wing remained attached to the fuselage at the root with the wing strut intact.  The tailboom was fractured about 2 ft aft of the fuselage consistent with impact forces.  It was retained by the elevator and rudder cables.  The empennage remained attached to the tail boom.  The upper portion of the vertical stabilizer and rudder were deformed consistent with the impact sequence.

Figure 1 – Accident Site
Aileron control continuity was continuous from the control stick to the wing roots, and from the wing roots to the ailerons. Aileron control rod end separations at the wing roots appeared consistent with overstress failures resulting from the impact.  The torque tube from the control stick to the aft fuselage was deformed consistent with the impact damage. Both ailerons remained attached to the wings at the hinges.  Control cable continuity from the control stick to the elevators and from the rudder pedals to the rudder horn was confirmed.
At the time of the on-scene examination, the engine was separated and rested adjacent to the fuselage.  The engine assembly appeared intact.  Both intake air filters and carburetors were separated. The left carburetor was located in the debris path.  The right carburetor was retained by the fuel inlet hose. Internal engine and gearbox continuity were confirmed via rotation of the crankshaft.  Two propeller blades remained attached to the hub and appeared intact.  One propeller blade was separated at the root and located in the debris path.  The separated blade was deformed and delaminated consistent with ground impact.
The engine ignition modules and engine monitor were retained for further evaluation.

On July 20, 2025, about 0800 eastern daylight time, a Piper PA-46-500TP Meridian airplane, N819MA, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident in Lititz, Pennsylvania. The pilot was the sole person on board and was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
Prior to the accident flight, the airplane was towed from its hangar by line service personnel and the fuel tanks topped off with 74 gallons of Jet A and Prist fuel additive, for a total of approximately 170 gallons. Shortly afterward, airport surveillance video showed the instrument-rated private pilot arriving at the airplane. He performed a brief preflight inspection of the airplane, then entered the airplane and closed the main cabin door.
The engine was started and preliminary air traffic control (ATC) data showed that the pilot called for his instrument flight rules (IFR) clearance from Lancaster Regional Airport (LNS), Lancaster Pennsylvania to State College Regional Airport (UNV), State College Pennsylvania. The readback of the clearance instructions to the clearance controller was correct and the pilot was cleared to taxi to the runway.
Upon arrival at the hold-short line for departure, the ATC recording indicated that the tower controller advised the pilot to hold short while they waited for his IFR release. Three minutes later, the release was received, and the pilot was cleared for takeoff with a left turn on course. There was no readback of this instruction, and the surveillance video showed the pilot enter the runway and start his takeoff roll.
Preliminary Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) data showed that the airplane reached rotation speed and lifted off. As the airplane cleared the departure end of the runway, having climbed to 650 ft mean sea level  at a ground speed of 136 knots, the airplane suddenly pitched down to a descent rate of -1600 feet per minute. Approximately 9 seconds later, the airplane impacted a corn field 1/4 mile from the end of the runway on an estimated heading of 070° and a descent angle of approximately 39°and the left wing slightly down. The estimated flight time from the moment the wheels left the runway to impact was approximately 20 seconds. Nineteen seconds after takeoff, the control tower attempted to establish communication with the pilot multiple times without result.
The airplane came to rest 164 ft beyond the point of impact. The airframe was compressed due to impact forces. The engine and propeller created an impact crater 11 ft long, 6 ft wide, and 20 inches deep. The leading edges of the wings left an impression mark in the soil at the base of angle-cut corn stalks 3-6 inches deep along the entire wingspan. The surrounding corn throughout the debris field from the point of impact forward to the end of the debris field showed evidence of fuel blight with a strong odor of jet fuel throughout the accident site.
All flight surfaces were accounted for at the accident site. The left wing, wing-flap, and left aileron were fragmented into multiple sections. The left wing separated from the fuselage at the wing root and was found laying on top of the engine. The right wing remained attached to the airframe. The leading edge was found 20 ft behind the main airplane wreckage. The tail section was intact with the left horizontal spar broken but still attached. The vertical stabilizer remained attached and upright with leading edge damage.
The propeller, propeller shaft and forward reduction gear box broke free of the engine. The propeller shaft separated from the propeller and was found in the corn several feet beyond the propeller. The propeller was found 60 ft forward and to the right of the impact crater. It exhibited rotational damage including the separation of one of the four blades with two of the blades fractured at their midpoint.  
The recorded weather at LNS, at 0753, included: wind from 200° at 3 knots, 5 miles visibility, broken clouds at 400 ft agl and 900 ft agl, mist, temperature 25° C, dew point 24° C, and an altimeter setting of 30.03 inches of mercury.
According to Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)  records, the pilot held a private pilot certificate with ratings for airplane single-engine land and instrument airplane. His most recent FAA third-class medical certificate was issued on September 19, 2024. He reported on that date that he had accrued approximately 2,350 total flight hours.
According to FAA and airplane maintenance records, the accident airplane was manufactured in 2015. The airplane's most recent annual inspection was completed on March 14, 2025. At the time of the inspection, the airplane had accrued approximately 1,336 total hours of operation.

The wreckage was retained for further examination.

ProbableCause: The failure of the left brake to release due to corrosion and pitting of the caliper piston and bore, which resulted in a runway excursion.
AnalysisNarrative:
The pilot reported that when the wheels touched down during landing the airplane pulled hard to the left and departed the runway despite his control inputs to correct the airplane’s direction of travel. The airplane nose landing gear collapsed during the runway excursion and the airplane came to rest inverted in the adjacent cornfield. The wings and empennage sustained substantial damage.
After the accident a bystander attempted to turn the left wheel of the airplane and told the pilot he could barely move it. Later when the pilot tried to move the left wheel it turned freely.
A post-accident examination of the airplane showed that the brake caliper pistons and piston bores for both main landing gear were corroded and pitted. It is likely the left brake caliper failed to release after being used during the landing due to the corroded brake components.
InvestigationClass: Class 4 - Basic report with no Prelim publish

ProbableCause: The failure of the pilot to set the flaps to the proper configuration for takeoff.
AnalysisNarrative: During takeoff roll, while rotating, the pilot noted that there was insufficient airspeed and responded by pushing the nose down. Subsequently, the nose gear impacted the runway and collapsed, and the airplane veered off the right side of the runway resulted in substantial damage to the fuselage. The pilot reported that the flaps were extended more than 10° takeoff setting, and that he did not check where they were set during the attempted takeoff.  Additionally, an airport video showed the airplane porpoising down the runway and the flaps were observed extended pass the typical takeoff setting. The pilot stated that there were no mechanical failures or malfunctions that would have precluded the normal operation of the airplane.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to maintain clearance from powerlines, which resulted in a wire strike.
AnalysisNarrative:
The pilot stated that he was flying over the river to examine a long gravel bar that he intended to land on. While looking for powerlines for the approach he had lost some altitude and was attempting to recover when a power line flew overhead and collided with the vertical stabilizer. The pilot attempted to regain control of the airplane, which then impacted terrain next to the riverbank. 
The airplane sustained substantial damage to both wings and fuselage. The pilot stated that there were no pre-impact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operations.

PrelimNarrative:
On July 17, 2025, about 1447 mountain standard time, a Cessna TR182, N182KC, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Tuba City, Arizona. The pilot and passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulation Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot reported that he departed with 62 gallons of fuel onboard and that he had verified the fuel quantity multiple times with a calibrated dipstick prior to departure. While enroute, and after switching to the right tank, which indicated about 31 gallons at the time, the engine began to run rough and sputter. He attempted to switch to BOTH fuel tanks, but the engine continued to sputter. The pilot activated the fuel boost pump, which displayed no fuel pressure at which time the engine lost all power. He executed a forced landing to the side of road to avoid vehicular traffic and with the landing gear stowed due to rough terrain. During landing the airplane belly contacted the ground, which substantially damaged the right wing and left elevator. Postaccident examination of the fuel tanks revealed that they were both empty; however, the pilot suspected a leak in the fuel delivery system. 
The airplane was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.

On July 17, 2025, about 1600 mountain daylight time, a Cessna 425, N425D, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Round Rock, Arizona. The pilot receiving instruction and the flight instructor were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.

The pilot under instruction and the flight instructor reported that they were about 1.5 hours into the flight from Centennial Airport (APA), Denver, Colorado to Phoenix Dear Valley (DVT), Phoenix, Arizona. They reported that during cruise flight at an altitude of about 26,000 ft msl, they heard a loud noise from the left engine, followed by an immediate and total loss of engine power. While troubleshooting the left engine, the right engine lost total power, as confirmed by the torque and engine temperature gauges. They declared an emergency with air traffic control and attempted to restart the right engine, but the primary flight display “flickered for a moment” followed by a total loss of electrical power. The pilot initiated a forced landing to an open desert area and during the landing sequence on a dry, rough surface, the main landing gear separated. The airplane came to rest upright, and the left wing sustained substantial damage. 

The airplane was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.

ProbableCause: The departing pilot’s failure to see and avoid the landing airplane during the takeoff, which resulted in a mid-air collision.
AnalysisNarrative:
The pilot of the Cirrus reported that he was conducting the RNAV GPS runway 31 approach in visual conditions. While crossing the threshold of the runway he saw what he thought was a wing and he heard a loud bang. The airplane nosed over and impacted the runway. 
The pilot of the RV-8 reported that he taxied to the beginning of the runway, near the fire base [CAL FIRE hangars]. The pilot looked for traffic and did not see any. The pilot applied power, rotated and the airplane began to climb. When the airplane was about 50 to 100 ft above ground level, he saw something from below and on the right side, then experienced “the inflight collision.” The pilot then reduced power and landed on the remaining runway. 
A video, from an airplane on a taxiway, captured the infight collision between the Cirrus and RV-8 airplanes. White flashing lights were in view near the runway that were consistent with runway end identifier lights (REIL) for runway 31. The Cirrus was descending to a point beyond the relocated threshold. The RV-8 was airborne prior to the relocated threshold and while climbing, struck the empennage of the Cirrus. The Cirrus rapidly descended to the runway, which substantially damaged the fuselage and empennage. The RV-8 landed on the runway. 
Both pilots reported no mechanical malfunctions or failures, with their respective airplanes, that would have precluded normal operations. 
According to 14 Code of Federal Regulations §91.113(g), “Landing. Aircraft, while on final approach to land or while landing, have the right-of-way over other aircraft in flight or operating on the surface…”

PrelimNarrative:
On July 20, 2025, about 1545 central daylight time, a Questair Venture airplane, N53TL, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident at Oshkosh, Wisconsin. The pilot and passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91. 
According to the pilot, he extended his landing gear over Fisk during the approach to the airport. The pilot confirmed that he had three green lights illuminated on his instrument panel and he continued the approach. During the landing flare to runway 9, the airplane touched down on both main landing gear. As the nose of the airplane came down, the propeller struck the runway; the airplane slid for several feet before it came to rest on its nose. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the engine mounts.
A postaccident assessment revealed that the nose landing gear was not extended at the time of landing. During the recovery, the pilot attempted to extend the nose landing gear; however, the nose landing gear would not extend. The circuit breaker for the nose landing gear motor was popped. The pilot reset the circuit breaker and attempted to extend the nose landing gear a second time. The nose landing gear extended and locked in place. The airplane was recovered to a secure hangar for further examination.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to avoid power lines during an aerial application flight.
AnalysisNarrative: The pilot reported that he was completing an aerial application flight in the helicopter. During a spray pass, he noticed a car on the nearby road, so he slowed the helicopter to avoid the applicant drifting onto the car. He then noticed power lines in front of him and attempted to fly underneath them but collided with the lower line. The pilot lost control of the helicopter which impacted in a field and came to rest on its left side. The helicopter sustained substantial damage to the fuselage and tail boom. The pilot added that he was not aware of the powerlines before the flight, even though he had sprayed this field many times before.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s mismanagement of the airplane’s available fuel supply, which resulted in fuel starvation and a subsequent total loss of engine power.
AnalysisNarrative: The pilot was on a multi-stop cross country flight, and after fueling the airplane, had departed for the next leg of the trip. While in cruise flight at an altitude of 11,500 ft msl, the pilot felt an engine vibration, and despite activating the alternate air, the vibration did not improve. He requested radar vectors from air traffic control to a nearby airport, and while descending through 3,500 ft, the engine lost power completely. The pilot then switched from the right to the left fuel tank, activated the fuel boost pump, and unsuccessfully attempted to restart the engine. He subsequently performed a forced landing to a field, during which the airplane’s horizontal stabilizer was substantially damaged. Following the accident, the pilot realized that the quantity of fuel available in the left tank was less than that tank’s unusable amount. With the right fuel tank selected, the engine was started and run with no anomalies noted. Based on this information, the loss of engine power that occurred during the accident flight was most likely the result of fuel starvation.

ProbableCause: The pilot’s failure to attain a positive climb rate due to airplane’s improper takeoff configuration.
AnalysisNarrative:
The pilot of the aerial application flight stated that he landed on a company grass strip and loaded the airplane with liquid fertilizer. He then departed to spray the fertilizer and returned to the airstrip about 30-40 minutes later. He loaded the airplane with the same quantity of fertilizer for a second flight. He said that during the second takeoff, he was turning the airplane and powering up the engine, when he hit the wing flap rocker switch to extend flaps. During the takeoff roll, which was to the east, the sun was in his eyes and when the airplane tail lifted off the ground, he saw that the airplane had veered a little to the left into an area of taller grass. He returned the airplane along the intended takeoff path down the runway, and toward the runway end, he rotated the airplane, but the airplane settled into a soybean field. The airplane impacted the field and sustained substantial damage to the left wing. The pilot was not wearing tinted glasses, and the helmet visor that he was wearing was also not tinted at the time of the accident takeoff.
The pilot stated that after the accident he observed that the wing flaps were retracted. The pilot stated there was no mechanical malfunction or failure of the airplane that would have precluded normal operation. The pilot believed that during the accident takeoff, the airplane settled into the soybean field because the airplane lost takeoff speed when it went into the area of taller grass on the runway.
